item.title: AppFollow
item.description:
Reviews can be tagged, translated, and routed to the right team. AI-assisted replies and review summaries help with high volume. Its keyword and competitor tracking supports store listing updates.

Subscription pricing depends on app count and features. It connects to tools like Slack and Jira so feedback reaches product teams.

AppTweak and Sensor Tower are alternatives. AppFollow suits app store optimizers and support teams that manage reviews.

item.title: AppTweak
item.description:
Marketers use it to find keyword ideas, check search volume estimates, and monitor changes in ratings and reviews. AI features suggest metadata and summarize review themes. It covers Apple App Store and Google Play.

Plans are subscription based. Results depend on store algorithms, which change.

AppFollow and Sensor Tower are alternatives. AppTweak suits app store optimizers and growth teams.

item.title: Atlan
item.description:
It connects to warehouses, BI tools, and pipelines, and builds a searchable catalog. Users tag assets, request access, and see downstream impact of changes. AI helps write descriptions.

It targets modern data stacks.

Collibra and Alation are alternatives. Atlan suits data governance managers on modern stacks.

item.title: Avid Media Composer
item.description:
Editors work with large bin structures, shared storage, and detailed timeline tools. Collaboration features let several editors work on one project. Newer versions add AI-based transcription and script search (PhraseFind and ScriptSync).

It is sold by subscription or as a perpetual license, and a free first version exists with limits. The interface has a longer learning curve than consumer editors.

Premiere Pro, DaVinci Resolve, and Final Cut Pro are alternatives. Media Composer suits film editors working on large productions.

item.title: CalTopo
item.description:
Users draw routes, add waypoints, and view layers such as slope angle shading and forecast data. Teams can share a live map during an operation. Maps print to scale, and the mobile app supports offline use.

A free tier covers basic planning, and paid tiers add advanced layers, printing, and team features. The interface is dense, and new users usually need a short tutorial.

Gaia GPS and AllTrails are alternatives with friendlier interfaces. CalTopo suits guides, avalanche professionals, and rescue teams.

item.title: Felt
item.description:
Users import GIS files and spreadsheets, draw on the map, and add comments. Maps share by link and embed in websites. AI features can help style layers and transform data from a plain-language request.

It is lighter than desktop GIS and lacks some advanced analysis. A free plan has limits.

QGIS and ArcGIS offer deeper analysis. Felt suits planners and cartographers who share maps with non-specialists.

item.title: Frontify
item.description:
Brand managers publish guidelines online and share approved assets. Templates let non-designers create on-brand materials. AI features help tag assets and search the library.

It is aimed at mid-size and larger companies, with custom pricing.

Brandfolder and Bynder are alternatives. Frontify suits brand managers who need consistency across teams.

item.title: GitHub Actions
item.description:
Workflows are YAML files that call reusable actions from a marketplace. Hosted runners run on Linux, Windows, and macOS, or teams can run their own. Secrets and environments control deployments.

Public repositories use it free, and private ones get a free allowance with paid usage after.

GitLab CI and CircleCI are alternatives. GitHub Actions suits DevOps engineers on GitHub.

item.title: IBM Maximo
item.description:
It stores maintenance history for equipment, creates work orders, and tracks inspections. Add-on modules apply AI to predict failures, read inspection images, and monitor condition. Aviation operators use its aviation edition for aircraft maintenance records and task cards.

It is a heavy enterprise system that needs configuration and training. Smaller operations may find lighter tools easier.

SAP, Fiix, and UpKeep cover similar maintenance work. Maximo suits large maintenance organizations.

item.title: Jellyfish
item.description:
Leaders see how engineering time splits between roadmap work, support, and tech debt, and track delivery. Resource planning and AI impact reports show effects of tools such as coding assistants.

It is an enterprise product with custom pricing.

LinearB and Swarmia are alternatives. Jellyfish suits engineering managers and executives.

item.title: LinearB
item.description:
Engineering managers see where work waits, such as in review, and set rules to route pull requests. AI features summarize changes and speed up code review.

Pricing is per developer, with a free tier for small teams. Metrics should be used to support teams, not to rank individuals.

Swarmia and Jellyfish are alternatives. LinearB suits engineering managers.

item.title: OpenSpace
item.description:
A worker walks the site wearing a camera, and the system builds a navigable record. AI maps images to drawings and tracks progress by area. Teams review conditions remotely and compare changes over time.

It is sold to contractors and owners with custom pricing.

StructionSite and Doxel are alternatives. OpenSpace suits construction managers.

item.title: Propared
item.description:
Stage managers build cue sheets, share call times, and send updates to crew. Calendars sync to phones. Documents and rider details stay with each event.

Free and paid plans exist.

Airtable and Notion are general alternatives. Propared suits stage managers and production teams.

item.title: Recorded Future
item.description:
Analysts look up indicators like domains and hashes, read risk scores, and see related campaigns. Alerts flag leaked credentials and brand abuse. An AI assistant answers questions about reports and threats.

It is an enterprise product, now part of Mastercard, with custom pricing.

Mandiant and CrowdStrike Falcon Intelligence are alternatives. Recorded Future suits threat intelligence analysts.

item.title: StudioBinder
item.description:
Producers build a schedule from a script breakdown and send call sheets to the crew. Shot lists and storyboards help directors plan coverage. A free plan covers basics, and paid plans add team features.

It suits small and mid-size productions more than large studios.

Movie Magic and Celtx are alternatives. StudioBinder suits filmmakers who run their own productions.

item.title: Swarmia
item.description:
Managers see cycle time, review speed, and where effort goes between features and maintenance. Teams set working agreements and get Slack nudges. Surveys capture developer experience.

It is a subscription product.

LinearB and Jellyfish are alternatives. Swarmia suits engineering managers who care about team health.

item.title: Tabletop Simulator
item.description:
Users import card images, boards, and custom pieces. Scripting with Lua adds rules and automation. Players join online, so designers can run tests with people in other cities.

It is a one-time purchase, and many community games are available through the Steam Workshop.

Tabletopia is an alternative. Tabletop Simulator suits board game designers who want remote playtests.

item.title: Tenable
item.description:
Scanners find missing patches, misconfigurations, and exposed services across servers, cloud accounts, and web apps. Risk scores combine severity with exploit activity and asset importance, and generative AI features summarize attack paths for analysts.

Nessus is widely used for individual scans, while Tenable One targets enterprise programs. Plans and pricing vary.

Qualys and Rapid7 are alternatives. Tenable suits cybersecurity analysts who run vulnerability programs.

item.title: 11x
item.description:
11x’s pitch is that AI can do the work of a sales development representative. Alice researches prospects, writes personalized outreach, sends messages across email and LinkedIn, and tries to book meetings. A voice agent, Julian, makes phone calls and follows up. The company presents them as digital workers that run around the clock.

Customers connect their CRM and define the audience and message guidelines, and the agents work through lead lists and hand interested prospects to human salespeople. The approach can raise the volume of outreach well beyond what a small team could do by hand, though response quality depends on targeting and data.

item.title: Adobe Captivate
item.description:
Captivate is a long-standing tool for instructional designers. They build courses from slides with interactive elements like quizzes, branching scenarios, drag and drop exercises, and video. A standout feature is software simulation, where the tool records on-screen steps in an application and turns them into demonstrations or practice exercises, which helps train employees on new systems.

Courses are responsive, so they work on desktops and mobile devices, and they publish in formats that learning management systems can track, including SCORM, xAPI, and HTML5. Assets from Adobe’s other tools can be reused. Recent versions add AI help, such as text to speech for narration and automatic generation of some content.

item.title: Amazon SageMaker
item.description: SageMaker started as a way to run machine learning on AWS without managing servers. Data scientists use notebooks to prepare data and write code, then train models on managed compute that scales up as needed. Once a model is trained, SageMaker can deploy it behind an endpoint, monitor its performance, and handle versioning, which turns a notebook experiment into a production service. It supports popular frameworks such as PyTorch and TensorFlow.

item.title: Animaze
item.description:
Animaze lets people appear as a character instead of themselves. It uses a webcam to track your face and, with some setups, your body and hands, then moves an avatar to match. The result is delivered through a virtual camera, so it shows up in OBS, Zoom, Teams, Discord, and other apps.

Users can pick from a library of avatars, import custom models, or create their own, and add props, backgrounds, and effects. Streamers and VTubers use it to build an on-screen persona, while others use it for presentations, teaching, or just privacy on calls. Support for expressions and triggers allows more lively performances.

item.title: Basecamp
item.description:
Basecamp takes a different approach from most project tools. Each project is a self-contained workspace with sections for to-dos, a message board for announcements and discussions, a shared schedule, documents and files, and a group chat called Campfire. Instead of dozens of views and customization options, it offers a fixed, simple structure that’s easy to learn, and encourages asynchronous communication over constant meetings.

The company that makes it, 37signals, is outspoken about its philosophy: calm, focused work and fewer meetings. Features like automatic check-ins replace status meetings, Hill Charts show progress visually, and notifications are designed to be quiet by default. Clients can be invited into projects, which makes it popular with agencies and small businesses.

item.title: Better Stack
item.description:
Better Stack started with uptime monitoring, checking websites and APIs and alerting the team when something fails. It has since added more of the operations toolkit. Telemetry covers logs and metrics, with fast search over large volumes, and incident management handles on-call schedules and escalation, with calls, texts, and chat alerts.

Public and private status pages let companies tell customers what is going on during an outage. The pieces work together: a failed check can open an incident, notify the person on call, and update the status page. The pitch is lower cost and less setup than assembling Datadog, PagerDuty, and Statuspage.

item.title: Claude Design
item.description: Claude Design lets you make visual material by talking to Claude. Instead of dragging shapes in an editor, you ask for what you need, such as a slide deck for a product update, a landing page mockup, or a clickable prototype, and Claude builds a first version. You refine it with follow-up messages, like asking for a calmer color palette, a different layout, or an extra section, and the design updates.

item.title: Codacy
item.description:
Codacy connects to repositories on GitHub, GitLab, and Bitbucket and analyzes code as it changes. It runs static analysis across many languages, checks for style problems, bugs, security issues, and complexity, and posts results as comments on pull requests. Teams can set quality gates that block merges when code does not meet agreed standards.

Dashboards show trends over time, including code coverage, duplication, and issue counts per repository, which helps engineering leads see whether quality is improving. Security features scan dependencies and secrets, and recent AI features suggest fixes and help review code produced by AI assistants. It integrates with CI systems and IDEs.

item.title: DaVinci Resolve
item.description: DaVinci Resolve started as a color grading system used on Hollywood films and grew into a complete post-production suite. It combines a video editor, the Color page for grading, Fusion for visual effects and motion graphics, Fairlight for audio mixing, and a delivery page for exporting. Because all of these are in one application, a project can move from edit to color to sound without being exported or relinked. It runs on Windows, macOS, and Linux.

item.title: Decagon
item.description:
Decagon builds AI agents for customer service. Companies connect it to their help center, policies, and internal systems, and the agent answers questions, looks up orders, processes refunds, and handles account changes. It aims to resolve the issue instead of only deflecting people to articles.

A key idea is that support teams control the agent without engineers. They write instructions in natural language, called Agent Operating Procedures, that define how to handle scenarios, which keeps the behavior consistent and reviewable. Testing and monitoring tools show how the agent performs, and analytics highlight why customers contact support.

item.title: Deepnote
item.description:
Deepnote reimagines the Jupyter notebook for teams. Several people can edit a notebook at once, comment on cells, and run code on managed cloud machines without setup. It connects to data sources such as Snowflake, BigQuery, and Postgres, and supports SQL blocks alongside Python, so analysts can mix queries and analysis.

Results are easy to share. Notebooks can be published as interactive apps or dashboards with inputs, charts can be built without code, and scheduled runs keep outputs fresh. Version history and permissions help with team workflows, and it works with common libraries and Jupyter files.

item.title: eMastered
item.description:
eMastered applies automatic mastering to a mixed track. A musician uploads the song, the service analyzes it, and an algorithm processes it for balance, loudness, and clarity so it sounds polished on streaming platforms. Users can adjust settings such as intensity, EQ, and reference tracks before downloading.

It is designed for independent artists and producers who cannot afford a mastering engineer for every release. The process takes minutes and costs less than hiring a professional, and a subscription can cover unlimited masters on some plans.

item.title: Excalidraw
item.description: Excalidraw has a distinct look: lines and shapes appear as if drawn by hand, which lowers the pressure to make diagrams perfect and encourages quick sketching. It runs in the browser without an account. You draw boxes, arrows, and text, drop in shapes from libraries, and share a link so others can edit with you in real time. It’s popular with developers for architecture sketches and with teachers and designers for brainstorming.

item.title: FullStory
item.description:
FullStory lets teams see how real people use their websites and apps. It captures sessions, which can be replayed like a video of the user’s screen, and detects signals such as rage clicks, dead clicks, and error clicks that suggest frustration. Searching across sessions helps teams find all users affected by a particular bug or those who abandoned a checkout step, instead of guessing from numbers alone.

Beyond replays, it offers analytics such as funnels, heatmaps, and journey maps, and tools for tying issues to revenue impact. AI features summarize sessions and surface patterns, so teams don’t have to watch hundreds of recordings, and help prioritize the problems that matter most. Privacy controls mask sensitive information, and integrations send findings to engineering and support tools like Jira and Slack.

item.title: GitLab Duo
item.description:
GitLab Duo integrates AI into the places where developers already work in GitLab. In the editor, it suggests code and generates tests, in merge requests it summarizes changes and helps with code review, and a chat assistant answers questions about code, issues, and GitLab itself. For DevSecOps, it can explain security vulnerabilities and propose fixes, and help find the root cause when a CI/CD pipeline fails.

The company has also introduced agent capabilities that can take on tasks across the software lifecycle, such as planning, coding, and review, with human oversight. Because it works within GitLab, it has access to context from repositories, issues, and pipelines, which general assistants lack. Self-managed customers can use it with their own deployment, and organizations control which models and features are available.

item.title: Google Document AI
item.description:
Document AI turns paper and PDF documents into structured data. Prebuilt processors read common document types: invoices with their line items, expense receipts, bank statements, government IDs, and forms. An OCR processor extracts text with layout information, and a layout parser prepares documents for use with language models by splitting them into meaningful chunks.

Customization is a strength. A custom extractor, based on Google’s Gemini models, can be set up with a few examples to pull specific fields from a company’s own documents, even if they vary in layout. A workbench lets teams train and evaluate processors, and a human-in-the-loop option sends uncertain results to reviewers. The output integrates with BigQuery, Cloud Storage, and workflow tools, which helps feed data to analytics and AI systems.

item.title: Google Stitch
item.description:
Stitch is designed to get from an idea to an interface quickly. You describe an app screen or a website, upload a sketch or screenshot, and Stitch generates a designed layout with components, colors, and text, which you can modify through further prompts or by editing directly. It can produce multiple variations, so you can explore directions before settling on one.

Output is meant to be practical. Designs can be pasted into Figma for further work by designers, or exported as front-end code, such as HTML and CSS, to give developers a starting point. The tool incorporates technology from Galileo AI, which Google acquired, and runs on Gemini models, with experimental features that improve over time.

item.title: Heap
item.description:
Heap approaches analytics with automatic capture. Once its snippet is on a site or app, it records user interactions without developers adding tracking code for each event. Product managers can then define what counts as a signup or a purchase later and look back at historical data, which avoids the gaps that come from forgetting to instrument something.

Analysis tools include funnels, retention, user paths, and session replay, and a feature that surfaces friction points and drop-offs. It supports building segments of users and comparing their behavior, and it can send data to a warehouse. Heap was acquired by Contentsquare, which combines its quantitative analytics with Contentsquare’s digital experience tools.

item.title: Invoke
item.description:
Invoke is built for people who want control over AI images. Beyond typing a prompt, the layered canvas lets users paint, mask, and inpaint specific areas, combine generated elements, and iterate on a composition like in an image editor. Control features guide pose, depth, and structure.

It works with Stable Diffusion and other open models, and users can add their own checkpoints and fine-tunes. The open-source release runs on a local machine with a capable GPU, which keeps images private, and the company provides a hosted version for teams with management features.

item.title: Kinexon
item.description:
Kinexon is a real-time location system. Small sensors worn by athletes or attached to a ball or a piece of equipment communicate with fixed anchors around a venue, and the system calculates positions many times per second. Teams use the data to measure distance, speed, accelerations, and tactical positioning.

In sports, coaches and sports scientists monitor workload to manage fatigue and reduce injury risk, and analysts study movement patterns. The company has been used in leagues for handball, basketball, hockey, football, and others. Broadcasters use the tracking data for graphics.

item.title: Klue
item.description:
Klue is a competitive enablement platform. Product marketing teams gather information on rivals from news, websites, reviews, and internal sales feedback, and organize it into battlecards with talking points, strengths, weaknesses, and objection handling. Sales reps access these cards in their CRM or Slack during deals.

AI helps keep the content fresh. It scans for changes, summarizes updates, and helps draft battlecard sections. Win/loss analysis tools collect feedback from deals and reveal patterns. Reports show which competitive content is used and how it relates to outcomes.

item.title: LangGraph
item.description:
LangGraph models an agent as a graph. Each node is a step, such as calling a model, running a tool, or checking a condition, and edges define the flow between steps, including loops and branches. A shared state object passes information along. This explicit structure gives developers control over what the agent does and when, which makes complex agents easier to reason about than a free-running loop.

Features aimed at production use set it apart. Checkpointing saves state so a run can pause and resume, or recover from failure. Human-in-the-loop steps let an agent wait for approval before taking an action, and time-travel debugging lets developers replay and edit earlier steps. It supports streaming of intermediate results, long-term memory, and multi-agent designs, in Python and JavaScript.

item.title: Lumen5
item.description:
Lumen5 is built for people who have words but no video. You paste in a link or text, and the tool breaks it into scenes, picks suggested footage and images from its library, and adds captions and music. You then edit the storyboard, swap clips, and adjust colors, fonts, and timing in a simple editor.

The service suits content marketing teams, publishers, and small businesses that want to turn articles into social clips quickly. Brand settings keep logos and colors consistent, and templates provide formats for different platforms and aspect ratios. AI can summarize text into short scene copy and suggest visuals.

item.title: Maltego
item.description:
Maltego is known for visual link analysis. An investigator starts with an entity such as a domain name, email address, or company, then runs transforms that pull related data from sources like DNS records, social media, breach databases, and corporate registries. The results appear as a graph that shows how things connect, which makes patterns easier to see than in a list.

The tool is widely used in cybersecurity and open-source intelligence work. Threat analysts trace infrastructure behind attacks, fraud teams look for networks of related accounts, and journalists and researchers map ownership and connections. A marketplace of data integrations extends what the graph can query, and collaboration features let teams share findings.

item.title: Meltano
item.description:
Meltano treats data integration like software development. A project defines extractors and loaders in a configuration file, and Meltano runs them to move data from sources into a warehouse. Because everything is code, pipelines live in Git, run in CI, and can be reviewed like other changes.

It builds on the Singer standard, which has hundreds of community connectors, and integrates with dbt for transformations and Airflow for orchestration. Teams can write custom connectors with a software development kit, which is handy for sources that commercial tools do not cover.

item.title: Microsoft 365 Copilot
item.description: Microsoft 365 Copilot is the business version of Microsoft’s AI, and its main advantage is context. It can see your files, emails, calendar, chats, and meetings through Microsoft Graph, within the permissions you already have. In Word it drafts and rewrites documents based on other files, in Outlook it summarizes long threads and drafts replies, and in Teams it recaps meetings, lists decisions, and answers questions about what was discussed. PowerPoint can build a deck from a document, and Excel can explain formulas and analyze data with plain-language prompts.

item.title: Microsoft Copilot Studio
item.description:
Copilot Studio lets organizations create their own AI agents without heavy coding. In a visual editor, makers describe an agent’s purpose, connect knowledge sources such as SharePoint sites and websites, add topics and actions, and test it in a chat window. The finished agent can be published to Teams, Microsoft 365 Copilot, websites, and messaging channels, and can answer questions, complete tasks, or hand off to people.

Its strength is connection to business systems. Hundreds of connectors reach tools like Salesforce, ServiceNow, SAP, and Dynamics 365, and agents can use Power Automate flows to run processes. Autonomous agents can respond to triggers such as a new email or record, not only a chat message, and the platform supports the Model Context Protocol to reach more tools. Administrators manage governance, data loss prevention, and access through Microsoft’s admin centers.

item.title: MongoDB Atlas
item.description:
MongoDB stores data as flexible JSON-like documents instead of rows and columns, which suits applications whose data shape changes often. Atlas runs it as a managed service: it handles provisioning, backups, scaling, and security, and works across the major clouds. Developers connect with drivers for most languages, and features like replication and sharding support high availability and large datasets. A free tier allows small projects and learning.

For AI, Atlas offers vector search alongside the regular database, so applications can store embeddings and run similarity queries without moving data to a separate vector database. This supports retrieval-augmented generation, recommendations, and semantic search. MongoDB has also acquired a company that builds embedding and reranking models, and integrates with common AI frameworks such as LangChain and LlamaIndex. Full-text search, time-series, and analytics features sit in the same platform.

item.title: MURAL
item.description:
MURAL gives distributed teams a shared canvas. Participants add sticky notes, diagrams, images, and text to a large board at the same time, and facilitators run sessions with tools such as timers, private mode for individual thinking, voting, and guided agendas. A big library of templates covers retros, roadmaps, design sprints, and strategy exercises.

AI assists with the messy part of workshops, which is making sense of dozens of notes. It can group sticky notes by theme, summarize a board, and generate ideas to get a session started. Integrations with Microsoft Teams, Zoom, Jira, and Slack connect boards to the tools where work gets done.

item.title: Optimizely
item.description:
Optimizely began as an A/B testing tool and grew into a suite for digital experiences. Teams use web experimentation to compare versions of pages, feature experimentation to test changes in apps behind feature flags, and personalization to show different content to different audiences. Statistical engines determine which variations win, and rollouts can be controlled to reduce risk.

The platform also includes content management and commerce. A CMS lets marketers create and manage web content, and commerce products support B2B and B2C stores, so a company can build, publish, test, and optimize in a single environment. AI features, under the Opal brand, help generate content, suggest experiment ideas, and run agents that automate steps in marketing workflows.

item.title: Pendo
item.description:
Pendo helps product teams understand and improve their software. After adding a snippet to an application, Pendo records usage automatically: which pages and features people use, where they drop off, and how behavior varies by customer or segment. Product managers use dashboards, funnels, and retention reports to decide what to build and what to fix.

The platform lets teams act on insights without waiting for developers. In-app guides, tooltips, announcements, and checklists guide users through features, surveys and NPS collect feedback, and a roadmap tool captures feature requests. Session replay shows what people did, and AI features summarize feedback, suggest improvements, and analyze conversations with AI features inside products, which is a growing need as software adds assistants.

item.title: Pigment
item.description:
Pigment is a modern take on planning software. Finance teams build models of their company, including headcount, revenue, and spend, in an environment that feels familiar to spreadsheet users but works with large data volumes and multiple dimensions. Plans link across departments, so a hiring plan updates the budget automatically.

It supports scenario planning, which lets teams test the impact of different assumptions side by side, and produces dashboards and reports for executives. AI agents help analyze variances, generate commentary, and build parts of models from prompts. Integrations bring in data from ERP and CRM systems and data warehouses.

item.title: Planhat
item.description:
Planhat is a customer platform built for subscription businesses. It connects to a company’s tools and data, builds a profile for each account, and shows health, usage trends, revenue, and conversations in one place. Teams use it to prepare for renewals and spot upsell opportunities.

Automation and workflows trigger tasks and outreach when something changes, such as a drop in usage or an upcoming renewal. Dashboards and reports show retention and growth, and AI summarizes accounts and suggests actions.

item.title: Questel
item.description:
Questel serves people who work with patents and trademarks. Its search tools let users query large databases of patents from many countries, apply classifications, and find prior art for patentability and infringement questions. Analytics show landscapes of who is filing in a field and trends over time.

The company also offers portfolio management, with docketing, renewals, and workflow tools for tracking deadlines across jurisdictions, along with services for filing and annuity payments. AI features assist with semantic search, summarization, and drafting, helping professionals review large numbers of documents faster. Its products come from combining several IP software companies.

item.title: Redis
item.description: Redis stores data in memory, which makes reading and writing it extremely fast. Developers use it as a cache that sits in front of a slower database, as a session store for logged-in users, as a message queue, and for leaderboards, rate limiting, and counters. Its data types, such as lists, sets, sorted sets, hashes, and streams, make these patterns easy to build with simple commands. It’s one of the most widely deployed pieces of infrastructure on the web.

item.title: Snorkel AI
item.description:
Snorkel started as an academic project that asked whether people could label data programmatically. Instead of tagging thousands of examples one by one, a domain expert writes labeling functions, which are rules, patterns, or model calls that vote on a label. Snorkel combines their noisy outputs into training labels, a technique called weak supervision.

The company has moved toward the needs of generative AI. Its platform helps enterprises curate data for fine-tuning and evaluating language models, with experts reviewing samples and defining what good answers look like. A network of expert annotators supplies specialized data in areas like law, medicine, and finance, and tools measure how models perform on custom benchmarks.

item.title: Storylane
item.description:
Storylane is an interactive demo platform. A user records their product with a browser extension that captures screenshots or the underlying page, then adds hotspots, tooltips, and callouts to guide viewers through a story. The result is a demo that prospects can click through on their own, without needing a sandbox or a live call.

Teams use it across the sales cycle. Marketing embeds demos on landing pages, sales sends personalized versions in outreach emails, and customer success uses them for onboarding. AI features add voiceovers, translations into other languages, and personalization of names and logos for each prospect. Analytics show who viewed a demo and where they dropped off.

item.title: Surge AI
item.description:
Surge AI supplies the human judgment that goes into modern language models. Labs need people to compare answers, write ideal responses, and grade quality, and these ratings train models through techniques like RLHF. Surge recruits and manages annotators with specialized skills, such as coding, writing, and expertise in science, law, or medicine.

Its pitch is quality over crowd volume. Careful screening, training, and quality checks aim to produce data that is more accurate than what general crowd platforms deliver. Services include building evaluation sets, adversarial testing to find model weaknesses, and custom datasets for specific tasks. The company works with large AI developers and publishes research on data quality.

item.title: Temporal
item.description:
Temporal addresses a hard part of building reliable software: making long-running, multi-step processes survive failures. Developers write workflows in an ordinary programming language such as Go, Java, Python, or TypeScript, and Temporal records each step and its state, so if a server crashes or a network call fails, the workflow continues from where it stopped without losing progress. Retries, timeouts, and timers are built in.

That makes it suitable for processes that take minutes to months, such as payment flows, order fulfillment, customer onboarding, infrastructure provisioning, and data processing. Increasingly, teams use it to orchestrate AI agents, where tasks call models and tools over long durations and need reliability and observability. Temporal Cloud provides a managed service, and the open-source server can be self-hosted.

item.title: Trello
item.description: Trello organizes work on a board. Lists represent stages like To Do, Doing, and Done, and each task is a card that you drag from list to list. Cards can hold descriptions, checklists, due dates, attachments, comments, and assigned members. The simplicity is the point: most people learn it in minutes, which makes it popular for small teams, personal projects, content calendars, and simple workflows like hiring or event planning.

item.title: Webex
item.description:
Webex is one of the older names in video conferencing, and Cisco has kept it competitive by adding hardware, calling, and collaboration tools. Companies use it for meetings, webinars, team messaging, a phone system, and conference room devices, with security and compliance controls that suit regulated industries and government.

The AI Assistant adds help across these pieces. It writes meeting summaries and action items, answers questions about what was discussed, catches up people who join late, and summarizes long message threads. Audio features remove background noise and can isolate a speaker’s voice in a loud room, and real-time translation and captions help international teams. Cisco also sells AI agents for contact centers.

item.title: Wrike
item.description:
Wrike is used by teams that coordinate lots of work. Projects can be viewed as lists, boards, Gantt charts, or calendars, and tasks carry dependencies, owners, due dates, and custom fields. Request forms and approvals let outside teams submit work in a structured way, which helps marketing, creative, and operations groups manage intake.

AI features reduce routine effort. Wrike’s tools can summarize long comment threads, create tasks from text, draft project descriptions, and predict which projects are at risk of missing deadlines. Dashboards show workloads and progress across portfolios, and integrations connect to Slack, Salesforce, Microsoft 365, and Adobe tools. Proofing helps creative teams review assets.

item.title: Conduyt
item.description:
Conduyt takes an approach to CRM pricing that departs from the per-seat model. A team pays a single price no matter how many people use the product, which suits small sales teams and agencies that would otherwise pay for every added user.

The basics are familiar: a contact database, deal pipelines, and activity tracking, with AI features that draft follow-up messages, summarize interactions, and reduce routine data entry. Positioned as AI-native, it aims to have the software do the admin work that salespeople dislike.

item.title: Aquant
item.description:
Aquant is a service intelligence platform. Equipment makers and service organizations hold years of repair history, manuals, and technician notes, which are hard to search in the moment. Aquant uses AI to learn from that data and recommend probable causes and fixes for a given symptom.

For a technician on a job, this works like an expert on call. They describe the problem or enter an error code, and the system suggests what to check, which parts are likely needed, and what has worked on similar cases. Service managers use the same data to see recurring failures and to reduce repeat visits and unnecessary parts.

item.title: AspenTech
item.description:
AspenTech sells engineering software to process industries. Chemical engineers use Aspen Plus and Aspen HYSYS to model how reactions, separations, and heat flows behave across a plant, which lets them design and test processes on screen before building them, and tune existing plants for efficiency, safety, and emissions.

The company also sells operations software. Optimization tools help plants decide how to run units to hit targets for cost and throughput, and asset performance products use machine learning on sensor data to predict equipment failures before they cause downtime. Digital twins of plant units connect design models to real operating data.

item.title: Bluebeam
item.description:
Bluebeam Revu is a PDF tool built for construction. Teams review plans on screen, add markups such as clouds, callouts, and stamps, and measure lengths, areas, and counts directly on drawings to prepare quantity takeoffs for estimates. Custom tool sets store commonly used markups.

Collaboration is a big part. Studio Sessions let many people mark up the same document at the same time, and Studio Projects store drawing sets in the cloud. Overlay and comparison features show what changed between revisions, with AI helping to line up sheets and highlight differences, which reduces missed updates.

item.title: ComplyAdvantage
item.description:
ComplyAdvantage provides financial crime tools for banks, fintechs, and other regulated firms. At onboarding, it checks whether a customer or company appears on sanctions lists, politically exposed person lists, or negative news, and continues to monitor them over time. Transaction monitoring flags unusual activity that may signal money laundering.

Its data comes from a large collection of sources that is structured and updated continuously, and machine learning ranks matches to cut down on false alarms that compliance staff would otherwise review by hand. Case management tools help analysts document decisions for regulators, and risk assessment features support a risk-based approach.

item.title: Duve
item.description:
Duve is a guest experience platform. Before arrival, guests receive a digital check-in flow, can upload documents, and see offers for upgrades and extras. During the stay, a messaging assistant answers questions about the property and the area, and requests are routed to staff when a person is needed.

The platform includes a digital guidebook, upsell tools that present add-ons at the right moment, and integration with property management systems. For hoteliers and vacation rental managers, this reduces repetitive messages and brings extra revenue per booking.

item.title: FiscalNote
item.description:
FiscalNote is a policy intelligence platform. Government relations and compliance teams set up alerts for topics they care about, and the system monitors legislation, regulatory dockets, and court cases in many jurisdictions, notifying them when something changes. This replaces manual tracking of dozens of websites.

AI summarizes long documents, estimates which bills are likely to move, and helps teams assess the impact on their organization. The platform also supports collaboration, so teams can share notes, assign tasks, and report to executives. Related products cover policy research and the news in a field.

item.title: FourKites
item.description:
FourKites is a supply chain visibility platform. It collects location and status data from carriers, telematics devices, and ocean and air sources, and shows shippers where each load is. Predictive estimates of arrival time account for traffic, weather, and dwell time at facilities, which are more accurate than static schedules.

Alerts warn teams of delays so they can reroute or notify customers. Yard and dock scheduling tools coordinate appointments, and analytics help identify problem carriers or lanes. AI agents handle tasks like checking on late shipments and communicating with carriers.

item.title: HiredScore
item.description:
HiredScore applies AI to the early stages of hiring. When applications arrive, it grades candidates against the requirements of the role, surfaces people who might be good fits, including past applicants and current employees, and helps recruiters focus on promising profiles first.

It integrates with applicant tracking systems and HR platforms, and Workday acquired the company to build AI into its talent products. Features include internal mobility recommendations, which help companies fill roles from within, and reporting to monitor process fairness and compliance.

item.title: Keela
item.description:
Keela helps small and mid-sized nonprofits manage supporters. It keeps donor records, gifts, and communication history, processes online donations, runs email campaigns, and supports events and volunteer tracking. The platform aims to be affordable and approachable for teams without a dedicated data staff.

AI features guide outreach. Engagement scoring highlights supporters likely to give again or increase gifts, timing suggestions prompt contact when it is most effective, and a writing assistant drafts appeals and thank-you notes. Reports show campaign results and giving trends.

item.title: Moveworks
item.description:
Moveworks brings an assistant to employee support. Workers ask for help in Slack, Teams, or a portal, and the system understands the request, finds the answer in company knowledge, or completes the action by connecting to IT and HR systems. Common examples are unlocking an account, requesting software, or finding a policy.

The company grew by focusing on large enterprises and on language understanding specific to workplace requests. It added generative AI and agent capabilities, with a platform for building custom agents and connecting to many business systems.

item.title: Muck Rack
item.description:
Muck Rack is a public relations platform. PR professionals search its database to find journalists who cover a topic, see what they have written recently, and build media lists. They send pitches and track responses, and the platform monitors news to show where their company or clients are mentioned.

Reporting tools measure coverage by reach and sentiment, and dashboards show how campaigns perform. AI features summarize articles, suggest journalists, and help draft pitches, saving time on research and writing. The company also publishes research about the relationship between journalists and PR.

item.title: NationBuilder
item.description:
NationBuilder is designed for people building a movement. A campaign or organization keeps records of supporters, volunteers, and donors in one database, runs a website, sends email and texts, organizes events, and takes donations. Having everything together helps small teams manage a large network.

Tools support organizing, such as lists, tags, and tasks for volunteers, and reporting on progress toward goals. AI features help draft messages and summarize supporter information. The platform is used by campaigns, community groups, and associations around the world.

item.title: Physna
item.description:
Physna is a geometric search engine. Instead of searching for a part by name, a user uploads a model and the system finds others with similar shapes, even if they were named differently or came from different CAD programs. This helps find existing parts to reuse and detect duplicates.

Manufacturers use it to cut costs from redundant parts, speed up quoting, and manage large catalogs. It also supports analysis such as comparing a design with a reference and checking for intellectual property overlap.

item.title: Productboard
item.description:
Productboard is a product management platform. Feedback from many sources flows into a central place, where it is linked to features and customers. Product managers see which problems come up most and who is asking, which grounds roadmap decisions in evidence.

AI helps process the volume of input. It groups similar requests, summarizes calls and tickets, and drafts specs and release notes. Prioritization frameworks score ideas against objectives, and roadmaps can be shared with stakeholders at different levels of detail.

item.title: Propeller Aero
item.description:
Propeller serves construction, mining, and quarry sites. A drone flies a site, often with ground control targets, and the images are processed into accurate maps and 3D models. Users measure stockpiles, cut and fill volumes, and compare the site with design plans.

Dashboards share progress with project teams, and tools track haul roads, compare surveys over time, and generate reports for clients. Its PPK-enabled hardware and workflow aim to improve accuracy and reduce the need for ground control points.

item.title: Quorum
item.description:
Quorum is a public affairs platform. Users track legislation and regulations, follow lawmakers, and keep a record of their outreach, all in one system. Alerts notify them when a bill moves or a hearing is scheduled, and a database of officials supports advocacy campaigns.

AI summarizes long bills, flags relevant provisions, and helps draft messages and reports. Constituent engagement tools let organizations mobilize supporters to contact officials. Teams use the data to plan strategy and measure impact.

item.title: Rayyan
item.description:
Rayyan streamlines a laborious step in evidence synthesis. Researchers import search results from databases, and multiple reviewers screen titles and abstracts, marking papers as included or excluded, often blind to each other’s decisions. The tool tracks conflicts and helps resolve them.

Machine learning ranks the unscreened papers by likelihood of relevance, so the likely includes surface earlier and screening can end sooner. Highlighting of keywords and filtering by terms speeds reading. Newer features use AI to assist with extraction and summaries.

item.title: Seequent
item.description:
Seequent software helps geologists understand what lies underground. Its flagship Leapfrog creates 3D models from drill holes, geophysics, and maps, so teams can see ore bodies and structures, plan drilling, and estimate resources. Other products handle geotechnical data, groundwater, and geophysical modeling.

Mining companies, geotechnical engineers, and environmental consultants use these models for decisions. Cloud tools allow collaboration and centralized data management, and newer features apply machine learning to modeling tasks.

item.title: Trinka
item.description:
Trinka is built for scholarly and professional documents. It reviews text for grammar, style, and consistency with academic conventions, and understands field-specific terms in areas like medicine, engineering, and law. Suggestions explain why a change is recommended.

Extra tools check for plagiarism and consistency, offer paraphrasing, and run publication readiness checks. Plugins work with Microsoft Word and browsers, and a web editor is available.

Trinka has a free tier and paid plans. Authors should follow journal policies on AI-assisted editing. Alternatives include Paperpal, Grammarly, Writefull, Wordvice AI, and QuillBot. Trinka suits researchers and students polishing manuscripts.

item.title: Yoodli
item.description:
Yoodli is an AI speech coach. A user records themselves or practices with an AI role-play partner, and the tool analyzes delivery: filler words, speaking rate, pauses, and word choice, and gives a report with suggestions and trends over time.

Role-play scenarios cover interviews, sales calls, and presentations, where an AI plays the other party and responds. Organizations use Yoodli for sales and leadership training, with private practice that removes the embarrassment of rehearsing in front of others.

item.title: QA Wolf
item.description:
QA Wolf offers testing as a service. Instead of a company writing and maintaining its own automated tests, QA Wolf’s team creates Playwright tests for the critical flows, runs them in parallel on every release, and fixes tests when the app changes. They report real bugs, and filter flaky failures.

AI generates and repairs tests, while engineers verify results. The aim is high coverage without the burden of test maintenance, which often overwhelms small teams. Tests are written in open frameworks, so customers own the code.

item.title: TypingMind
item.description:
TypingMind is a front end for AI models. A user supplies API keys, and gets a clean chat app with conversation folders, prompt libraries, and tools. Pay-per-use API pricing can be cheaper than several subscriptions, especially for light users.

Features include support for multiple models in one place, custom assistants, plugins, and knowledge uploads, and teams can share setups with controlled access. It is a paid product with a one-time or subscription license depending on the plan.

item.title: Ando
item.description:
Ando rethinks team chat for a workplace where software agents work next to people. In most chat tools, AI is an add-on bot. In Ando, agents have identities, inboxes, and permissions, and they can join channels, read ongoing conversations, and message teammates, just like human members.

The product has the familiar parts of a messaging platform, including channels, direct messages, group conversations, and calls. The difference is how agents are treated: a person can assign work to an agent in a thread, and the agent can respond, ask questions, and report back. Teams can bring agents built on different models.

item.title: Scholé
item.description:
Scholé rethinks workplace learning. Instead of asking employees to finish courses on the side, it delivers short, relevant learning moments tied to real tasks, adapting to what a person already knows and needs to do. Principles from learning science, such as practice and spaced repetition, shape the design.

Teams can use it to build skills in areas like communication, sales, or technical topics, with AI creating content and feedback. The idea is learning that fits into work and sticks.

item.title: Claude Docs
item.description:
Claude Docs brings document writing into the chat. Instead of copying an answer from a conversation into another app, you ask Claude to draft a report, memo, or plan, and it appears as a document you can edit beside the conversation. You can revise it by typing changes directly or by asking Claude to rework sections.

Documents are stored in the Artifacts tab, so they are easy to find later and update across sessions. When the draft is ready, it can be exported to common formats such as Word, PDF, Google Docs, or Markdown. The tool handles headings, lists, and tables, and it works with files and context shared in the conversation.

item.title: Claude Slides
item.description:
Claude Slides makes decks from a conversation. You describe the audience and the point of the presentation, share notes or source files, and Claude produces a set of slides with an outline, text, and layout. You can then ask for changes, such as a different order, a tighter message, or new visuals, and edit individual slides directly.

The finished deck can be presented from within Claude or exported to PowerPoint or PDF for use elsewhere. Because it lives in the same place as the conversation, you can pull information from uploaded documents and revise based on feedback without switching tools. It sits alongside Claude’s other creation features, including Docs.

item.title: MosMos
item.description:
MosMos is a dictation and meeting tool for Mac. A user speaks and text appears in the active app, formatted to fit the context: casual in a chat, structured in a document, code-friendly in an editor. A personal glossary learns names and technical terms, reducing repeated mistakes.

In meetings, MosMos can record and transcribe with labels for each speaker and produce notes and action items afterward. Combining dictation and meeting features in one app saves switching between tools.

item.title: MagiCrew
item.description:
MagiCrew packages agent capabilities in one open-source system. A general agent can plan and complete tasks with tools, a visual workflow editor lets users build repeatable processes, and messaging and collaboration features let teams work with agents in shared spaces.

Because it is open source, organizations can host it themselves and adapt it, which appeals to teams with privacy requirements or specific needs. It extends an existing open-source project, which gives it a base of users and code to build on.

item.title: GitNexus
item.description:
GitNexus gives coding agents a map of a codebase. It analyzes repositories and builds a graph in which nodes are symbols, files, functions, and services, and edges show how they relate, such as which function calls another. Agents query the graph over the Model Context Protocol to answer questions like what will break if this function changes.

The aim is more reliable context than searching text or embeddings, which can miss relationships. The graph can span multiple repositories, which helps in organizations with many services. It works with different agents and editors, and the vendor claims it lowers cost and errors.

item.title: Magic Hour
item.description:
Magic Hour brings several AI video tools together. A user can animate a still image, generate a clip from a prompt, convert a video into an anime or painted style, sync a character’s lips to audio, or swap faces. The tools run in the browser and export short videos for social media.

It is aimed at creators and marketers who want a variety of effects without learning several apps. A credit system covers the different features, and templates help with common formats such as memes and talking-head videos.

item.title: OpenCode
item.description:
OpenCode is a coding agent that works in a developer’s terminal. It reads a repository, plans changes, edits files, and runs commands, with a text interface for conversation. The same engine also runs behind a desktop app, editor extension, and web client.

Provider freedom is the main appeal. Users connect models from Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, and others, or open models run locally, and can switch between them. Configuration files add project rules, custom agents, and Model Context Protocol tools, and sessions can be shared.

item.title: QueryStory
item.description:
QueryStory approaches analytics with agents. A team connects its data sources and describes the business, such as its metrics and definitions, and then asks questions in natural language. The agents write queries, analyze results, and respond with explanations and visuals.

The point is to go beyond a static chart. When a number moves, a user can ask why, and the agent investigates by looking at breakdowns and related data. Business context helps the agent interpret questions the way an analyst on the team would.

item.title: Viktor
item.description:
Viktor lives where teams already talk. Instead of a separate app, a colleague mentions Viktor in a channel and asks for something, such as pulling numbers from a dashboard, building a report, or writing a script, and it replies in the thread. It watches how the team works and picks up context over time.

It connects to a very large number of business tools, so it can read from and act in systems like CRMs, analytics, and ad platforms, and it can produce artifacts such as documents and simple web apps. Skills can be added for specialized work.

item.title: Zetik
item.description:
Zetik is a personal research assistant. A user picks topics, and the system monitors many source types, ranks what matters, and delivers a concise brief, so they stay informed without scanning feeds. It aims to surface signal across places that are hard to follow manually.

This suits founders, investors, and researchers who track fast-moving fields. Summaries need to link back to sources, and personalization improves as the tool learns what the user finds relevant.

item.title: Ivo
item.description:
Ivo is an AI contract review tool built for in-house legal teams. A lawyer opens an incoming contract, and Ivo compares it with the team’s preferred positions, flags issues, and suggests redlines in the document, using the editor the lawyer already works in.

Beyond review, Ivo has added tools to manage the whole flow. Business users submit requests, contracts are routed to the right reviewers, negotiations are tracked, and approvals are collected. A repository holds executed agreements for analysis.

item.title: BrowserStack Test Companion
item.description:
Test Companion is an AI agent for quality assurance. Instead of a separate dashboard, it works in the developer’s editor, where it can generate test scripts from a description or from the code, run them on BrowserStack’s device and browser cloud, and investigate failures.

Maintenance is a major use. Tests break when interfaces change, and fixing them takes time. The agent can update selectors, adjust steps, and rerun, which reduces the upkeep that makes automated testing costly. It works with common frameworks and connects to BrowserStack’s testing infrastructure.

item.title: Algolia AI Search
item.description:
Algolia is a hosted search service known for speed. Developers send it their data, such as products, articles, or help center pages, and use its APIs and UI libraries to add search that responds as the user types, with typo tolerance, filters, and facets. Many e-commerce and media sites use it.

Its AI search layer extends that with newer methods. Hybrid search blends keyword matching with vector similarity so queries find results by meaning, and tools can personalize ranking from user behavior. Merchandisers can adjust relevance with business rules without code, and the platform supports retrieval for conversational and agent experiences, where an AI model answers using the retrieved content.

item.title: Braintrust
item.description:
Braintrust helps teams treat AI quality like software quality. Developers log each model call and agent step, then build datasets of test cases from real traffic. Scorers, including programmatic checks and language model judges, rate outputs, so a change to a prompt or model can be tested before it ships.

The product combines several pieces. A playground lets teams compare prompts and models side by side, experiments track results over time, and online monitoring scores production traffic and raises alerts. A gateway can route calls to different model providers, and collaboration features let engineers and non-engineers review outputs.

item.title: Cohere North
item.description:
North is Cohere’s platform for putting agents to work inside companies. Employees use a chat interface and can build agents without code for tasks in HR, finance, IT, and other areas, connecting them to the apps and documents they already use. Search across company data is powered by Cohere’s own retrieval technology.

Security and control are the main pitch. Organizations can deploy North in a private cloud, on premises, or in air-gapped settings, which appeals to banks, governments, and defense contractors with strict data rules. Cohere designs the models for enterprise use and works with customers on custom solutions.

item.title: Dataiku
item.description:
Dataiku aims to let analysts, data scientists, and engineers work in the same environment. Teams connect to data sources, clean and prepare data with visual recipes or code, build models, and deploy them as applications or services. The visual interface lowers the barrier for business users, while coders can use notebooks and libraries.

The platform has added tools for generative AI, including connecting to language models, building retrieval applications, and creating agents. Governance features track models and projects, assess risk, and document decisions, which large organizations need to meet internal and regulatory requirements.

item.title: Elastic AI Assistant
item.description:
Elastic AI Assistant is built into the Elastic stack, which many companies use for search, logs, and security monitoring. Users ask questions in plain language, such as what caused a spike in errors or what an alert means, and the assistant queries the data, explains findings, and suggests next steps.

For security teams, it helps triage alerts, write queries, and summarize incidents using the organization’s own data. For observability, it assists with investigating logs and metrics. Retrieval from indexed content grounds answers in real information, and administrators choose which language model provider to connect.

item.title: Figma Make
item.description:
Figma Make lets designers and product teams bring ideas to working form. A user describes an app, or starts from a Figma design, and the AI builds an interactive version using code. They can then edit it by chatting, adjusting on the canvas, or changing the code directly.

Because it connects to Figma, designs, components, and styles can serve as the starting point, which keeps results consistent with a design system. Teams use it to test ideas with realistic prototypes before involving engineering, and to share working demos with stakeholders. Backend features such as data storage let prototypes behave more like real apps.

item.title: FLUX
item.description: FLUX comes from Black Forest Labs, a company founded by researchers who previously worked on Stable Diffusion. Its models became popular because they produce sharp, detailed images that follow prompts closely, including difficult cases like readable text in a picture and complex scenes with several subjects. For many people, FLUX became the best open alternative to closed services such as Midjourney, because the weights for several versions can be downloaded and used locally.

item.title: GPT Image
item.description:
GPT Image brings image generation into the same model family that handles text. A user describes an image or uploads one to edit, and the model generates or modifies it, following detailed instructions and rendering readable text, which earlier image models struggled with. It can edit photos, change styles, and keep a subject consistent across images.

The model is available inside ChatGPT, where conversation lets users refine results step by step, and through the API for developers building apps. It replaced the DALL-E models in OpenAI’s lineup. Smaller and faster variants exist for cost-sensitive use.

item.title: Futurepedia
item.description:
Futurepedia is a directory of AI tools with a focus on helping people choose. Visitors browse by category or use case, filter by price, and read short descriptions and reviews. New listings are added regularly, so it can serve as a way to keep up with launches.

The site also publishes tutorials, courses, and a newsletter aimed at people who want to apply AI in their work. Like other directories, it relies on submissions and editorial choices, and some listings may be promoted.

item.title: Altern Newsletter
item.description:
The Altern Newsletter comes from Altern, a site that catalogs AI tools. Each issue gathers newly launched products and resources the team found that week, with a short description of what each does. It is organized so a reader can skim for tools relevant to their work.

A weekly cadence keeps it manageable for busy readers. The content leans toward product discovery, not deep analysis, so it works well alongside news-focused newsletters. Items come from the team’s directory and community submissions, which means selection reflects what makers share.

item.title: AICode
item.description:
AICode targets a problem many AI coding tools handle poorly: older systems with hundreds of files and years of accumulated decisions. Where an assistant that autocompletes in a single file struggles, a tool built for legacy code needs to understand how modules depend on each other and what a change will affect.

The pitch includes helping developers navigate unfamiliar code, explain what a function does and why, plan refactors, and write documentation or tests. Teams that inherit a system with little documentation can use that kind of help to get productive faster. Work on large code usually depends on good context retrieval and on careful human review of suggested changes.

item.title: Anomaly AI
item.description:
Anomaly AI is for people who work with data that is too big or messy for a normal spreadsheet. A user uploads Excel or CSV files or connects sources such as databases, warehouses, and Google Sheets, then asks questions in natural language. The tool answers with tables, charts, and written explanations.

The vendor emphasizes traceable answers, meaning the analysis is run as code against the data so results can be inspected and not just generated by a language model. It can merge files with database data in one analysis, find trends, and flag unusual values. A connector allows assistants like Claude to hand questions about your data to the service.

item.title: ZOOOP
item.description:
ZOOOP gathers generative tools on one canvas. A user creates images, video, and audio, arranges them as a project, and collaborates with teammates. AI agents can operate the canvas through an interface, which suits automated workflows.

Instead of a monthly subscription, it uses a consumption model, so people pay for what they generate. That can suit irregular use.

Independent information is limited. Check which models are available and the terms for commercial use. Alternatives include Krea, Freepik, Leonardo AI, Runway, and Flora. ZOOOP suits creators who want flexible pricing and a canvas workflow.

item.title: AIPRM
item.description:
AIPRM saves people from writing prompts from scratch. Its browser extension adds a prompt library to the ChatGPT interface, organized by topic such as SEO, sales, customer support, productivity, and writing. You pick a prompt template, fill in details like your topic or audience, and it sends a detailed, well-structured instruction to the AI. Users can also create, save, and share their own prompts.

The library grew from community contributions, which means quality varies, though ratings and usage counts help identify useful ones. Paid plans add private prompts, team sharing, and prompt management for organizations, plus integrations with other AI tools. It is popular with marketers and SEO professionals who run the same kinds of tasks repeatedly, such as keyword clustering or content briefs.

item.title: Alli AI
item.description:
Alli AI addresses a common obstacle in SEO: implementing recommended changes often requires developer time. Alli installs a snippet on a website, and then SEO teams can edit and push on-page elements, such as titles, meta descriptions, headings, schema markup, and internal links, directly from its dashboard to many pages at once. Changes can be tested and rolled back, and the platform tracks results.

AI features suggest optimizations. The tool analyzes pages and recommends improvements, can generate titles and descriptions in bulk, and automates tasks such as adding structured data. Agencies value it for managing many client sites through one interface, and enterprises use it to speed up large-scale optimization where release cycles are slow.

item.title: Amplemarket
item.description:
Amplemarket helps sales teams find and contact potential customers. It combines a database of B2B contacts and companies with search filters and intent signals, so reps can build lists of people who match their ideal customer and show signs of interest, such as hiring, funding, or website activity. Contact data is verified and enriched to reduce bounced emails and wrong numbers.

Outreach happens through multichannel sequences that mix email, phone calls, and social steps such as LinkedIn messages. A parallel dialer lets reps call through lists quickly. The AI layer researches each account and prospect, drafts personalized emails and call notes, and surfaces the best people to contact first. Duo Intelligence is Amplemarket’s approach of AI preparing the work while the rep reviews and sends, instead of fully automatic sending.

item.title: Anyscale
item.description: Anyscale was founded by the creators of Ray, a framework that makes it easier to spread Python code across many machines. Ray is widely used in AI for tasks such as distributed model training, large-scale data processing, reinforcement learning, and serving models, and it is the engine behind a number of big AI systems. Anyscale offers a managed platform that handles cluster setup, scaling, and monitoring, so teams do not have to operate the infrastructure themselves.

item.title: Arcade
item.description:
Arcade makes interactive demos simple to create. A person records their screen using a Chrome extension, and Arcade turns the clicks into a step-by-step walkthrough with highlights and captions. The result can be edited, branded, and shared as a link or embedded on a website or in an email.

Teams use demos for several purposes. Marketing places them on landing pages to show a product in action, sales sends them to prospects, and customer success uses them for onboarding and help content. AI features add voiceovers, generate captions, and personalize demos by changing names and details. Analytics show who watched and where they stopped.

item.title: Baseten
item.description:
Baseten runs models for companies that build AI products. A team packages a model, often with the Truss open-source tool, and deploys it as an endpoint that scales up and down with demand. The platform handles GPU provisioning, scaling, and monitoring, which are chores that distract from building the product.

It focuses on performance. Optimized inference engines, quick cold starts, and support for the latest GPUs help serve models with low latency and cost. Teams can deploy open models from a library, bring their own, or fine-tune, and use dedicated deployments for steady traffic. Options for running in a customer’s own cloud address security needs.

item.title: Bloomfire
item.description:
Bloomfire is a knowledge management platform. Employees add articles, files, videos, and Q&A to a central library, tag them, and find them later with search. The platform is meant to hold what a company knows so that people do not keep asking colleagues the same questions.

AI features make retrieval easier. Users ask questions in plain language and get answers drawn from the company’s own content with links to sources, and the system can suggest related material and flag content that needs updating. Analytics show what people search for and where gaps exist.

item.title: Cal.com
item.description:
Cal.com is an alternative to Calendly built around openness. Users connect their calendars, define when they are free, and share a link that lets others book a slot. Event types handle one-on-one meetings, group sessions, and team round-robin assignments, and bookings sync to video tools and calendars.

Because the code is open source, companies can self-host it and customize it, or embed scheduling inside their own products with APIs and components. Workflows send reminders and follow-ups, payments can be collected at booking, and routing forms direct prospects to the right person. AI assistants can handle scheduling conversations.

item.title: ChurnZero
item.description:
ChurnZero is built for customer success teams at software-as-a-service companies. It pulls in product usage data, support tickets, and CRM information to give each account a health score, so a team can see which customers are thriving and which are at risk of leaving before a renewal conversation turns bad.

Automation handles routine outreach. Playbooks trigger tasks and emails when a customer hits a milestone or goes quiet, in-app messages guide users inside the product, and dashboards track renewals, adoption, and revenue. AI features summarize accounts, draft messages, and suggest next actions, and a customer-facing portal can share progress with clients.

item.title: Cognism
item.description:
Cognism helps salespeople reach the right people. Its database covers companies and contacts across regions, with a reputation for strong coverage in Europe and for verified mobile numbers, which are valuable for cold calling. Users filter by role, industry, size, and technology, then export or sync contacts to their CRM.

Intent data adds timing. Signals show which accounts are researching topics related to a product, so teams can prioritize outreach. Compliance is a selling point: the company screens contacts against do-not-call lists and says it follows privacy rules like GDPR, which matters for outreach in Europe.

item.title: Cutout.Pro
item.description:
Cutout.Pro offers a set of web tools for common image tasks. Its background remover isolates a subject in a few seconds, and other features upscale resolution, colorize old photos, remove objects, retouch portraits, and generate passport-style photos. A bulk processing option helps stores prepare many product photos.

An API lets developers build these functions into their own products, and plugins connect with tools like Photoshop. Creators and sellers use it for listing photos, social content, and design assets, often at lower cost than hiring a retoucher.

item.title: Databricks
item.description:
Databricks started with Apache Spark and grew into a unified platform for data work. Companies store data in open formats in their cloud, then use Databricks for pipelines, SQL analytics, notebooks, and machine learning, with a governance layer called Unity Catalog that controls access and tracks lineage across it all.

AI has become central to the pitch. The platform supports training and fine-tuning models, serving them through endpoints, vector search for retrieval, and a framework for building agents grounded in enterprise data. The company acquired MosaicML to strengthen model training, and offers tools to monitor and evaluate AI systems. An assistant helps write code and queries.

item.title: DataStax
item.description:
DataStax grew up around Apache Cassandra, a database designed for large, always-on applications. Its Astra DB service runs Cassandra in the cloud without servers to manage, and adds vector search so developers can store embeddings and find similar items by meaning. That makes it a base for retrieval-augmented generation, recommendations, and chat features.

The company also supports the tools around AI development. Langflow is a visual builder for agent and retrieval workflows, and its data APIs let developers use document or table models. Pairing a scalable database with AI tools gives teams a path from prototype to large production workloads.

item.title: DeepInfra
item.description:
DeepInfra hosts open models and sells access by the token or by usage. A developer picks a model from its catalog, which includes chat models, embeddings, image generators, and speech tools, and calls it with an API compatible with OpenAI’s format. The company handles GPUs, scaling, and optimization.

The appeal is price and simplicity. Because open models are widely available, hosting providers compete on cost and speed, and DeepInfra positions itself at the low end. Developers can also deploy custom models or fine-tuned versions in some cases, and use dedicated GPUs for steady workloads.

item.title: Gainsight
item.description:
Gainsight was one of the first platforms for the customer success discipline. It pulls usage, support, survey, and billing data to produce a health score for every customer, so teams can see who needs attention before a renewal is at risk. Playbooks guide the steps a manager should take for each situation.

AI features predict churn, suggest next actions, summarize account history, and draft communications. Surveys, in-app engagement, and a community product complete the suite, and the company has expanded into customer education. Reports help leaders show the effect of customer success on retention.

item.title: Genmo
item.description:
Genmo works on video generation with an open approach. Mochi 1 is a large video model released with open weights, so researchers and developers can study it, run it on their own hardware, and fine-tune it. It was noted for strong motion and for following prompts well among open models at release.

The company also offers a hosted product where users generate clips from text prompts without managing hardware. Creators use it for experimentation, short clips, and concept work. Running the open model locally takes a powerful GPU and some technical skill.

item.title: Glassbox
item.description:
Glassbox captures user sessions on digital properties. Teams can replay a visit to see what a customer clicked, where they hesitated, and what errors they hit. Heatmaps summarize click and scroll behavior across many sessions, pointing to confusing pages or broken flows.

The platform adds analytics and detection. Journey analysis shows where users leave a funnel, and automatic detection flags frustration signals such as repeated clicks.
