It has features for regulated industries like banking, including data masking so that sensitive information is not stored. The company has expanded through acquisitions into areas like anomaly detection.

item.title: Hex
item.description:
Hex combines notebooks with business intelligence. Teams connect their data warehouse, write SQL and Python in a notebook, and turn the results into interactive apps that non-technical colleagues can use without code. Everything lives in one place with version history and comments.

AI is built into the workflow. Magic helps write and fix queries and code, and agents let business users ask questions of governed data in plain language. A semantic layer keeps definitions of metrics consistent, so answers match across reports. Scheduled runs keep outputs fresh.

item.title: Highspot
item.description:
Highspot helps sales organizations make sure reps find and use the right material. Marketing publishes decks, case studies, and playbooks in one library, reps search or get recommendations based on the deal stage and customer, and managers see which assets are used and which correlate with wins.

Training and coaching tools are part of the platform, including practice exercises, call reviews, and guided selling plays. AI features recommend content, summarize accounts, and generate tailored messages and presentations. Integrations with CRMs and communication tools bring this into reps’ daily workflow.

item.title: Hour One
item.description:
Hour One produces videos with AI avatars. A user chooses a virtual presenter, pastes a script, and the platform generates a video of the presenter speaking, with options for language, voice, and background. Custom avatars can be created from real people with their consent.

It is aimed at companies that need to make many videos, such as training modules and product updates, without arranging film shoots each time. Changing a script and regenerating the video is faster than reshooting, and translations extend the same video to new languages.

item.title: Instapage
item.description:
Instapage focuses on the page that visitors reach after clicking an ad. Marketers build pages in a drag-and-drop editor with templates, connect them to ad campaigns, and track conversion rates. Collaboration features let teams and clients comment directly on designs.

Optimization tools set it apart. A/B testing compares versions, heatmaps show where visitors engage, and personalization changes page content depending on the ad or audience that sent the visitor. AI helps write copy and suggests improvements.

item.title: Kaspr
item.description:
Kaspr is a contact data tool for outbound sales. While browsing a LinkedIn profile, a user clicks the Kaspr extension to reveal a professional email address and phone number, then saves the contact to a CRM or a list. It also supports bulk searches and enrichment of existing records.

The company emphasizes European data and compliance with privacy rules like GDPR, and offers ways for individuals to opt out of the database. Credits limit how many contact details a user can reveal each month, and integrations connect with CRMs and sales engagement tools.

item.title: Keyword Insights
item.description:
Keyword Insights helps turn a long keyword list into a content plan. A user uploads thousands of keywords or discovers them in the tool, and the platform clusters them based on how search results overlap, which indicates whether a group of terms should be targeted by one page or several.

It also determines search intent for each cluster, suggests content types, and produces briefs that outline what a page should cover based on top results. Rank tracking and content tools support the workflow after publishing, and AI assists with drafting.

item.title: Kommunicate
item.description:
Kommunicate combines a chatbot builder with a shared inbox for agents. Businesses add a chat widget to their site or app, train a bot on help articles and FAQs, and let it answer routine questions, handing the conversation to a person when the bot cannot help or the customer asks.

The platform supports generative AI models and connects to knowledge bases, so answers draw on company content. Multi-channel support extends to messaging apps, and analytics show deflection rates and satisfaction. Integrations with CRMs and helpdesks keep data in sync.

item.title: Landbot
item.description:
Landbot lets non-developers design conversations visually. A user drags blocks onto a canvas to ask questions, branch based on answers, and connect to other tools, then publishes the flow on a website, a landing page, or WhatsApp. The conversational format often gets more responses than a plain form.

AI features add the ability to answer free-text questions from a knowledge base and to build flows from a description. Integrations send leads to CRMs and spreadsheets, and handoff routes complex chats to human agents. Templates cover lead generation, support, and onboarding.

item.title: Laxis
item.description:
Laxis joins online meetings, records and transcribes them, and produces summaries with action items and key points. Sales teams use it to log call notes in the CRM automatically, and researchers and recruiters use it for interviews. Search across past meetings helps find specific topics.

Extra features include templates for different meeting types, follow-up email drafts, and analytics on conversations. Integrations connect with Zoom, Google Meet, Microsoft Teams, and CRMs such as Salesforce and HubSpot.

item.title: Let's Enhance
item.description:
Let’s Enhance takes a small or low-quality image and makes it larger. The AI adds plausible detail as it increases resolution, so a photo can be printed bigger or used on a high-resolution display with less blur. It also reduces noise and compression artifacts and improves color and lighting.

E-commerce sellers use it to improve product photos, designers to rescue old assets, and photographers to prepare prints. Batch processing and an API handle large volumes, and extra tools cover background removal and image generation.

item.title: Lindy
item.description:
Lindy lets people create agents without code. A user describes a task or chooses a template, connects apps like Gmail, Slack, and a CRM, and defines triggers and steps. The Lindy then runs on its own: sorting an inbox, drafting replies, booking meetings, or updating records.

Workflows can include several steps with conditions, and Lindies can hand tasks to each other or ask a human for approval. A phone agent product handles calls, and a large catalog of integrations connects to business tools.

item.title: memoQ
item.description:
memoQ helps translators work faster and stay consistent. As a translator works through a document, the tool shows matches from a translation memory of earlier work and terms from a glossary, so repeated phrases are translated the same way. Machine translation can provide suggestions that the translator edits.

For teams, memoQ’s server and cloud products manage projects, assign work to translators and reviewers, and track deadlines and costs. It supports many file formats and quality checks, and integrates with machine translation engines and AI services, including large language models for suggestions and review.

item.title: MotherDuck
item.description:
MotherDuck takes the DuckDB analytical database, which runs on a laptop, and adds a cloud service. A user connects from their local DuckDB, queries data in the cloud, and combines it with local files, in what the company calls hybrid execution, using each machine for what it does best.

It targets teams that do not need a large data warehouse. Features include shared databases, collaboration, integrations with common data tools, and an AI assistant that helps write SQL. The pitch is simple, fast analytics at lower cost for data in the gigabytes to terabytes range.

item.title: Movio
item.description:
Movio is an avatar video generator. A user selects a digital presenter, pastes or writes a script, chooses a voice and language, and the platform renders a video of the avatar speaking. Backgrounds, text, and images can be added in an editor that works like a slide deck.

The pitch is speed and cost. Filming a presenter needs scheduling, equipment, and editing, while an avatar video can be revised by changing the script and regenerating. Translation into other languages makes the same video usable in several markets, and templates cover common formats.

item.title: Navattic
item.description:
Navattic helps companies show software without a live demo. A marketer captures a product’s screens or pages, adds callouts and steps, and publishes a tour that visitors can click through. Gated or ungated, these demos let prospects see the product before talking to sales.

Analytics show who viewed a demo and how far they went, giving sales a signal about interest. Personalization lets teams tailor tours by account, and integrations send engagement data to CRMs and marketing tools. AI helps create and edit demos and write copy.

item.title: Neon
item.description:
Neon rebuilt Postgres for the cloud by separating storage from compute. That design lets a database scale up under load and scale down to zero when idle, so you pay for use instead of keeping a server running. Developers get standard Postgres, which means existing tools, drivers, and extensions work, including pgvector for storing embeddings in AI applications.

The standout feature is branching. Because storage is copy-on-write, you can create a full copy of a database in seconds, like a Git branch, for testing a migration, running a preview environment for each pull request, or giving each developer an isolated copy. The same ability makes Neon attractive to AI coding agents and platforms that spin up many short-lived databases. Connection pooling, read replicas, and integrations with Vercel and other platforms are available.

item.title: Phrasee
item.description:
Phrasee focuses on the words in marketing messages. A team sets up a brand voice, and the platform generates many variations of subject lines, push text, or ads, predicts which will perform best, and tests them against audiences. Results feed back to improve future suggestions.

The company has become part of Jacquard Group, which combines it with other brand messaging tools. Large retailers, financial institutions, and travel brands used it to squeeze more from large campaigns, where small improvements in open rate add up.

item.title: Planable
item.description:
Planable is built around approval workflows. Marketers create posts in a view that looks like the final social post, share it with teammates or clients, collect comments and approvals, and schedule it once signed off. This replaces long email chains and screenshots.

Features include a content calendar, multiple approval stages, and support for many networks. AI tools help draft captions and ideas. Agencies find it useful for client work where sign-off is required.

item.title: Prome AI
item.description:
Prome AI helps designers see concepts early. A user uploads a sketch, a screenshot of a 3D model, or a reference photo and writes a prompt, and the tool produces a realistic rendering with chosen materials, lighting, and style. This speeds up exploration before detailed modeling.

Architects use it for building massing and facades, interior designers for room concepts, and product designers for form studies. Variations can be generated quickly to compare options with clients.

item.title: Promptfoo
item.description:
Promptfoo helps developers test AI systems systematically. A user defines test cases and criteria in a configuration file, runs prompts across models, and compares outputs side by side, with assertions that check for expected content, format, or safety. It runs from the command line and in CI pipelines.

Red-teaming features generate adversarial inputs to probe for jailbreaks, prompt injection, data leaks, and other vulnerabilities, and report where an application fails. It supports many providers and local models and has been widely adopted.

item.title: Ragas
item.description:
Ragas helps teams measure how well a RAG system works. A developer feeds in questions, retrieved passages, and generated answers, and Ragas uses language models to score aspects like whether the answer is supported by the context, whether it addresses the question, and whether the retrieved context was relevant.

Because it does not require hand-labeled answers for every case, teams can evaluate quickly, and it can generate synthetic test sets from documents. It integrates with frameworks such as LangChain and LlamaIndex and with observability tools.

item.title: Render
item.description:
Render simplifies hosting. A developer connects a repository, and Render builds and runs the app, handles TLS certificates, and scales as needed. It supports web services, static sites, cron jobs, private services, and managed Postgres and Redis.

Preview environments build each pull request automatically, and infrastructure can be defined in a file. Teams like its predictable pricing and straightforward interface, and it works for AI apps that need background workers and databases.

item.title: Rewatch
item.description:
Rewatch is built on the idea that useful knowledge is trapped in recordings no one rewatches. It captures meetings and async videos, transcribes them, and organizes them into channels and playlists, so employees can find the moment they need by searching words said.

Features include summaries, chapters, comments on moments in the video, and integrations with Zoom, Slack, and calendars. The goal is to let people catch up on meetings quickly and reduce the number of live sessions.

item.title: Seamless AI
item.description:
Seamless.AI helps salespeople find who to contact. Users search by title, industry, and location, or use a browser extension to look up contacts on websites, and the platform returns emails and phone numbers pulled from public sources and its database. Lists export to CRMs and engagement tools.

Real-time search and enrichment aim to keep data fresh, and intent signals show which accounts may be in a buying cycle. AI features help write outreach and prioritize accounts.

item.title: Seismic
item.description:
Seismic organizes marketing and sales content so reps can find and use it. Instead of searching shared drives, a seller gets recommended decks, case studies, and playbooks based on the deal stage and customer, and can assemble personalized presentations quickly.

Analytics show which content gets used and which correlates with wins, and engagement data tells sellers how buyers interact with shared materials. Coaching and training modules, and AI that writes tailored messages and summaries, add to the suite.

item.title: Showpad
item.description:
Showpad helps sellers find and use approved content. Marketing publishes decks, videos, and guides, and reps get recommendations based on the customer and deal stage. Buyers receive shared links that track engagement, which tells sellers what resonated.

Coaching and training are the other half. Reps practice pitches and receive AI feedback, learning paths build skills, and managers see progress. The platform integrates with CRMs and works well in industries such as manufacturing, healthcare, and technology.

item.title: Smartling
item.description:
Smartling connects content systems to translators. Websites, apps, and documents flow in through integrations, and Smartling applies translation memory and machine translation, then routes text to human linguists where quality matters most. Translations return to the source system.

Features include visual context for translators, glossaries, quality scoring, and AI that translates and edits at scale. The company has pushed AI-first workflows to reduce cost and time, and reports on translation quality and spend.

item.title: Snowflake
item.description:
Snowflake pioneered the cloud data warehouse built on this separation. Companies load data, run SQL queries with elastic compute, and share datasets securely with partners. It runs on the major clouds, and teams of analysts and engineers use it as a central data foundation.

The platform has grown into an AI data cloud. Cortex provides language model functions, search over documents, and agents that run inside the platform, close to the data, with governance. It also supports machine learning, Python workloads, and apps built on Snowflake data.

item.title: Sprinklr
item.description:
Sprinklr serves very large organizations. It manages publishing across social channels, listens for brand mentions, handles customer care across messaging and voice, and analyzes market trends, using a shared data layer so teams see the whole customer picture.

AI runs through the platform: models classify conversations, detect sentiment, route cases, suggest replies, and generate content, and agents handle some customer interactions. Governance tools suit regulated industries and large teams.

Sprinklr is sold on enterprise subscriptions, with high cost and complexity. Alternatives include Hootsuite, Sprout Social, Khoros, Emplifi, and Salesforce. Sprinklr suits large brands managing many channels.

item.title: Stack AI
item.description:
Stack AI offers a visual builder for AI workflows. Users drag together components such as inputs, language models, document search, and outputs, then connect them to enterprise tools. The result can be deployed as a chatbot, form, or API.

Common cases include document processing, internal knowledge assistants, and support triage. The platform emphasizes security and governance, with options for private deployment. Templates give a starting point.

Stack AI has a free tier and paid plans. Workflows need testing and monitoring. Alternatives include Relevance AI, Dify, Flowise, n8n, and Microsoft Copilot Studio. Stack AI suits business teams building AI workflows without code.

item.title: Supademo
item.description:
Supademo makes product demos quickly. A user records clicks through an app with a browser extension, and Supademo converts them into a step-by-step interactive demo with callouts, which can be edited, branded, and embedded on a site or emailed.

AI adds voiceover narration and translations, and helps write step text. Analytics show who viewed a demo and where they stopped. The tool is also used for onboarding guides and help documentation.

item.title: Sylvera
item.description:
Sylvera brings independent analysis to the carbon market. Analysts and models assess projects, such as forest protection or renewable energy, against criteria like additionality and permanence, and issue ratings. Satellite data and machine learning help measure forest carbon and detect deforestation.

Buyers use the ratings to choose credits, and sellers use them to demonstrate quality. The platform tracks market prices and supply, and supports due diligence.

Sylvera is sold on subscription to enterprises and financial institutions. Carbon markets remain contested, and ratings reflect methodology choices. Alternatives include BeZero Carbon, Pachama, MSCI Carbon Markets, Calyx Global, and Renoster. Sylvera suits buyers evaluating carbon credits.

item.title: Talkwalker
item.description:
Talkwalker monitors the public conversation about brands and topics. Users set up searches, and the platform collects posts, articles, forums, and broadcast mentions from around the world, then analyzes volume, sentiment, and who is talking. Alerts flag spikes that may signal a crisis or opportunity.

Image and video recognition detect logos in pictures even when the brand name is not written, and AI summarizes themes and trends. Marketing and communications teams use the findings to measure campaigns, track competitors, and shape messaging, and a generative assistant helps analysts query the data.

item.title: Totango
item.description:
Totango helps subscription companies keep customers. It gathers usage and account data, scores health, and triggers playbooks when customers need attention. Modules called SuccessBLOCs package best-practice workflows that teams can adopt and adjust.

The company merged with Catalyst, another customer success platform, and the combined product serves teams from startups to enterprises. AI features summarize accounts and draft communications, and analytics show retention and expansion.

Totango has had a free tier and paid plans. Alternatives include Gainsight, ChurnZero, Planhat, Vitally, and HubSpot. Totango suits customer success teams at software companies.

item.title: Transifex
item.description:
Transifex helps product teams translate content into many languages. Developers connect repositories such as GitHub and GitLab, or use a command-line tool, and new text is sent to Transifex for translation. Translators and reviewers work in an online editor with translation memory, glossaries, and context, and approved translations flow back to the codebase.

A distinctive piece is Transifex Native, which lets apps fetch translations through an SDK, so updating a translation doesn’t require a new release. AI and machine translation pre-translate content, and quality checks flag issues, while workflows route text through reviewers or professional translation vendors. Integrations cover design tools, content management systems, and help centers.

item.title: Transistor
item.description:
Transistor is designed for people who run more than one podcast. A single account can host unlimited shows, which suits agencies, companies, and networks, and plans are based on downloads and team size instead of per-show fees. Episodes distribute to Apple Podcasts, Spotify, and other apps through an RSS feed Transistor manages.

Other features address professional needs. Private podcasts let companies share internal or members-only audio, embeddable players and a branded website help promote shows, and detailed analytics show downloads and audience. Collaboration features give team members access to specific shows, and integrations connect with Zapier and other tools. AI tools support transcripts and episode copy.

item.title: Typeform
item.description:
Typeform changed the feel of online forms. Instead of showing a long page of fields, it presents one question at a time with large type and smooth transitions, which tends to make forms feel friendlier and often improves completion rates. People use it for surveys, quizzes, lead capture, registrations, feedback, and onboarding. Design options and templates make it easy to match a brand.

Behind the interface are capable features. Logic jumps change the next question based on earlier answers, calculators and scoring support quizzes, payments can be collected, and files can be uploaded. Integrations send responses to tools like Google Sheets, HubSpot, Slack, and Zapier. AI features help generate a form from a short prompt, suggest questions, and summarize responses so teams can understand results faster.

item.title: Vizcom
item.description:
Vizcom speeds up concept design. A designer draws a rough sketch of a shoe, car, or gadget, picks materials or style, and Vizcom generates a realistic render, which can be refined with further drawing and prompts. It can also turn renders into 3D models.

Teams use it to explore many ideas quickly and communicate them to stakeholders. Collaboration tools allow shared workspaces and feedback. Automotive, footwear, and consumer product designers are common users.

item.title: Warmbox
item.description:
Warmbox addresses a deliverability problem. New or little-used email accounts sending outreach often land in spam. Warmbox connects an account to a network of inboxes that exchange emails, open and reply to them, and gradually build a positive sending history.

It is used before and during cold email campaigns, with dashboards that show inbox placement and health. Settings control volume and ramp-up.

Warmbox is paid, with plans by mailboxes. Warm-up does not fix poor targeting or bad content, and spam laws still apply. Alternatives include Instantly, Smartlead, Lemwarm, Mailreach, and Warmup Inbox. Warmbox suits teams sending cold email.

item.title: Writecream
item.description:
Writecream offers many small tools in one place. Users generate cold emails with personalized openers based on a prospect’s profile, write blog posts and ad copy, create images, and clone voices or make avatar videos.

Its outreach features appeal to sales teams that want personalization at scale, such as icebreakers for LinkedIn or email. Other tools cover general content needs.

Writecream has a free tier and paid plans. Generic AI personalization can feel obvious to recipients, and outreach must follow spam and privacy law. Alternatives include Lemlist, Copy.ai, Jasper, Instantly, and Clay. Writecream suits small teams wanting varied content tools.

item.title: Writer
item.description:
Writer targets large organizations that need AI output to stay on brand and compliant. Teams set style guides, terminology, and rules, and the system applies them as people draft, with checks for claims and tone. A knowledge graph lets AI answer from company data.

The company builds its own Palmyra language models and a platform for building agents that handle multi-step work across tools. Governance features such as permissions, logging, and fact checks support regulated industries.

item.title: Zilliz
item.description:
Zilliz Cloud runs Milvus as a service. Teams avoid operating clusters themselves and get a managed database for embeddings with features such as automatic scaling, backups, and security controls. It supports search for recommendations, retrieval for AI applications, and image or audio similarity.

Zilliz created Milvus and contributes to the open-source project, which means customers can move between self-hosting and the managed service. Hybrid search, filtering, and multi-tenant setups serve production workloads.

item.title: Datawrapper
item.description:
Datawrapper was built by journalists for journalists. A user pastes or uploads data, chooses a chart type such as a bar, line, scatter plot, or map, and adjusts labels, colors, and annotations. The result is a responsive graphic that works on phones and desktops, and can be embedded in a story or exported as an image.

Its design defaults follow good data visualization practice, so charts look clear without fiddling. Features include color-blind friendly palettes, tables with inline bars, locator maps, and a way to update charts automatically from a linked data source. News organizations around the world use it, and teams can share themes to keep a consistent style.

item.title: Looker
item.description:
Looker takes a modeling-first approach. Data teams define dimensions and measures in LookML, a code-based language, and users explore data and build dashboards on top of those shared definitions. This keeps numbers consistent and cuts arguments over whose revenue figure is right.

The platform queries data warehouses directly, so it works with the company’s data without extracting it. It supports embedded analytics, letting companies put dashboards in their own products. Gemini in Looker adds conversational analytics and help writing LookML and building reports.

item.title: PagerDuty
item.description:
PagerDuty is an incident management platform. Monitoring tools send alerts, and PagerDuty decides who should respond based on schedules and escalation rules, notifying them by phone, text, or app. It groups related alerts so one problem does not create a flood of pages.

During an incident, it supports coordination: a timeline, chat integrations, status pages, and runbooks for common fixes. AI features summarize the situation, suggest causes based on past incidents, and help write postmortems. Automation can run diagnostic or remediation steps.

item.title: FoodDocs
item.description:
FoodDocs is a digital food safety system. A restaurant, producer, or caterer answers questions about what it makes and how, and the software generates a food safety plan with hazard analysis and control points, along with the daily tasks to carry it out. Staff complete checklists on a phone or tablet.

Monitoring features include temperature logging, cleaning schedules, and alerts when tasks are missed or readings are out of range. Records are stored and ready for inspectors, and AI helps adapt the plan when menus or processes change. Sensors can send temperature readings automatically.

item.title: Meltwater
item.description:
Meltwater is a media monitoring and social listening platform. Users set up searches for brand names, competitors, and topics, and the system collects mentions from news sites, blogs, social networks, forums, and broadcast sources, with alerts and dashboards.

Analytics show volume, sentiment, and reach, and AI highlights trends and unusual spikes, such as the start of a negative story. Tools for PR teams include media databases for finding journalists, and distribution of press releases. Reports demonstrate the impact of campaigns.

item.title: Qualtrics
item.description:
Qualtrics is an experience management platform. Organizations use it to run customer satisfaction surveys, product research, brand studies, and employee engagement programs. A powerful survey builder handles complex logic, and results flow into dashboards segmented by customer, team, or time.

AI features turn feedback into action. They analyze comments for sentiment and themes, spot issues as they emerge, predict which customers may leave, and suggest next steps. The platform also pulls in data from support calls, reviews, and social media.

item.title: Relativity
item.description:
Relativity is a leading e-discovery platform. Legal teams load documents collected in a case, and the system processes them, makes them searchable, and lets reviewers tag and code them for relevance, privilege, and confidentiality. RelativityOne runs in the cloud.

AI helps lawyers cut review volume. Active learning ranks documents by likely relevance, clustering groups similar items, and generative features summarize documents and find key evidence. Analytics show patterns in communications, and audit trails support defensible processes.

item.title: Unit21
item.description:
Unit21 is a risk and compliance platform. It ingests transaction and customer data, flags suspicious activity with rules and machine learning, and routes alerts to analysts through case management. Teams build and adjust rules in a no-code interface.

The platform covers fraud prevention, anti-money laundering monitoring, and onboarding checks, and generates reports such as suspicious activity filings. AI agents help summarize cases and speed investigations.

Unit21 is sold to fintechs, banks, and marketplaces on custom pricing. Alerts need tuning to avoid overload. Alternatives include Sardine, Feedzai, Alloy, ComplyAdvantage, and Actimize. Unit21 suits risk teams at financial companies.

item.title: JITX
item.description:
JITX approaches board design as software. Instead of drawing a schematic by hand, an engineer describes circuits and requirements in code, and the system selects parts, creates connections, and generates a board layout that satisfies rules for signal integrity, power, and manufacturing. Changes can be made by editing the description and regenerating.

That makes it easier to reuse designs, check them automatically, and explore alternatives. The platform’s solvers handle routine layout tasks, so engineers concentrate on architecture. It targets hardware teams that build complex boards and want faster iteration.

item.title: 8th Wall
item.description:
8th Wall made AR available through a link. Developers built experiences using web technologies, and users opened them in a phone browser by scanning a QR code or tapping a link, with no app download. Brands used it for marketing campaigns, product try-ons, games, and events, and agencies liked that it worked across iOS and Android. Features included world tracking, image targets, face effects, and, later, location-based AR.

Niantic, the company behind Pokémon Go, acquired 8th Wall, and its technology was used alongside Niantic’s mapping and spatial work. Niantic Spatial, the spinoff focused on geospatial AI, then ended access to the 8th Wall platform. Hosted projects were given time to keep running, and the engine was released as open source, so developers can still use its code.

item.title: Agiloft
item.description:
Agiloft is a configurable system for managing contracts from request to renewal. Teams create agreements from templates and clause libraries, route them through approvals, negotiate with redlining, collect signatures, and store them in a searchable repository. Alerts remind owners of renewals and obligations, and reports show how contracts are performing, so legal, procurement, and sales teams share a single source of truth.

Its design emphasizes flexibility without custom coding. Organizations can adjust fields, workflows, and rules through no-code tools, which suits companies with unusual processes, and it connects with systems such as Salesforce, SAP, and DocuSign. AI features extract data from existing contracts, identify risky or missing clauses, summarize agreements, and let users ask questions in plain language, which speeds up migration from messy archives.

item.title: Appen
item.description:
Appen is one of the long-standing companies behind AI training data. Machine learning models need large amounts of labeled examples, such as transcribed speech, tagged images, ranked answers, and annotated documents, and Appen supplies them through a global crowd of contributors plus managed teams. Its customers have included major technology companies, and its work has fed search, voice assistants, and recommendation systems.

The services now lean toward generative AI. Appen provides data for aligning large language models, such as human preference rankings, expert-written examples, and red-teaming to find unsafe behavior. It also offers multimodal and speech datasets, coding data, and model evaluation services that test how a system performs in many languages and regions. A platform manages the workflows, quality checks, and contributor payments.

item.title: Archbee
item.description:
Archbee helps teams write and publish documentation. The editor supports rich text, code blocks, diagrams, and embedded content, and spaces organize material into sections with navigation and search. Teams can keep docs private for internal use or publish them as polished public sites with custom domains and branding, which makes it suitable for product help centers and developer portals.

Features for technical documentation include API reference generation from OpenAPI specs, Git integration to sync docs with repositories, version control, and review workflows. AI features provide smarter search and an assistant that answers questions from your documentation, plus writing help. Analytics show which pages are read and what readers search for but cannot find.

item.title: Avalara
item.description: Avalara helps businesses get indirect taxes right. Sales tax rules vary by state, city, product type, and customer, and rates change often, which makes manual calculation risky. Avalara integrates with online stores, accounting software, and ERP systems to calculate the correct tax at checkout or invoicing based on the transaction’s location and product, then helps file returns and remit payments in many jurisdictions. It covers sales and use tax, VAT, and other transaction taxes around the world.

item.title: AWS IoT Core
item.description:
AWS IoT Core is the entry point for Internet of Things devices into AWS. Devices connect using MQTT, HTTPS, and other protocols, authenticate with certificates, and publish and receive messages, with the service scaling to billions of devices and trillions of messages. A device registry tracks each device, and Device Shadows keep a copy of the device’s state so applications can interact with it even when it is offline.

A rules engine processes incoming data and routes it to other AWS services such as Lambda, S3, DynamoDB, Kinesis, and SageMaker, so data can be stored, analyzed, or used to trigger actions. Related services handle device management, fleet monitoring, over-the-air updates, and edge computing with AWS IoT Greengrass, which runs code and machine learning models on the device. Security features include fine-grained policies, and logging and monitoring tools.

item.title: Azure Content Moderator
item.description:
Content Moderator was Microsoft’s tool for checking user-generated content. It scanned text for profanity and personal data, analyzed images for adult or racy content, and screened video, returning scores and flags that platforms could use to filter or send items for human review. Online communities, marketplaces, and apps with user uploads used it as an automated first line of defense.

Microsoft has deprecated the service and no longer allows new projects, directing customers to Azure AI Content Safety. The newer service uses more advanced models, handles multiple severity levels across categories such as hate, sexual content, violence, and self-harm, supports many more languages, and adds features aimed at generative AI, including prompt shields and groundedness detection. Existing Content Moderator projects continue to work until the retirement date.

item.title: Azure IoT Hub
item.description: Azure IoT Hub is the messaging backbone for connected devices on Azure. Devices send telemetry such as sensor readings to the cloud, and the cloud can send commands and configuration back. Each device has its own identity and credentials, so the platform can authenticate it, and connections use standard protocols like MQTT and AMQP. The hub scales to large fleets and can route messages to storage, stream processing, and analytics services.

item.title: Benchling
item.description: Benchling brings the scattered tasks of a research lab into one cloud system. Scientists use the notebook to record experiments, design DNA and protein sequences with molecular biology tools, and register the samples and materials they create, so everything is traceable. Teams track workflows, share results, and connect lab instruments, which replaces a mix of spreadsheets, paper notebooks, and separate databases. It is common at startups and large biopharma companies.

item.title: BigID
item.description:
BigID starts with a question many companies cannot answer: where is our sensitive data? It scans databases, file shares, cloud storage, SaaS apps, and data lakes to discover personal information, financial records, and other regulated data, then classifies it using machine learning. The results build a catalog showing what data exists, where it sits, and who can access it. That map is the basis for privacy and security work.

Several functions build on the catalog. Privacy teams use it to respond to access and deletion requests, track consent, and meet rules like GDPR and CCPA. Security teams use it to find overexposed data, fix permissions, and reduce risk through remediation workflows. A newer focus is AI governance: the platform identifies which AI agents, copilots, and models can reach sensitive data, helps limit that access, and checks against frameworks such as the NIST AI Risk Management Framework and the EU AI Act.

item.title: Bizzabo
item.description: Bizzabo is a software platform for corporate and large-scale event teams. Planners build event websites, sell tickets and handle registration, manage speakers and agendas, and track who attends. On site, it supports badge printing and check-in, and a mobile app lets attendees see the schedule, message each other, and use polls or Q&A during sessions. For virtual and hybrid events, it can stream sessions and bring remote attendees into the same experience.

item.title: Blinkist
item.description:
Blinkist is designed for people who want the main ideas of a book without reading all of it. Editors and writers distill nonfiction titles in business, psychology, science, health, and self-improvement into short summaries, with key takeaways and often a quick audio version. Users listen on a commute or skim on a break, and it’s used as a way to preview a book before deciding to read it fully.

The app has broadened with audiobooks, original content, and tools such as highlighting and collections of titles by topic. AI features include personalized recommendations and generated summaries or answers based on its library, and an AI assistant that lets users ask questions about topics. Audio can be downloaded for offline listening.

item.title: Bugsnag
item.description: Bugsnag tells engineering teams what is breaking in their software and for whom. A small SDK in a web, mobile, or server app reports crashes and handled errors with a stack trace, device and browser details, user information, and the actions that led up to the failure. Instead of a flood of raw events, Bugsnag groups similar errors together, so a single bug appears as one issue with a count of affected users.

item.title: Buildxact
item.description:
Buildxact is built for builders who work from plans and spreadsheets and need a more organized way to price jobs. Users can create estimates from templates and cost catalogs, perform takeoffs from digital plans, and turn the estimate into a professional proposal. After a job is won, the same data feeds purchase orders, schedules, and cost tracking, so you can compare what you estimated with what you spent.

The software covers the flow of a residential project: estimating, quoting, selections, job scheduling, subcontractor coordination, and invoicing, with integrations to accounting software such as QuickBooks and Xero. AI features help read plans and speed up takeoffs, suggest items, and draft proposals. It targets small to mid-sized companies, such as custom home builders, remodelers, and specialty trades.

item.title: Catapult Sports
item.description: Catapult makes the small wearable devices that professional teams use to measure what athletes do. A tracker worn in a vest sits against the athlete’s upper back and records movement with GPS and inertial sensors, capturing distance, speed, accelerations, impacts, and the intensity of effort. Coaches and sports scientists use the data to see how hard each player is working, compare training with match demands, and adjust loads to reduce the risk of injury.

item.title: Clarifai
item.description: Clarifai started as an image recognition API and has grown into a broader AI platform. Teams use it to find and call models for vision, language, and audio tasks, to train their own models on labeled data, and to run them in production. It includes tools for organizing and labeling data, searching images and video, and building workflows that chain several models together. Industries such as retail, media, and public sector have used it to classify content and find objects in large collections.

item.title: CloudHealth by VMware
item.description: CloudHealth was one of the first tools built for managing cloud costs across several providers. Companies connect their AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud accounts and get a consolidated view of spending, broken down by team, project, or application using tags and rules. Reports show where money goes, budgets raise alerts when spending drifts, and recommendations point to unused resources and oversized instances. That helps finance and engineering teams share a view of cloud costs.

item.title: Coggle
item.description:
Coggle keeps mind mapping simple. In the browser, you start with a central idea and add branches by clicking, using colors, images, and text, and the diagram grows into a tidy tree. It can also draw flowcharts, with free-form connections between nodes, so the same tool covers brainstorming, note taking, planning, and basic process diagrams. The look is clean, with auto-arranged branches that make diagrams easy to read.

Collaboration is a core feature. Several people can edit the same diagram at once and see each other’s changes, and a full history lets you review and restore earlier versions. Diagrams can include notes and images, be shared by link, and be exported as PDF, image, or text outlines. Students, teachers, and small teams use it for study notes, lesson plans, and project outlines.

item.title: Confluence AI
item.description:
Confluence is where many teams keep their documentation. It organizes pages into spaces, with templates for meeting notes, product requirements, runbooks, project plans, and knowledge bases. Pages support rich formatting, comments, and embedded content from Jira and other tools. Version history and permissions help control who can edit and read what. Teams in engineering, product, IT, and operations use it as a shared source of truth.

AI features come through Atlassian’s Rovo. Inside Confluence, you can summarize a long page, draft content from a short prompt, improve or translate writing, and ask questions in natural language and get answers drawn from the knowledge in your spaces. Rovo search reaches across Confluence, Jira, and connected tools like Google Drive and Slack, and agents can take on tasks such as turning a meeting note into action items.

item.title: Creately
item.description:
Creately combines diagramming and whiteboarding in one workspace. You can draw flowcharts, org charts, mind maps, UML diagrams, process maps, wireframes, and more using shape libraries and templates, then connect them with smart connectors that stay attached when you move things. An infinite canvas supports brainstorming and planning, and teams can edit together in real time with comments and cursors.

Some features go beyond plain drawing. Diagrams can be linked to data, so a shape can show information from a spreadsheet or tool, and cards and tables let you build lightweight planning boards. AI features generate a diagram from a text description, summarize or expand notes, and suggest ideas for brainstorming. Presentations and exports in common formats help you share work, and integrations connect with Slack, Confluence, Google Workspace, and Microsoft Teams.

item.title: Crowdin
item.description:
Crowdin helps teams make products available in many languages. Developers connect their repositories, such as GitHub or GitLab, and Crowdin picks up new source strings, makes them available to translators, and syncs completed translations back, so localization keeps pace with development. It works with files from mobile, web, and game projects, and with content from design tools like Figma and from help centers.

The translation environment supports several workflows. Professional translators, in-house reviewers, and community volunteers can work in an editor with context, screenshots, glossaries, and translation memory that reuses past translations for consistency. Machine translation and AI features pre-translate content and suggest improvements, and quality checks catch errors. Project managers track progress and can order work from translation vendors through the platform.

item.title: CrowdStrike
item.description: CrowdStrike’s core product is Falcon, a cloud-based endpoint security platform. A small agent on laptops, servers, and cloud workloads sends behavior data to CrowdStrike’s cloud, where machine learning and threat intelligence look for malicious activity such as ransomware or hands-on-keyboard attacks. Because analysis happens in the cloud, the agent is light and updates quickly. The company’s detection and response model, known as EDR and XDR, is widely used by large enterprises and governments.

item.title: CVAT
item.description: CVAT was created at Intel and released as open source, and is now maintained by a company called CVAT.ai along with a community. It is a web-based tool for labeling data for computer vision: drawing bounding boxes, polygons, polylines, points, and masks, and tagging images or video frames with classes. It handles tasks such as object detection, segmentation, tracking across video, and classification, and exports to common formats such as COCO, YOLO, and Pascal VOC.

item.title: Datadog
item.description: Datadog is software-as-a-service for watching what your systems are doing. You install an agent on servers, containers, or cloud accounts, or connect it through one of hundreds of integrations, and it begins collecting metrics, logs, and traces. Dashboards and alerts then show how hosts, databases, queues, and services are behaving. The value for most teams is having infrastructure monitoring, application performance monitoring, log management, and real user monitoring in one place instead of stitching together separate tools.

item.title: Derwent Innovation
item.description:
Derwent Innovation serves IP professionals who need thorough patent research. It provides search across patent documents from many countries, with tools to construct complex queries, filter results, and analyze trends. Its distinguishing asset is the Derwent World Patents Index, in which Clarivate’s editors rewrite patent abstracts in clear language and standardize names and classifications, making it easier to find relevant documents despite varying terminology.

Analytics and workflow tools support decisions about filing, licensing, and litigation. Users can visualize technology landscapes, compare competitors’ portfolios, and track legal status, and AI features help with semantic search, summaries, and finding similar patents. Teams collaborate on search results and export reports. Clarivate also offers related products for trademark and scientific research.

item.title: DNAnexus
item.description: DNAnexus gives life science organizations a place to work with very large datasets. Sequencing a genome produces enormous files, and analyzing thousands of them takes substantial computing and careful data management. The platform provides cloud storage, scalable compute, workflow tools, and a catalog of bioinformatics pipelines, so teams can run analyses without managing their own servers. It is built to meet regulatory and privacy requirements for clinical and health data.

item.title: Drata
item.description:
Drata addresses the burden of proving security compliance. Companies selling to enterprises are often asked for a SOC 2 report or other certifications, and preparing for an audit traditionally takes months of gathering screenshots and documents. Drata connects to systems such as AWS, Google Workspace, GitHub, Okta, and HR tools, automatically checks whether controls are in place, and collects evidence continuously, so the company remains audit-ready.

The platform covers more than evidence. It manages policies and employee training, tracks vendor risk, supports risk assessments, and offers a trust center that lets customers see a company’s security posture. Auditors can work directly in the platform. AI features help fill out security questionnaires, summarize risks, and map controls across multiple frameworks, saving time for small security teams.

item.title: Dune Analytics
item.description:
Dune made blockchain data accessible. Raw on-chain information is hard to work with, so Dune indexes data from many blockchains into databases that anyone can query with SQL. Users write queries to answer questions such as how many people used a decentralized exchange last week or how much value is locked in a protocol, and publish results as charts on dashboards that others can fork and extend.

The community aspect is a key feature. Analysts share dashboards openly, so you can find ready-made views of NFT markets, stablecoin flows, protocol metrics, and more, and learn from other people’s queries. Dune AI features help generate and explain SQL from natural language, and APIs allow developers to use query results in applications. Data teams use it for research and reporting.

item.title: Flexport
item.description:
Flexport is a freight forwarder with a software platform. Companies that import and export goods book shipments, track containers, manage documents, and handle customs through a single interface, instead of coordinating by email with many parties. It also offers financing, warehousing, and trade services.

Technology handles repetitive work. AI reads shipping documents, checks customs data for errors, and predicts delays based on port, carrier, and weather information. An assistant answers questions about shipment status and helps with classification of goods. Data from many shipments feeds analytics on cost and performance.

item.title: Formant
item.description:
Formant solves operational problems that arise once robots leave the lab. Companies running fleets of mobile robots, drones, or arms need to know what each machine is doing, diagnose problems, and sometimes take control. Formant collects telemetry, video, and sensor data from robots, shows it in dashboards, and raises alerts when something goes wrong, working with robots running ROS or other software.

Teleoperation is a key feature: an operator can view a robot’s cameras and drive or guide it remotely, which helps with situations where autonomy fails. Teams can capture and tag data to improve machine learning models, schedule and analyze missions, and manage software updates across a fleet. Integrations connect with cloud services and business systems, and AI tools help find anomalies.

item.title: Geneious
item.description:
Geneious gives molecular biologists a graphical environment for work that would otherwise need command-line tools. Researchers import sequence data from sequencers or databases, then view, align, annotate, and compare it in a visual interface. It supports de novo assembly and mapping of reads to a reference, building phylogenetic trees, designing primers, and planning cloning experiments, so a lab can do many routine tasks in one program.

A plugin system extends it with additional algorithms and workflows, including tools for antibody discovery, metagenomics, and variant analysis. Results are shared through a collaboration feature, and a server product lets teams work with common databases. The software is part of Dotmatics, which also owns other scientific R&D tools. Machine learning appears in specific tools and plugins instead of as a general assistant.

item.title: GitBook
item.description:
GitBook helps teams publish documentation that people can actually navigate. Writers use a clean editor to create pages, organize them into spaces and collections, and publish them as a polished documentation site with search, navigation, and versioning. Software companies use it for product docs, API references, and internal knowledge bases, and the same content can be shared publicly or restricted to teams.

Developer-friendly features set it apart. Content can sync with a GitHub or GitLab repository, so docs can live alongside code and be reviewed through pull requests, and a change request workflow lets teams review edits before publishing. OpenAPI imports generate API reference pages, and integrations connect analytics, support tools, and chat. AI features include an assistant that answers readers’ questions from the docs, AI-enhanced search, and help with writing and editing pages.

item.title: Gretel.ai
item.description: Gretel helps teams get usable data when real data is sensitive or scarce. Developers connect a dataset, such as customer records or medical tables, and Gretel trains a model that produces new records with the same statistical patterns but no direct link to real individuals. Teams use the results to test software, share data across departments, and train machine learning models without waiting for privacy approvals. It also generates text and tabular data for fine-tuning language models.

item.title: Headspace
item.description:
Headspace is one of the best-known meditation apps, with a friendly style and a structured approach for beginners. It offers guided meditations of different lengths, sleep content, movement and breathing exercises, focus music, and courses on topics such as stress, anxiety, and relationships. Short daily sessions are designed to build a habit, and progress features encourage consistency.

The company has expanded beyond meditation into broader mental healthcare. Depending on the market and plan, users can access coaching and therapy services, and employers offer Headspace as a benefit. An AI companion, Ebb, provides conversational support for reflecting on feelings and finding relevant exercises. It is meant to support wellbeing, not to diagnose or treat conditions, and Headspace points users in crisis toward professional help.

item.title: Honeycomb
item.description:
Honeycomb works from the premise that modern systems fail in unpredictable ways. Engineers send rich events and traces with many attributes, and can slice and filter by any of them to find what is different about slow or failing requests. High-cardinality fields such as user IDs are supported, which many tools handle poorly.

Visual tools highlight outliers, compare groups, and follow a request across services, and service level objectives alert teams when users are affected. The platform embraces OpenTelemetry for data collection, so teams can instrument once. AI features let users ask questions in natural language and help interpret data.

item.title: Hopin
item.description:
Hopin offered an all-in-one environment for online events. Organizers sold tickets, ran live sessions on a main stage, hosted breakout rooms and video networking, and set up virtual expo booths, and attendees moved between these areas as if walking around a venue. It grew explosively as conferences moved online, with large funding rounds and acquisitions of other event and streaming companies.

As in-person events returned, demand for virtual events dropped sharply, and Hopin shrank and restructured. It sold its events platform to RingCentral, which continues to operate it as part of its own offering, and the company’s other products, such as streaming and community tools, were separated or spun out. The brand is no longer the same independent business.

item.title: Insomnia
item.description:
Insomnia is a desktop application that lets developers send requests to APIs and inspect responses. You build requests with headers, authentication, and bodies, organize them into collections, and use environment variables to switch between development and production. It supports REST, GraphQL, gRPC, WebSocket, and Server-Sent Events, and can import definitions from OpenAPI specifications.

Beyond manual testing, it supports design and automation. An API design editor helps write specs, test suites run collections of requests with assertions, and command-line tools run tests in CI. Plugins extend functionality, Git sync stores collections with code, and AI features help generate requests, tests, and documentation. Insomnia can store data locally or in the cloud, a choice that matters to teams concerned about privacy.

item.title: Intrinsic
item.description:
Intrinsic works on a long-standing challenge in manufacturing: robots are powerful, but programming them is slow, specialized, and expensive. The company develops a software platform that lets developers build robotic applications, using skills and tools that can be reused across different robots and tasks. The idea is similar to how an operating system and app tools made computers easier to program for a wide range of hardware.

AI and simulation play a central role. Perception tools help robots see and understand objects, motion planning handles collisions, and simulation lets teams test and refine an application virtually before running it on the factory floor. Intrinsic works with robot makers and system integrators, and it has explored combining its platform with advanced AI models so that robots can handle more varied tasks without extensive reprogramming.

item.title: IPlytics
item.description:
IPlytics focuses on the overlap between patents and technical standards. Many technologies, from 5G to Wi-Fi to video codecs, depend on standards, and companies hold patents they declare essential to implementing them. IPlytics links patent databases with standards documents, declarations, and standardization meeting contributions, helping users understand who owns what and how influential each player is.

Typical users are IP and licensing professionals, R&D strategists, and legal teams. They use it to search for standard-essential patents, benchmark portfolios against competitors, find licensing opportunities, and see which companies are shaping emerging standards. The platform includes analytics, dashboards, and data feeds, and AI features help classify patents and find relevant documents.

item.title: Labelbox
item.description:
Labelbox helps AI teams turn raw data into labeled datasets. Its tools let annotators draw boxes and masks on images and video, tag text, transcribe audio, and rate model responses. Project management features assign work, review quality, and measure agreement between labelers, so teams can catch mistakes early. The platform supports both in-house labelers and external workforces.

The company has focused on generative AI. Tools support reinforcement learning from human feedback and model evaluation, where experts compare and rank responses, and a labeling service provides specialist annotators for domains such as coding, math, and medicine. Model-assisted labeling uses a model to pre-label data so humans only correct it, and data curation tools help find the most valuable examples. Integrations connect with cloud storage and ML pipelines.

item.title: Leetify
item.description:
Leetify is an analytics and coaching tool for Counter-Strike players. After a match, it reads the demo data and produces a report with ratings across aim, positioning, and use of grenades, plus round-by-round breakdowns that show why a round was won or lost. Players compare themselves with others at their level.

Team features support scrims and coaching. Coaches review stats across players, see where the team struggles, and track improvement over time. A public profile shows a player’s progress, and a leaderboard ranks users, with an optional paid tier for deeper analysis.

item.title: Lexalytics
item.description: Lexalytics builds natural language processing for businesses that need to make sense of large amounts of text. Its Salience engine reads reviews, survey comments, support tickets, social posts, and call transcripts and returns structured information: whether the sentiment is positive or negative, which products or people are mentioned, what themes recur, and what the author intends. Analysts can then count, trend, and compare these signals instead of reading comments one by one.

item.title: Mermaid Chart
item.description:
Mermaid is a popular open-source way to create diagrams by writing text. You describe a flowchart or sequence diagram in a few lines of code, and it renders as a graphic, which makes diagrams easy to version in Git, embed in documentation, and update alongside code. GitHub, GitLab, and many documentation tools render Mermaid natively, and developers like that diagrams stay in plain text.

Mermaid Chart is the company and product founded by the creator of Mermaid. It provides a web editor with live preview, a visual drag-and-drop editor for people who prefer not to write code, templates, and collaboration features such as sharing and comments. AI can generate diagrams from a description, fix syntax errors, and suggest changes, which lowers the barrier for beginners. Plugins integrate with VS Code, Confluence, Jira, and other tools.

item.title: MindMeister
item.description:
MindMeister helps you think in branches. You start with a central topic and add connected ideas around it, using keyboard shortcuts to build a map quickly. Maps can be formatted with colors, icons, images, links, and notes, rearranged freely, and turned into outlines. People use it for brainstorming, studying, project planning, meeting notes, and mapping out content such as articles or courses.

Collaboration is a core strength. Several people can edit a map at once, with comments and voting to gather input, and maps can be shared by link. A presentation mode turns a map into slides, and tasks can be assigned on map nodes and synced with the project tools in the same suite. Integrations connect with Google Workspace, Microsoft Teams, and other apps, and exports include PDF, image, and Word formats. AI features suggest ideas and generate map structures from a topic.

item.title: Mobalytics
item.description:
Mobalytics is a gaming analytics and coaching site. Players link their accounts, and the tool analyzes their games, scoring performance across areas like farming, vision, and teamfights. A profile shows trends over time and compares the player with others at their rank.

Coaching features set it apart. The platform highlights patterns in mistakes and suggests focus areas, offers guides for champions and builds, and provides an overlay with in-game tips. Premium plans add deeper analysis and AI-generated feedback.

item.title: MonkeyLearn
item.description:
MonkeyLearn let people analyze text without machine learning expertise. Teams could connect support tickets, survey responses, reviews, and social posts, pick a ready-made model for sentiment or topics, or train a custom classifier by tagging examples. Results appeared in dashboards and could be sent to spreadsheets, helpdesks, and BI tools, which made it popular with customer experience, product, and marketing teams.

Its approach was to make natural language processing approachable. A visual interface handled model creation and testing, and the API let developers add analysis to their own apps. Typical uses included tagging support requests by issue, tracking sentiment in reviews, and pulling themes from open-ended survey answers.

item.title: MOSTLY AI
item.description:
MOSTLY AI helps organizations use data that would otherwise be locked away by privacy rules. It trains a generative model on a real dataset, such as customer transactions or patient records, and then produces a new dataset that reflects the same patterns, relationships, and distributions but contains no real individuals. Banks, insurers, and healthcare companies use it to share data across teams and borders, test software, and develop models.

The platform handles multi-table relational data, preserving links between tables such as customers and their orders. Quality and privacy reports compare the synthetic data with the original and check for leakage, and features can rebalance datasets to reduce bias or fill in rare cases. An open-source SDK allows developers to run generation in their own environment, while the platform adds a user interface, scheduling, and enterprise controls.

item.title: NAVEX
item.description:
NAVEX serves compliance and risk teams at large organizations. Its best-known service is a reporting hotline and web portal where employees can raise concerns about misconduct anonymously. Reports flow into a case management system that assigns investigators, tracks actions, and keeps records.

The company also provides policy management, training courses, third-party risk tools, and analytics that reveal patterns across reports. Newer features use AI to summarize cases, categorize reports, and surface trends for compliance leaders.

item.title: New Relic
item.description:
New Relic helps engineering teams understand how their software behaves in production. You add agents or OpenTelemetry instrumentation to your applications and infrastructure, and it collects performance data, errors, logs, and traces of requests as they move through services. Dashboards and alerts show slow endpoints, failing deployments, and resource pressure, and distributed tracing helps pinpoint which service in a chain caused a delay.

The platform covers application performance monitoring, infrastructure monitoring, log management, browser and mobile monitoring, and synthetic checks that test your site from outside. Applied intelligence groups related alerts and reduces noise, and an AI assistant lets people ask questions about their systems in plain language, summarize incidents, and get suggested next steps. It also includes tools for monitoring AI applications, tracking model calls, latency, cost, and quality.

item.title: Niantic Lightship
item.description:
Lightship began as a set of tools for building location-based AR experiences. The ARDK SDK for Unity offered features such as depth sensing, occlusion, and meshing, and the Visual Positioning System let apps determine a device’s precise location and orientation by matching camera images to a map of the real world. The technology came from the infrastructure behind Pokémon GO and drew on scans collected from players.

Niantic’s geospatial work later moved into a separate company, Niantic Spatial, after the games business was sold. The developer platform was renamed the Niantic Spatial Platform, with an SDK for Unity, tools for scanning places through Scaniverse, and mapping services. The original Lightship website was shut down, and visitors are redirected, with guidance for migrating projects.

item.title: Okta
item.description:
Okta is one of the best-known providers of cloud identity. Companies use it as the central place where employees sign in to their applications: one login gives access to hundreds of apps through single sign-on, and multi-factor authentication adds protection against stolen passwords. The Universal Directory stores identities and groups, and lifecycle management automates giving people the right access when they join, change roles, or leave.

The platform covers more of the identity problem over time. Adaptive policies check device and context before allowing access, governance tools handle access reviews and requests, and privileged access tools protect administrator accounts. Okta also owns Auth0 for customer-facing apps. As companies deploy AI agents that act on behalf of users, Okta has added features for giving these agents their own identities and managing what they may do.

item.title: OneTrust
item.description:
OneTrust helps large organizations manage the rules about data. Its best-known product handles consent: the cookie banners and preference centers that appear on websites and apps and record what visitors agree to. Privacy teams use other modules to respond to data subject requests such as access and deletion, map where personal data is stored, run privacy impact assessments, and show regulators that they follow laws like GDPR and CCPA.

The platform has expanded into broader governance, risk, and compliance. Tools cover third-party and vendor risk, security and IT risk, ethics and policy management, and environmental and social reporting. A growing area is AI governance: inventorying the AI systems an organization uses, assessing their risks, and tracking compliance with emerging rules such as the EU AI Act. AI features in the platform help classify data and automate assessments.

item.title: Osano
item.description:
Osano began with cookie consent, the banner that asks visitors what tracking they accept. Its consent manager scans a site, categorizes cookies and scripts, shows region-appropriate banners, and records choices, which helps companies comply with laws such as GDPR and CCPA. Websites install it with a small piece of code, and it can block scripts until a visitor agrees.

The platform grew to cover the wider privacy program. Tools handle data subject access requests, data mapping, and assessments, and a vendor monitoring service tracks the privacy practices of third parties and flags risks. Osano also offers privacy rating information and a catalog of vendor reports. Features for managing AI use and policies are being added as regulation develops.

item.title: PatSnap
item.description:
PatSnap serves teams that need to understand the patent landscape. Its search covers a very large collection of patents and scientific literature worldwide, and semantic search finds relevant documents from a description of an invention instead of exact keywords. Users can analyze who is filing in a technology area, map clusters of related patents, track competitors, and check whether an idea has been patented before.

Several products fit different jobs. Tools help with prior art searches before filing, freedom-to-operate checks before launching a product, and landscape analysis to guide R&D strategy. AI assistants summarize patents, extract key claims, and answer questions about a technology, and workflows let teams share results and collaborate. The platform also covers non-patent literature and market information for innovation scouting.

item.title: Persona
item.description:
Persona lets companies verify who their customers and business partners are. A business builds a flow, choosing which checks to run: collecting and verifying a government ID, matching a selfie to the photo with liveness detection, checking databases and watchlists, verifying a business and its owners, or confirming an address. The flow can adapt based on risk, asking for more evidence only when something looks suspicious.

Configurability sets it apart. Companies can design the user experience, set rules for approvals, and route uncertain cases to human reviewers in a case management tool. Additional products detect fraud patterns across accounts, run ongoing monitoring, and verify employees and workforce identities. APIs and no-code builders connect the flows to existing systems, and the platform covers documents from many countries.

item.title: PlanetScale
item.description:
PlanetScale brought a workflow familiar from Git to relational databases. Developers create a branch of their database schema, make changes, and merge them through a deploy request, with checks that avoid downtime. Behind that is Vitess, the sharding system created at YouTube, which lets MySQL scale horizontally across many servers. This allows growth beyond the limits of a single database machine.

Features focus on safe changes and performance. Online schema changes let teams alter large tables without locking, insights show slow queries and suggest improvements, and connection handling supports large numbers of clients. Recent products emphasize high-performance storage and have extended the platform to Postgres. AI-assisted insights help identify problematic queries, and the service integrates with popular frameworks and hosting platforms.

item.title: Postman
item.description: Postman started as a simple way to send HTTP requests without writing code, and it is still the most common tool for poking at an API. You enter a URL, choose a method, add headers and a body, and see the response. Requests are saved in collections that can be shared with a team, and environments let you switch variables like base URLs and keys between development, staging, and production without editing every request.

item.title: Procore
item.description:
Procore is one of the most widely used software platforms in construction. It gives everyone on a building project a shared place to manage drawings and documents, RFIs and submittals, daily logs, schedules, budgets, change orders, and inspections. Instead of email chains and spreadsheets, project information lives in one system with a record of who did what, which reduces disputes and rework.

The platform spans the project lifecycle, from preconstruction bidding and estimating through construction and closeout. Financial tools handle cost tracking, invoicing, and payments, while quality and safety modules support checklists, observations, and incident reports. A marketplace of integrations connects accounting, scheduling, and design tools. AI features help search across documents, summarize information, and automate routine tasks, and agents are being added to take on project management work.

item.title: Repustate
item.description: Repustate focuses on understanding opinions in many languages. Its API reads text, such as tweets, reviews, news, or survey responses, and returns the sentiment, the topics and entities discussed, and the themes that recur, with attention to context so that sentiment about one aspect of a product can be separated from another. Language coverage is a selling point, including Arabic, Chinese, and many other languages that are less well served by some competitors.

item.title: Rookout
item.description:
Rookout solved a frustrating problem: figuring out what is happening inside production code. Normally, finding a bug means adding logging, redeploying, and waiting for the problem to recur. Rookout let developers set non-breaking breakpoints in live applications, so they could capture variable values, stack traces, and logs on demand without stopping the program or changing and restarting it.

It supported cloud-native environments with containers, serverless functions, and Kubernetes, and integrated with the tools developers already used for logging and monitoring. The data could be sent to existing observability systems, so debugging fit into current workflows. It was used by engineering teams that needed to debug complex, distributed applications quickly.

item.title: Sentry
item.description:
Sentry tells developers when their code breaks and why. By adding an SDK to an app, errors are reported with stack traces, the environment, the user’s actions leading up to the problem, and the release that introduced it. Sentry groups duplicate errors into single issues, sends alerts, and links to the relevant commit, so teams can fix a bug quickly rather than discovering it from user complaints.

Beyond error tracking, Sentry monitors performance with tracing that shows slow requests and database queries, and session replay records what the user saw. Cron monitoring watches scheduled jobs, and release health tracks crash-free sessions. Its AI assistant, Seer, analyzes issues to suggest root causes and can propose fixes, and tools for monitoring AI applications trace model calls. It supports most languages and frameworks, and integrates with GitHub, Slack, and Jira.

item.title: Shorthand
item.description:
Shorthand makes it possible to create the kind of immersive web story that once required a design and development team. You assemble a story from sections with full-width images, video backgrounds, parallax effects, and text, and the platform handles responsive layout and animation. The finished piece is published as a webpage that scrolls like a magazine feature, and works on phones and desktops.

Newsrooms, universities, nonprofits, and corporate communications teams use it for long-form journalism, annual reports, campaign stories, and case studies. Collaboration features let writers and editors work together with review stages, brand themes keep designs consistent, and analytics show readership. Stories can be embedded in a site or hosted by Shorthand, and a CMS integration helps publishing.

item.title: Sight Machine
item.description:
Sight Machine tackles the data mess inside factories. Machines, sensors, and systems produce data in many formats, and plants often cannot easily combine it. Sight Machine’s platform pulls in data from equipment, quality systems, and enterprise software, standardizes it into a common model of the production process, and creates a digital twin that shows how products move through the plant.

With that foundation, teams can analyze performance.
