Dashboards track throughput, yield, scrap, and downtime across lines and sites, machine learning finds the factors that drive defects or slowdowns, and alerts flag issues in near real time. An AI assistant lets operators and engineers ask questions about production data in plain language, and the platform supports sustainability tracking such as energy use.

item.title: Spacemaker AI
item.description:
Spacemaker was a Norwegian startup that applied AI to the first phase of building design. Given a site and a set of goals, it generates many layouts for buildings, then analyzes each for sunlight, daylight, wind comfort, noise, views, and the amount of floor area it provides. Designers can compare options and adjust parameters, rather than testing a few ideas by hand.

Autodesk acquired the company and integrated its technology into Autodesk Forma, a cloud platform for early design. Forma combines site context, environmental analysis, and design tools, and connects to Revit and other Autodesk products so early decisions can be carried into detailed design. The platform serves architects, developers, and city planners evaluating projects.

item.title: Spot.io
item.description:
Spot started as Spotinst, a company that helped users run workloads on cheap but interruptible cloud capacity. Its Elastigroup service predicts when spot instances will be reclaimed and moves workloads to keep applications running, which can reduce compute costs sharply. Ocean applies the same ideas to Kubernetes clusters, scaling nodes and choosing instance types automatically, and Eco manages savings plans and reserved instances.

NetApp acquired Spot, branded it Spot by NetApp, and later sold the Spot FinOps portfolio to Flexera, which now develops it alongside its other cloud cost tools. The tools support AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud, with dashboards showing savings, and they are sold on a model tied to a percentage of savings or capacity. Customers have included engineering teams running large container and batch workloads.

item.title: Stem AI
item.description:
Stem began by installing battery storage systems for businesses, and its software, Athena, became the heart of the company. Athena uses forecasts of energy prices, demand, and generation to decide when a battery should charge or discharge, balancing cost savings for the owner with revenue from grid services. This kind of optimization can make storage economically viable.

The business has shifted from selling hardware toward software and services. Athena manages solar plus storage, standalone batteries, and other distributed assets for developers and owners, and also offers analytics and asset performance tools. Machine learning helps predict conditions and handle the complexity of electricity markets, which differ by region.

item.title: StoryChief
item.description:
StoryChief helps marketing teams run a content workflow in one place. Teams plan content on a calendar, write articles in a shared editor, route them through review and approval, and then publish to multiple channels with a click, including their website, social networks, newsletters, and platforms like Medium. It reduces the work of copying content between tools and keeps assets organized.

SEO and analytics features support performance. An optimizer scores drafts against target keywords, and reports track traffic and engagement across channels. AI features help generate outlines and drafts, rewrite content, and adapt posts for social networks, and a library of integrations connects WordPress, HubSpot, and other tools. It’s popular with agencies that manage multiple clients, and with in-house teams.

item.title: Tonic AI
item.description:
Tonic.ai solves a common development problem: engineers need realistic data to test software, but production data contains sensitive information. Tonic Structural connects to a database, identifies sensitive fields, and replaces them with fake but realistic values, preserving relationships and formats so applications behave as they would with real data. This allows teams to build and test with representative data without exposing customers’ details.

Other products broaden the range. Tonic Fabricate generates synthetic data from scratch for new applications or demos, and Tonic Textual finds and redacts sensitive information in unstructured data such as documents and text, which helps prepare data for training or retrieval in AI systems. Integrations support popular databases and data warehouses, and subsetting tools cut large databases down to smaller, usable test sets.

item.title: Transcend
item.description:
Transcend takes a developer-oriented approach to privacy compliance. It connects to a company’s databases, SaaS tools, and warehouses to discover where personal data is stored, then automates responses to requests from individuals to access or delete their data. Instead of manually searching dozens of systems, the platform executes the request across them and keeps a record.

Other products cover related needs. Consent management controls cookies and tracking according to each visitor’s choices and location, a gateway can enforce those choices in what data flows to third parties, and data mapping documents processing activities. Newer tools address AI governance, helping teams track what data feeds models and meet emerging regulations.

item.title: Tulip
item.description:
Tulip brings software to the factory floor. Engineers and operators build apps using a drag-and-drop editor, with steps that guide workers through assembly, inspection, or maintenance, collect data, and trigger actions. Connecting sensors, machines, and tools lets the apps read real-time values, and the platform replaces clipboards and spreadsheets with digital work instructions and quality checks.

Analytics and automation extend the value. Dashboards show production performance, quality, and downtime, and machine learning models can detect anomalies or predict issues. Generative AI helps create apps from a description and analyze data in plain language. As a lightweight manufacturing execution system, it can be adopted gradually, line by line.

item.title: Turbonomic
item.description: Turbonomic tries to answer a question that infrastructure teams face constantly: is each application getting the resources it needs without wasting money? The platform monitors applications and the infrastructure they run on, including virtual machines, containers, and cloud services, and uses analytics to decide where workloads should run, how large they should be, and when to scale. It can take actions automatically, such as resizing instances, moving workloads, or adjusting Kubernetes resources.

item.title: Vanta
item.description:
Vanta helps companies prove they run secure operations. It integrates with tools such as AWS, Google Workspace, GitHub, Okta, and HR systems, continuously checks whether controls like encryption, access reviews, and employee training are in place, and collects the evidence auditors need. This replaces manual screenshots and spreadsheets and keeps a company audit-ready year-round.

The platform has grown into a broader trust management suite. It tracks vendor risk, manages security policies and employee onboarding tasks, runs risk assessments, and provides a trust center where customers can see a company’s security posture. AI features answer security questionnaires, map controls across frameworks, and help prioritize remediation, saving time for small security teams.

item.title: Virtuous
item.description:
Virtuous aims to help nonprofits treat donors as individuals. Its CRM unifies donor records, giving history, communications, and activity from the website and email, and uses scoring to show which supporters are likely to give again or give more. Fundraisers use the data to plan outreach and prioritize relationships, rather than sending the same message to everyone.

Additional tools expand the system. Marketing automation builds journeys and email campaigns triggered by donor behavior, online giving forms and text-to-give accept gifts, and volunteer management tracks service. Newer AI features help write appeals, summarize donor histories, and recommend next steps for each supporter, and an analytics layer shows campaign performance.

item.title: Wanderlog
item.description:
Wanderlog combines a travel notebook with a map. You create a trip, add places such as hotels, restaurants, and attractions, and arrange them by day. The app shows everything on a map with travel times between stops, and can optimize the order to reduce backtracking. It imports reservations from your email, tracks expenses, and works offline on mobile apps, which is handy while traveling.

Collaboration is a main feature. Friends and family can edit the same itinerary at once, vote on places, and share notes and budgets. AI tools suggest destinations and activities, generate draft itineraries from a few preferences, and recommend nearby places based on reviews and guides. A catalog of lists and guides provides inspiration for popular destinations.

item.title: Weglot
item.description:
Weglot lets a site add languages without rebuilding it. You install a plugin or add a snippet, Weglot finds the text on your pages, translates it with machine translation, and creates versions of the site in the languages you choose. It also adds a language switcher and handles the technical parts of international SEO such as hreflang tags and translated URLs.

Quality control happens in a dashboard. You can edit any translation, use a glossary to keep brand terms the same, and order professional translations through partners for key pages. Translations are stored and reused, and visual editing lets you fix text in the context of the page. AI features improve consistency, and it works with many popular platforms.

item.title: Whoop
item.description: WHOOP is a screenless wearable worn on the wrist or in apparel. It records heart rate, heart rate variability, skin temperature, blood oxygen, and movement around the clock, and its app turns that into daily scores for recovery, strain, and sleep. The idea is to show how prepared your body is to train hard or rest, and to give athletes and health-conscious people a sense of how habits like alcohol or late nights affect them.

item.title: Wiz
item.description: Wiz became one of the fastest-growing security companies by making cloud risk easier to see. It connects to cloud accounts through APIs and snapshots, without installing agents on every machine, and builds a graph of resources, identities, networks, and data. From that graph it finds problems such as exposed storage, over-permissive roles, unpatched software, and secrets in code, and it shows how they could be chained together into an attack path to something valuable.

item.title: 6sense
item.description:
6sense helps B2B teams find buyers who are not yet raising their hands. It collects signals from many sources, such as web visits, content consumption, and third-party research activity, identifies the companies behind the anonymous traffic, and uses machine learning to predict which accounts are in the market and at what stage of the buying journey. Teams see lists of target accounts ranked by readiness to buy.

The platform acts on those insights. Marketing can run advertising aimed at accounts showing interest, sales gets alerts when key accounts spike in activity, and workflows enroll contacts in email sequences. AI agents help with outreach and qualification, and integrations with CRMs and marketing automation tools keep data in sync. Predictions rely on data from many sources, so they are probabilistic.

item.title: Ada
item.description: Ada helps companies handle customer support questions without adding staff. Its AI agent answers inquiries on websites, in apps, and over messaging channels by drawing on a company’s knowledge base and systems, and it can take actions such as checking an order, changing an address, or processing a return by connecting to back-end tools. When a request is too complex or sensitive, it hands the conversation to a human agent with context.

item.title: Adalo
item.description:
Adalo lets people without programming skills build mobile apps. You design screens with a drag-and-drop editor, add components such as lists, forms, and buttons, set up a database for your data, and define what happens when users interact. It handles user accounts, payments, and push notifications, and produces apps that can be published to the Apple App Store and Google Play, as well as web apps.

AI features speed up the first draft: you can describe an app and have the builder generate screens and data structures, then refine them manually. A marketplace of components and integrations extends functionality, and connections to external databases and APIs allow more complex apps. Typical projects include community directories, booking apps, marketplaces, internal tools, and simple social apps.

item.title: Agno
item.description:
Agno, formerly called Phidata, aims to make agent building straightforward and fast. A developer defines an agent in a few lines: choose a model, give it instructions and tools, and optionally attach memory and a knowledge base. Agents can search the web, query databases, call APIs, and work with text, images, and audio. Multiple agents can be combined into teams that collaborate on complex tasks.

The framework emphasizes performance and production use. It is designed to start agents quickly and use little memory, which helps when many run at once, and it includes features such as session storage, retrieval from vector databases, structured outputs, and reasoning steps. AgentOS, a runtime layer, lets teams serve agents through an API with a control interface, and monitoring tools show runs and performance.

item.title: Airtable
item.description: Airtable looks like a spreadsheet but behaves like a database. Records live in tables with typed fields such as dates, attachments, checkboxes, and links to records in other tables, which allows relationships that spreadsheets cannot handle. The same data can be shown as a grid, kanban board, calendar, gallery, or timeline, and filters and groups tailor each view. It’s used for content calendars, product roadmaps, CRM, event planning, and operations.

item.title: AIVE
item.description:
AIVE was described as a video enhancement service that used deep-learning super-resolution to sharpen detail, reduce noise, and raise the resolution of existing footage. That kind of tool takes low-resolution or damaged video, such as old family tapes, archival film, or compressed web clips, and reconstructs a clearer version. The idea is sound, and a number of products do it well.

The domain listed for AIVE no longer hosts a video enhancement tool. It now shows an unrelated media site, and searches turn up no active product of this name with the features described. A separate company called Aive makes a platform for automating video post-production for brands, which is a different kind of product. Because the original service cannot be confirmed, this entry should not be used as a recommendation.

item.title: AlphaSense
item.description: AlphaSense is a search engine for business information. Analysts, investors, and strategy teams use it to find what companies and experts are saying across a large body of documents: earnings call transcripts, SEC filings, broker and industry research, press releases, news, and expert call transcripts. Its search understands financial language, so a query for supply chain risk or pricing pressure returns relevant passages instead of just keyword matches, with highlights and context.

item.title: Amplitude AI
item.description: Amplitude helps product teams see what users actually do. You instrument your app or website to send events, such as signing up, clicking a button, or finishing a purchase, and Amplitude turns them into funnels, retention curves, user paths, and cohorts. These views answer questions like where new users drop off and which features bring people back. It is used by product managers, designers, and data analysts at companies from startups to large enterprises.

item.title: Anima
item.description:
Anima sits between designers and developers. A designer working in Figma, Sketch, or Adobe XD installs the plugin, and the tool turns the design into code that uses real layout rules, so pages respond to different screen sizes. Developers receive a starting point for components in frameworks like React and Vue.

It also helps with prototypes. Designers can add interactions and publish a clickable prototype for user testing, and Anima’s AI features generate designs and code from text prompts or from existing screens. Teams use it to cut the time between an approved design and a working front end.

item.title: Animaker
item.description:
Animaker lets people without animation skills make animated videos. You choose a template or start from scratch, add characters, props, backgrounds, and text, and arrange them on a timeline. A character builder customizes avatars with facial expressions and actions, and ready-made assets cover business, education, and storytelling scenes. It also supports whiteboard-style videos, infographic videos, and live-action editing, with exports up to 4K.

AI tools shorten the production steps. Text-to-animation turns a script into a rough animated scene, voiceover tools generate narration in many voices and languages, and translation and auto-subtitle features help localize videos. Teams use it for training videos, product explainers, school lessons, social media clips, and internal communications, where hiring an animation studio would be too costly.

item.title: Anyword
item.description:
Anyword’s distinguishing feature is its performance prediction. When you ask for ad copy or an email subject line, the platform generates several versions and gives each a predicted score, based on models trained on large amounts of marketing performance data, along with an estimate for different audiences. The idea is to help marketers choose which copy to test or publish instead of guessing.

It works across typical marketing needs: ad copy for social and search, email campaigns, landing pages, blog content, and product descriptions. Brand voice settings and a knowledge base keep outputs consistent with a company’s tone and facts. Teams can integrate it with ad platforms and other tools, and an analytics layer connects the predictions with actual results. Targeting options adapt copy to specific audience segments.

item.title: Artbreeder
item.description: Artbreeder began with an unusual idea: instead of typing a prompt, you start with existing images and breed them together, like mixing genes. Each image has sliders for traits, such as age, expression, or lighting for a portrait, so you can nudge it in a direction and save the results. Children of images can be crossed again, which lets a visual idea evolve step by step. The community shares images that others can remix.

item.title: Asana
item.description:
Asana helps teams keep track of who is doing what by when. Work is organized into projects and tasks, viewable as lists, boards, timelines, or calendars, with dependencies, owners, due dates, and custom fields. Goals connect daily tasks to company objectives, and portfolios give leaders an overview of many projects.

AI features reduce the overhead of managing work. They can generate project plans from a description, summarize updates and conversations, answer questions about project status, and spot risks to deadlines. Asana has also introduced AI teammates that can be assigned work and operate inside projects, with controls to keep humans in charge. Automations handle routing and reminders.

item.title: Asana
item.description: Asana organizes work as tasks inside projects. Each task has an owner, a due date, and a place in a larger plan, and the same project can be viewed as a list, a kanban board, a timeline, or a calendar. Teams use it for campaign planning, product launches, client work, and operations requests, anywhere several people need to see who is doing what and by when. Portfolios and Goals roll individual projects up into a view managers can read without opening every one.

item.title: Avoma
item.description: Avoma joins sales, customer success, and recruiting meetings on Zoom, Google Meet, and Teams, then records and transcribes them and produces notes organized by meeting type. Instead of a generic summary, it uses templates suited to the call, such as a discovery call or a customer check-in, and pulls out action items, objections, and next steps. Notes and key fields can be pushed into CRMs like Salesforce and HubSpot, which saves reps from doing data entry after every call.

item.title: BambooHR
item.description:
BambooHR is built for companies without a large HR department. It keeps employee information in one place, tracks time off, handles onboarding checklists and documents, and offers an employee self-service portal. Applicant tracking helps with hiring, performance tools support reviews and goals, and payroll and benefits administration are available for U.S. customers. Reporting shows headcount, turnover, and other metrics.

The product is known for being easy to use, with a friendly interface and quick setup. AI features help HR teams with tasks such as drafting job descriptions and performance review language, summarizing feedback, and answering employee questions using company policies. Integrations connect with accounting, benefits, and productivity tools, and an app marketplace extends the platform.

item.title: Beautiful.ai
item.description:
Beautiful.ai tackles a common complaint about PowerPoint: you spend more time fiddling with alignment than thinking about content. Its slides are built from smart templates that rearrange themselves when you add or remove text, images, or chart elements, so the design stays clean. Rules keep spacing, fonts, and colors consistent, and a library of layouts covers timelines, comparisons, charts, team slides, and more.

AI features help create the first draft. You can describe a presentation, or paste in notes, and it generates an outline and slides in the app’s format, which you then edit. Teams can store brand colors, fonts, and logos in a shared theme, share slide libraries, and collaborate on decks with comments. Presentations can be exported to PowerPoint or PDF, or shared by link with view analytics.

item.title: BenevolentAI
item.description:
BenevolentAI built a platform that gathers large amounts of biomedical information, including scientific literature, clinical data, and experimental results, into a knowledge graph that connects diseases, genes, proteins, and drugs. Machine learning explores the graph to suggest which biological targets might be worth pursuing for a given disease and which molecules might act on them, aiming to speed up the early stages of drug discovery.

The company gained attention when its system flagged baricitinib, an existing drug, as a possible treatment for COVID-19, which was later supported by clinical trials. It has formed partnerships with large pharmaceutical firms and developed its own programs. The platform combines AI with scientists who validate predictions in the lab.

item.title: Bing Chat
item.description: Bing Chat was Microsoft’s first big move into AI-assisted search. It put a conversational assistant next to the Bing search box, so you could ask a question and get a written answer with links to sources instead of scanning a page of results. Microsoft later renamed and expanded it as Copilot, and the assistant now works across the web, in the Edge browser, in Windows, and in standalone mobile and desktop apps.

item.title: Biteable
item.description:
Biteable makes video creation approachable for non-editors. Users pick a template for something like a company announcement, training clip, or social promo, and replace text, images, and footage scene by scene. Brand settings keep colors, fonts, and logos consistent across a team.

AI features accelerate the first draft. A script or prompt can generate a sequence of scenes with suggested visuals, text can be turned into narration, and videos can be resized for formats such as vertical social posts and widescreen. Collaboration features let teammates review and edit, and analytics show how videos perform.

item.title: Bito AI
item.description:
Bito started as a chat and code-completion assistant inside VS Code and JetBrains IDEs and as a command-line tool. You could ask it to explain a function, write unit tests, find bugs, or generate documentation, and it used a model of your choice for the answers. Its early appeal was practical convenience: reusable prompts for common tasks and support for working with context from your project.

The product has increasingly centered on code review. The AI Code Review Agent examines pull requests on GitHub, GitLab, and Bitbucket, leaves comments on issues such as bugs, security problems, and style violations, and summarizes the change for reviewers. It builds a model of the codebase so its feedback accounts for how the changed code fits with the rest, which helps reduce noisy comments. Teams use it to speed up reviews and catch issues earlier.

item.title: Brandwatch
item.description:
Brandwatch is used by marketing, communications, and research teams to understand what people say online. It collects posts and mentions from social networks, news sites, forums, blogs, and reviews, and lets analysts build searches to track a brand, a competitor, a campaign, or a topic. Dashboards show volume over time, sentiment, demographics, top influencers, and emerging themes, which helps with campaign measurement, crisis monitoring, and product feedback.

AI plays a role in making sense of the data. Language models classify sentiment and topics, group conversations into themes, summarize large sets of posts, and answer questions about the findings in natural language. Image recognition finds logos in pictures posted without any text. Alerts warn teams when mentions spike, and the social management side supports publishing and responding to messages from one place.

item.title: Casetext
item.description: Casetext began as a community site where lawyers annotated and shared case law, then grew into a legal research service with tools such as a brief-checking feature called Parallel Search, which found relevant cases using natural language. It was among the first legal technology companies to build on large language models, and its CoCounsel assistant could review documents, summarize depositions, draft research memos, and help prepare contract analyses with citations to sources.

item.title: Causal
item.description:
Causal was created for finance teams that outgrew spreadsheets. Users build models from blocks that represent revenue, headcount, and costs, link them to data from accounting and CRM systems, and see results as charts and dashboards. The structure makes models easier to follow and share than a sprawling workbook.

Scenario planning is a core strength. Teams can change assumptions, such as hiring plans or pricing, and compare outcomes side by side, then present the results to executives and investors. AI features help create models from descriptions and explain changes in numbers.

item.title: CB Insights
item.description:
CB Insights tracks the innovation economy. Its database covers private companies, funding rounds, investors, acquisitions, patents, and news, and analysts and algorithms turn that into research on market trends. Corporate strategy teams, investors, and consultants use it to understand which sectors are growing and who the major players are.

Features include company profiles, market maps, forecasts of company outcomes, and an AI assistant that answers questions from the platform’s data and research. Alerts and newsletters keep subscribers up to date, and tools support building lists of companies matching specific criteria.

item.title: ChatGPT Canvas
item.description:
Canvas changes how you work with ChatGPT on longer projects. When a request involves writing a document or code, ChatGPT can open a separate pane next to the conversation, where the text or code appears as an editable file. You can edit it directly, highlight a passage and ask ChatGPT to change just that part, and see changes without the whole response being regenerated.

For writing, shortcuts adjust the length, reading level, and tone, add polish or emojis, and suggest edits inline like a collaborator leaving comments. For coding, Canvas helps review code, add comments and logs, fix bugs, and port a project to another language, and it can run some code, such as Python, within the interface. Version history lets you go back to earlier drafts.

item.title: Chorus.ai
item.description:
Chorus records sales calls and video meetings and turns them into searchable transcripts. Managers can look through conversations to see what customers say about price, competitors, or objections, instead of relying on reps’ summaries. The tool tags topics, tracks talk time and question patterns, and highlights key moments, which makes it faster to review a call than to listen to the whole recording.

The AI layer analyzes patterns across many conversations. It can surface deals that appear to be at risk, detect competitor mentions, summarize each call, and suggest next steps. Coaching features let managers share clips, give feedback, and compare reps against top performers. Integrations with Salesforce and other CRMs send call data and notes into the customer record so reps spend less time on updates.

item.title: Claap
item.description: Claap targets teams that want fewer live meetings. You can record your screen and camera as a short video, share a link, and let colleagues watch and respond on their own time. The same tool records live calls on Zoom, Google Meet, and Teams, then stores them with a transcript. Comments and reactions can be attached to specific moments, so feedback stays tied to the part of the video it refers to.

item.title: Claude
item.description: Claude is the AI assistant from Anthropic, a company that focuses on AI safety research. It comes in a few model tiers, with smaller and faster models for quick tasks and larger ones for harder reasoning and coding. People tend to pick it for writing that sounds less formulaic, careful reading of long documents, and code. It is also more willing than some competitors to say it is unsure or to disagree with you, which some users value and others find less accommodating.

item.title: Clickup
item.description: ClickUp tries to be a single home for everything a team does. At its center are tasks that can be shown as lists, boards, calendars, Gantt charts, or timelines, and each task can have subtasks, custom fields, dependencies, and checklists. Around that sit docs, wikis, whiteboards, forms, dashboards, goals, and built-in chat. Teams use it for software sprints, marketing calendars, client projects, and operations, and the same workspace can be shaped differently for each department.

item.title: Clockwise
item.description:
Clockwise worked inside Google Calendar and Slack to protect time for deep work. It looked at a team’s calendars, moved flexible meetings, and combined scattered gaps into longer blocks, aiming to cut the constant switching between tasks that fragments a workday. It could also find meeting times that worked for groups.

The product grew a following among engineering and product teams, and added AI scheduling features and a way to plan work around priorities. The company ended the service and the team joined Salesforce, where they work on AI agents. The product itself did not move over.

item.title: Coda AI
item.description:
Coda reimagines the document as something that can behave like an app. A Coda doc can contain text, tables, buttons, and automations, so a team can build a project tracker, a wiki, a CRM, or a planning tool in the same document where they write. Formulas, similar to those in spreadsheets, connect data across the doc, and Packs integrate with outside services such as Slack, Jira, and Google Calendar.

AI features run through the platform. Coda AI can summarize documents, draft text, fill table columns with generated content, categorize and extract information, and answer questions about the contents of a doc. AI blocks and agents can be placed in workflows to automate tasks. The company joined Grammarly, which has taken the name Superhuman, and its tools are being combined with Grammarly’s writing assistant and the Superhuman email app.

item.title: CodeRabbit
item.description:
CodeRabbit acts as a first reviewer. When a developer opens a pull request, it reads the diff along with surrounding code, writes a summary of the change, and leaves comments on potential bugs, missing tests, security concerns, and style. Developers can reply to its comments and ask it to explain or fix things, so the review becomes a conversation.

Configuration lets teams set rules and instructions in plain language so the review follows their standards. It learns from feedback, and can run linters and security scanners as part of the review. IDE and command line versions bring review earlier, before a pull request is opened.

item.title: CodeRabbit
item.description:
CodeRabbit gives every pull request a quick first review. When a developer opens a pull request, it summarizes the change, walks through the files, and leaves comments on potential bugs, security problems, performance concerns, and deviations from team conventions. It can also suggest fixes that developers apply with a click and answer questions in the comments, acting like a tireless reviewer available at any hour.

It improves with use. CodeRabbit learns from how reviewers respond to its suggestions and from guidelines the team defines, so comments become more relevant over time. It runs linters and security scanners as part of its review, can use context from the wider codebase, and has an IDE and command-line version for reviewing before code is pushed. It integrates with issue trackers to check that changes match requirements.

item.title: Codiga
item.description:
Codiga offered real-time code analysis inside the editor. Its plugins for VS Code, JetBrains IDEs, and other tools scanned code as you typed for security vulnerabilities, bugs, and violations of coding standards, and a rules engine let teams write their own checks. It also provided a code snippet assistant and, later, AI-based suggestions, and integrated with Git platforms to review pull requests automatically.

The company was acquired by Datadog, which wanted to bring code analysis into its observability and security platform. Codiga’s standalone products were shut down shortly afterward, with refunds for paid subscribers, and the team joined Datadog. The static analysis engine and its rules now underpin Datadog Code Security, and the analyzer is available as open source.

item.title: Colossyan
item.description: Colossyan targets companies that need a lot of video for learning and communication but do not want to film each one. You type or paste a script, or upload a document or slides and have it converted, choose an AI presenter and voice, and Colossyan produces a video. Editing works like slides, with scenes, text, images, and screen recordings, and changing the script means regenerating the video instead of reshooting.

item.title: Conversica
item.description:
Conversica automates the follow-up that sales teams often drop. When a lead comes in, the AI assistant sends personalized messages, reads replies, answers questions, and tries to book a meeting. If a prospect does not respond, it continues with a sequence of nudges, which keeps leads from going cold.

The assistants are used in industries such as automotive, education, software, and financial services, where large volumes of inquiries arrive. Conversation data flows into the CRM, so salespeople see which leads are qualified and what was said. The company has added generative AI to make conversations more natural.

item.title: Copy.ai
item.description:
Copy.ai began as one of the first popular AI copywriting tools. Users choose a template or write a prompt, and the tool generates headlines, product descriptions, email sequences, ads, and social captions. A brand voice feature helps keep the tone consistent.

The product later shifted toward workflows for go-to-market teams. Marketers and sales teams can chain steps that research accounts, draft outreach, and produce content at scale, using multiple language models. Chat and knowledge features let the AI draw on company information.

item.title: Copy.ai
item.description:
Copy.ai started in the first wave of AI writing tools. You picked a template, such as a product description, email, or social caption, answered a few prompts, and got several drafts to edit. It was popular with marketers and small businesses who needed a lot of copy quickly. Over time it moved away from one-off text generation and toward automating sales and marketing processes.

Its later product centered on workflows. A team could chain steps together, for example researching an account, pulling in data, drafting outreach, and writing a CRM update, and let AI agents run the sequence on a schedule or trigger. A data layer called Tables kept the inputs organized, and the aim was to replace manual go-to-market busywork with repeatable automations rather than just generating paragraphs.

item.title: Crimson Hexagon
item.description: Crimson Hexagon was a consumer insights company that analyzed social media, news, forums, and review data at large scale. It was known for its ForSight platform and for machine learning that classified posts by sentiment and topic with accuracy that researchers could tune. Market researchers, agencies, and brands used it to track what people said about products and campaigns, and its archive of historical social data was a draw for studying trends over time.

item.title: Crunchbase
item.description:
Crunchbase is a widely used database about startups and private companies. Users look up a company to see its founders, funding history, investors, and news, or search for companies by industry, location, and stage. Investors, salespeople, and researchers use it to find targets and track activity.

Predictive features add forward-looking signals. AI models estimate which companies are likely to raise money, grow, or be acquired, and alerts notify users when relevant events happen. Lists and integrations send data into CRMs for prospecting.

item.title: Culture Amp
item.description:
Culture Amp helps companies listen to employees. HR teams run engagement, onboarding, and exit surveys, analyze the results by team and demographic group, and compare against benchmarks from other organizations. Dashboards point out areas where scores are low and what drives them.

The platform also covers performance and development, with review cycles, goal tracking, and feedback. AI helps by summarizing open-ended comments into themes, drafting review text, and recommending actions to managers, which saves analysts days of reading. An assistant answers questions about results.

item.title: DataRobot
item.description:
DataRobot pioneered automated machine learning. A data team uploads a dataset, and the platform tries many algorithms and feature combinations, ranks them, and explains the best models, which lowers the barrier to building predictive models for tasks such as churn, demand, and risk. It also handles deployment and monitoring, tracking model accuracy and drift once models are live.

The company has pivoted toward generative AI and agents. Its platform now helps companies build and run AI agents and applications, with governance features such as documentation, bias checks, approvals, and audit trails that matter in industries such as banking, insurance, and healthcare. It can run in the cloud or on a company’s own infrastructure and integrates with major cloud providers and data platforms.

item.title: Dify
item.description: Dify gives teams a visual way to build AI applications without writing everything from scratch. In its workflow editor, you connect blocks for models, prompts, knowledge retrieval, code, conditions, and tool calls to create chatbots, agents, and automations. Knowledge pipelines ingest documents, split and index them, and let the application answer questions from your own data. You can test and debug each run, then publish the app as a web interface or API.

item.title: Dimensions
item.description:
Dimensions connects different kinds of research outputs. Instead of searching only for papers, users can see how a grant led to publications, which patents cite a study, and whether a trial or policy document refers to it. The linked structure helps trace the path from funding to impact.

Institutions, funders, and researchers use it for several purposes. Universities benchmark their output, funders track results of the grants they award, and companies look for experts and emerging fields. AI features summarize results, help with literature searches, and surface connections, and APIs let organizations pull data into their own systems.

item.title: Eraser
item.description:
Eraser is built around engineers’ diagrams. Users can write diagrams as code in a simple syntax, draw them visually, or describe them in plain language and let AI generate the first version. The result stays editable, with a clean style that looks good in documentation and design reviews.

The product also supports documents. Eraser has a docs editor where diagrams sit alongside text for design documents and runbooks, and integrations with GitHub allow diagrams to be generated from a repository and kept in sync. Teams share and comment on documents in real time.

item.title: Fathom
item.description: Fathom is known for making meeting notes free. It joins your Zoom, Google Meet, or Microsoft Teams calls, records them, and creates a transcript in real time. You can highlight important moments during the call with a click, and within seconds of the meeting ending, it produces a summary with decisions, action items, and key points that you can share. The free plan includes unlimited recordings and transcripts, which set it apart from competitors that cap free use.

item.title: Fellow
item.description:
Fellow helps teams run better meetings. Before a meeting, it provides shared agendas and templates for one-on-ones, team meetings, and client calls. During the meeting, an AI notetaker records and transcribes, capturing decisions and action items automatically. Afterward, summaries and tasks are sent to attendees.

The platform keeps a record of conversations over time, which suits managers who run recurring one-on-ones. Integrations connect with calendars, Slack, Zoom, Teams, and project tools. AI features answer questions across past meetings and draft follow-up messages. Feedback tools support regular check-ins and performance conversations.

item.title: Figma
item.description: Figma is where a lot of software gets designed before anyone writes code. It runs in the browser, so designers, product managers, engineers, and writers can open the same file at once, leave comments, and watch changes appear live. That ended the old habit of emailing design files back and forth. Its core strengths are vector editing, Auto Layout for components that resize correctly, and shared libraries that keep colors, type, and buttons consistent across a whole product.

item.title: Fireflies.ai
item.description: Fireflies sends a bot into your meetings, usually named Fred, that records the call and creates a transcript with speaker labels. After the meeting, it produces a summary with action items and key topics, and posts them where your team works. Every meeting becomes searchable text, so you can find what a customer said last month or when a decision was made. It supports dozens of languages and works with the main video call platforms and uploaded recordings.

item.title: FlutterFlow
item.description: FlutterFlow combines the speed of a visual builder with real code. You design screens by dragging widgets, define logic with a visual action editor, and connect to backends such as Firebase, Supabase, or any API. Because it generates Flutter code, apps run natively on iOS and Android and also on the web, and you can export the code to continue development in a standard IDE, which avoids the lock-in of many no-code tools.

item.title: Forta
item.description:
Forta provides security monitoring for blockchain applications. Independent developers write detection bots that scan transactions and state changes across networks, looking for patterns that signal attacks, such as sudden fund movements or unusual contract calls. Bots publish alerts to the network, which protocols and users can subscribe to.

Machine learning models are used for some detections, such as spotting scams or anomalies. Protocols use Forta alerts to trigger their own responses, such as pausing contracts. A marketplace of bots covers many threat types and chains, and its token supports staking and rewards for bot operators.

item.title: Frase
item.description:
Frase helps content teams plan and write articles that can rank. Enter a keyword, and Frase analyzes the top search results to show the topics, questions, and headings they cover and the terms they use, then creates a brief that guides a writer. As you draft, a score shows how well your article covers the topic compared with competitors, and suggestions help fill gaps.

AI features support writing and optimization. Frase can generate outlines and drafts, answer questions drawn from search data, and update existing articles to improve their performance. Newer tools track visibility in AI-generated answers from assistants and search engines, reflecting the shift in how people find information, and an agent can handle parts of the content workflow. Integrations with Google Search Console and publishing tools connect data to action.

item.title: Freshdesk
item.description: Freshdesk gives support teams a single place to handle customer requests. Messages from email, a web form, live chat, phone, and channels like WhatsApp, Messenger, and Instagram land in a shared inbox as tickets that can be assigned, tagged, prioritized, and tracked against service-level targets. A knowledge base lets customers find answers on their own, and a customer portal shows the status of their requests. It is used by companies from small startups to large support organizations.

item.title: Gemini in Workspace
item.description:
Gemini in Workspace brings Google’s models into the apps people use at work. In Gmail, it drafts replies and summarizes long threads. In Docs, it writes, rewrites, and proofreads, and can pull in information from files and email. In Sheets, it helps create formulas, tables, and analysis. In Slides, it generates slides and images, and in Meet it takes notes and summarizes.

A side panel gives a chat assistant that can search across a user’s Drive, Gmail, and Calendar, and answer questions using that content. Organizations can control access, and Google states that business data is not used to train models without permission. Newer features include agents and tools such as NotebookLM for deeper source work.

item.title: Glean
item.description:
Glean addresses the problem that company knowledge lives in dozens of separate tools. It connects to those systems through hundreds of connectors, builds an index of documents, messages, tickets, and other content, and lets employees search across everything from one box. Crucially, it mirrors the permissions of the source systems, so a person only sees results they would already have access to.

On top of search, Glean provides an AI assistant that answers questions in natural language using company information, with citations to the underlying sources. Employees ask things like how a process works, what was decided in a project, or what the latest customer feedback says, and receive a synthesized answer. Glean Agents let teams build automations and agents that take actions in connected apps, and a builder allows non-engineers to create them. Companies can choose among language models from several providers.

item.title: Glide
item.description:
Glide lets people build working apps from a spreadsheet. You connect a sheet or a table, and Glide generates an interface with lists, detail pages, forms, and actions, which you can customize with a visual editor. Because the data lives in a familiar place, small business owners and operations teams can create apps for inventory, field reports, event check-ins, and customer portals without writing code.

The platform has added more advanced features over time. Users can set up roles and permissions, run workflows that send emails or update records, and connect to services through integrations. AI features can generate apps from a description, extract data from images and documents, and add AI-powered actions such as summarizing or categorizing. Glide’s own database supports larger datasets than a typical spreadsheet.

item.title: Grain
item.description:
Grain records meetings on Zoom, Google Meet, Microsoft Teams, and other platforms and turns them into transcripts, summaries, and short clips. Its clip feature is a distinguishing idea: instead of sharing a whole recording, you highlight a moment, such as a customer’s feedback or a question about pricing, and share just that clip with colleagues. This makes customer insights easier to spread across product, marketing, and leadership.

AI features produce structured notes from each meeting using templates, such as discovery calls or customer interviews, and answer questions across a library of recordings. Integrations send notes and fields to Salesforce, HubSpot, Notion, and Slack, which cuts manual updates. A desktop capture option can record meetings without a visible bot joining the call, which some teams prefer for external meetings.

item.title: Grammarly
item.description:
Grammarly started as a grammar checker and became the writing helper people keep installed everywhere. A browser extension, desktop app, mobile keyboard, and plugins for Word and Google Docs underline mistakes in emails, messages, and documents as you type. It catches typos and grammar errors, flags wordy or unclear sentences, and suggests a different tone, such as more confident or more friendly. A free version covers the basics.

Generative AI is built into the same flow. You can ask it to rewrite a paragraph, shorten a message, draft a reply to an email, or brainstorm ideas from a prompt. AI agents focus on particular jobs, such as giving feedback on a student paper, predicting how a reader might respond, or checking citations. Paid tiers add full-sentence rewrites, tone detection, plagiarism checking, and an AI detector, and business plans add style guides, brand tone, and analytics for teams.

item.title: H2O.ai
item.description:
H2O.ai built its reputation on open-source machine learning. H2O-3 is a widely used library for training models on large datasets, with an AutoML feature that tries many algorithms and picks the best. The company’s commercial Driverless AI automated feature engineering and model building for business users, and its tools have been used in finance, insurance, and healthcare.

More recently, H2O.ai has focused on generative AI. H2O LLM Studio lets teams fine-tune language models without much code, h2oGPT is an open-source project for chatting with documents, and its enterprise platform lets companies deploy private assistants and agents, including on-premises or in air-gapped environments. It has also released small language models designed to run efficiently.

item.title: Happy Scribe
item.description:
Happy Scribe converts speech into text. You upload an audio or video file, or connect a source like Zoom or YouTube, and receive a transcript in minutes with speaker labels and timestamps. It supports many languages and dialects, which suits journalists, researchers, podcasters, and companies that work in several markets. A browser editor lets you listen while you correct the text.

Subtitling is a major use. The service can generate subtitles and captions for videos, translate them into other languages, and export in standard formats for YouTube, Vimeo, and video editors. For cases where accuracy matters more, such as legal or broadcast work, you can order human-made transcripts and subtitles, which cost more and take longer. An API and integrations connect it to workflows.

item.title: Height
item.description: Height set out to make project management less manual. It was a task and project tracker with a clean interface, and its main idea was that AI should do routine upkeep: sorting incoming requests, writing and updating subtasks, assigning work, and keeping descriptions consistent. Teams used it as a lighter alternative to Jira with more automation, and the product drew fans among startups for its design and its early AI features.

item.title: Helpshift
item.description:
Helpshift places support inside the app. Users reach help from a screen in a game or mobile product, without leaving to email, and conversations carry context about the device, account, and recent activity. Agents see this information and respond in the same thread.

AI reduces the load. Intent detection reads messages, classifies the issue, and routes it to the right team, while chatbots answer common questions and collect details before a human steps in. A knowledge base and automation tools support self-service, and analytics track satisfaction and resolution times.

item.title: Hootsuite
item.description:
Hootsuite is one of the oldest social media management tools. Teams connect accounts for networks such as Instagram, Facebook, LinkedIn, X, TikTok, and YouTube, plan content on a calendar, schedule posts, and respond to comments and messages in a shared inbox. Approval workflows suit larger organizations.

Listening and analytics tools track brand mentions and compare performance across channels. OwlyWriter, the AI assistant, helps write captions, suggest ideas, and repurpose content. Advertising management and employee advocacy products extend the suite for enterprises.

item.title: Hotjar AI
item.description:
Hotjar helps teams see what visitors actually do on a site. Heatmaps show where people click, move, and scroll, session recordings replay individual visits, and on-page surveys and feedback widgets ask visitors what they think. Together they reveal confusing layouts, broken elements, and places where people give up, which complements numbers from analytics tools that show what happened but not why.

AI cuts down the time it takes to find insights. Instead of watching hundreds of recordings, teams can get automatic summaries of sessions, highlights of common frustrations, and analysis of open-ended survey responses grouped into themes. This helps designers, product managers, and marketers decide what to fix first. Funnels and trends let you see where users drop out, and integrations send findings to tools like Slack, Jira, and HubSpot.

item.title: Hunter
item.description: Hunter is a tool for finding contact details for business outreach. A Domain Search shows the email addresses associated with a company along with the sources where they were found, and the email pattern the company uses. An Email Finder takes a person’s name and company and returns the most likely address with a confidence score. Email Verifier checks whether an address is valid and likely to deliver, which reduces bounces.

item.title: InVideo
item.description:
InVideo targets creators and marketers who need many videos fast. In InVideo AI, you describe the video you want, such as a product explainer, a faceless YouTube video, or a social ad, and it writes a script, selects stock clips, adds a voiceover and music, and assembles it. You can then give plain-language instructions to change scenes, tone, or length, which makes iteration quick for people without editing skills.

The traditional editor remains for more control. It provides templates, a timeline, text and effects, and a large stock library, and it can turn blog posts and scripts into videos. Voice features include text-to-speech in many languages and voice cloning, and recent versions have added AI-generated video clips and avatars alongside stock footage. Exports are available in formats for different social platforms.

item.title: InVision
item.description:
InVision was one of the leading prototyping and design collaboration tools of the 2010s. Designers uploaded static screens, linked them into clickable prototypes, and shared them with stakeholders for feedback. It also offered a design system manager and, later, Freehand, a collaborative whiteboard.

As Figma and other tools took over design work, InVision’s usage declined, and the company announced it would close its products. Teams moved their work to other platforms, and exports were offered for a period before shutdown.

item.title: Jasper
item.description:
For copywriting, Jasper offers more structure than a general chatbot. Marketers choose a format such as a Facebook ad, a product description, a landing page section, or an email sequence, supply the details, and get multiple options in their brand’s voice. The Brand Voice feature learns tone and style from examples, and a company knowledge base provides facts about products and audiences so the copy uses accurate claims.

Collaboration features suit teams. Shared templates and style guides keep writers consistent, and campaigns can be planned in one place with copy, images, and variations for different channels. An editor helps refine text, change tone, and check for plagiarism. Newer agent features help automate common marketing tasks, such as producing a set of assets from a brief.

item.title: Jasper
item.description:
As a marketing platform, Jasper aims to speed up the full path from a brief to a finished campaign. Marketers define their brand voice, audience, and product information once, then generate blog posts, social posts, ads, emails, and landing pages that follow those guidelines. Campaign tools help plan content around a launch, adapt messages for each channel, and keep versions organized.

The latest versions emphasize agents and workflows. Specialized agents handle tasks such as researching a topic, creating a content calendar, repurposing a webinar into several assets, and optimizing copy for search. Integrations connect with tools such as Google Docs, Webflow, and HubSpot, and analytics features tie content to performance. Controls let enterprises govern who can use what and ensure compliance with brand rules.

item.title: Jasper
item.description: Jasper was one of the first dedicated AI writing products and has focused on marketing teams that need a lot of on-brand content. You describe what you need, such as a product launch email or a set of ad variations, and it drafts the copy using your guidelines. Brand Voice learns your tone from sample content, and a knowledge base stores product details, audiences, and approved messaging, so output needs fewer corrections.

item.title: Juro
item.description:
Juro puts the contract workflow in a browser editor. Sales and business teams generate contracts from approved templates, negotiate with counterparties in the same document, collect signatures, and store the result in a searchable repository. Legal sets the rules and approvals, so routine deals move without a lawyer.

AI is part of the product. It can draft clauses from a plain-English description, review third-party paper against a company’s positions, summarize agreements, and answer questions about the contract portfolio. Integrations with CRMs and messaging tools keep the process connected to sales.

item.title: Kaedim
item.description:
Kaedim addresses a slow stage in game and digital content production: turning concept art into 3D assets. You upload an image of a character, prop, or environment piece, and Kaedim produces a 3D model that matches it. The aim is to give artists a solid starting point they can refine, which cuts down the days of modeling work needed for each asset.

The service has been known for mixing machine learning with human review. Models go through checks by 3D artists who clean up errors before they are delivered, which improves reliability compared with fully automatic generators, but may slow turnaround. Output can be downloaded in common formats and used in engines like Unity and Unreal or imported into Blender and Maya for editing. Teams use it for game props, virtual production, and prototyping product ideas.

item.title: Kapwing
item.description:
Kapwing is an online editor aimed at creators and teams who need fast, polished content. You upload video or start from a template, trim, add captions, music, and effects, and export in formats suited to platforms such as TikTok, Instagram, and YouTube. Because it runs in the browser, there is nothing to install, and collaborators can work in the same project and leave comments.

AI features are at the center of the workflow. Auto subtitles transcribe speech and add stylized captions in many languages, background removal works without a green screen, and tools can remove silences and filler words, translate and dub videos, and clean up audio. A repurposing tool cuts long videos into short clips for social media, and text-to-video and script features help generate drafts. Brand kits keep fonts and colors consistent.

item.title: Kira Systems
item.description:
Kira was one of the first widely adopted machine learning tools in legal work. It reads contracts and identifies provisions such as change of control, termination rights, assignment, and indemnification, then extracts the relevant text into a structured summary. Lawyers use it in mergers and acquisitions due diligence, where hundreds or thousands of agreements must be reviewed quickly, and in lease, finance, and compliance reviews.

Litera acquired Kira Systems and continues to develop it. The newer version adds generative AI to the original extraction models, with features like rapid clause analysis that organizes clauses across many documents. Users can start from built-in models for common provisions, train their own for specific needs, and review results in a side-by-side view that links back to the source text. Integration with Litera’s other tools connects review to drafting and transaction workflows.

item.title: Krisp
item.description: Krisp installs as a virtual microphone and speaker, so it sits between your hardware and whatever calling app you use. It removes noise before it reaches the other person: barking dogs, keyboard clatter, traffic, and other voices in the room. It can also clean incoming audio, so a participant on a bad connection or in a loud space sounds clearer to you. Because it works with Zoom, Teams, Meet, Slack, and nearly any other app, one setup covers all of them.

item.title: Lambda Labs
item.description:
Lambda started by selling deep learning workstations and servers to researchers and grew into a GPU cloud. Developers rent instances with NVIDIA GPUs, from single machines to large clusters, pre-configured with the Lambda Stack of machine learning software, so they can start training or running models quickly. Its focus on AI workloads and straightforward pricing has made it a favorite among startups, universities, and AI labs.

The company offers several ways to buy compute. On-demand instances are billed by the hour, reserved capacity provides discounted access for longer commitments, and 1-Click clusters let teams spin up multi-node setups for large training runs. Lambda also sells hardware for on-premises use, including workstations and servers, and offers inference services for deploying models.

item.title: Later
item.description:
Later started as a way to plan Instagram feeds visually. Users drag photos and videos onto a calendar, see how the grid will look, write captions, and schedule posts to go out automatically. It has since expanded to other networks, including TikTok, Pinterest, LinkedIn, Facebook, and X, with tools to manage a content library, collaborate with teammates, and track results.

Other features support social growth. A link-in-bio page lets creators send followers to multiple destinations, analytics show which posts perform best and when audiences are most active, and AI helps write captions, suggest hashtags, and repurpose content. The company also owns an influencer marketing platform, which helps brands find creators and manage campaigns.

item.title: Lattice AI
item.description:
Lattice helps companies run performance and development programs. Managers and employees complete reviews and give continuous feedback, set goals and OKRs, hold one-on-ones with shared agendas, and track growth plans. Engagement surveys measure how employees feel, and compensation tools support pay reviews and planning, while an HR information system keeps employee records.

AI is added to reduce busywork. It can help managers draft feedback and review summaries, analyze survey comments for themes, and suggest talking points for one-on-ones. Insights flag possible retention risks or teams with low engagement, and an AI assistant answers questions about company data. The company has also launched products for managing AI agents as part of the workforce, a controversial idea.

item.title: LawGeex
item.description:
LawGeex addresses the high volume of routine contracts that reach legal departments, such as NDAs and standard vendor agreements. Legal teams define a playbook that states what is acceptable in each type of clause, and LawGeex’s AI reads incoming contracts and checks them against it. Contracts that conform can be approved quickly, and those that deviate are flagged with the problem and suggested edits.

The idea is to let lawyers focus on contracts that really need judgment. Business users can submit documents for review through integrations and workflows, and reviewers see a clear summary of what matched, what did not, and where to look. The system learns from corrections, and reporting shows how many contracts were reviewed and how long approvals take. It supports a range of commercial agreements.

item.title: Lexion
item.description:
Lexion helped legal teams make sense of their contracts. It read agreements, pulled out terms like parties, dates, renewal windows, and liability caps, and stored them in a searchable repository. Alerts warned teams about upcoming renewals and obligations, and workflows routed new requests.

AI answered questions across the portfolio, such as which contracts have auto-renewal or a particular clause. The company was built for fast-growing technology companies that wanted contract management without a heavy implementation.

item.title: Linear
item.description: Linear is a project management tool aimed at product and engineering teams. Its pitch is that the tool should get out of your way: pages load instantly, nearly everything can be done from the keyboard, and the data model is opinionated about how software gets built. Work is tracked as issues, grouped into cycles (time-boxed sprints), projects, and initiatives, with roadmaps on top for the longer view. Many teams switch to it from Jira because there is far less configuration to maintain.

item.title: LinkedIn Sales Navigator
item.description:
Sales Navigator gives salespeople deeper access to LinkedIn’s network. It provides advanced filters for finding people and companies, such as by seniority, function, company size, industry, and recent job changes. Users save leads and accounts into lists, and the system sends alerts when something relevant happens, like a prospect changing jobs or a company hiring in a certain department, which can prompt a timely message.

Further features support outreach. InMail messages reach people outside your network, TeamLink shows how colleagues are connected to a prospect for warm introductions, and integrations sync with CRMs such as Salesforce and HubSpot to keep records current. AI tools recommend leads, summarize accounts, and suggest ways to start a conversation, using the profile and activity data on the platform.

item.title: Lokalise AI
item.description:
Lokalise helps teams ship products in multiple languages. Developers and designers connect their code repositories and design files, and Lokalise collects the text that needs translating, lets translators and reviewers work on it in an editor with context, and sends finished translations back. Integrations with GitHub, GitLab, Figma, and content systems keep localization in step with development rather than delaying releases.

AI sits at the center of recent versions. It can translate new strings with models that take glossaries, tone, and context into account, flag likely errors, and score translation quality so humans focus on the content that needs attention. Translation memory reuses approved translations for consistency and cost savings, and workflows route content to in-house teams or translation vendors. Reporting shows progress by language.

item.title: Loom
item.description:
Loom replaces many meetings and long emails with a short video. You click record, show your screen while talking, and Loom uploads the video instantly and gives you a link to share. Viewers can watch at their own pace, react with emojis, comment at specific timestamps, and get an automatic transcript. It’s widely used for product walkthroughs, bug reports, onboarding, feedback, and updates to distributed teams.

AI features cut the work around videos. Loom creates titles and summaries, chapters for easy navigation, and action items, and can remove filler words and silences or turn a recording into a written document or ticket. Integrations connect with Slack, Jira, Notion, and Gmail, and since Atlassian acquired Loom, it fits more closely with tools like Jira and Confluence.

item.title: Lottie
item.description: Lottie is an animation format created at Airbnb that exports motion from After Effects as small JSON files. The files are vector-based, so they scale to any size without blur, and they are far lighter than GIFs or videos. App and web developers use them for loading spinners, onboarding screens, icons, and illustrations. A Lottie animation can be changed in code, colors can be swapped, and playback controlled, which makes it interactive.

item.title: Lucidchart AI
item.description:
Lucidchart is a mature online diagramming tool from Lucid Software. Users create flowcharts, process maps, org charts, wireframes, network diagrams, and technical drawings with a large library of shapes and templates, and collaborate in real time with comments and version history. Because it runs in the browser and integrates with the tools that teams already use, it’s popular in business and IT.

Several features go beyond drawing. Data linking can generate org charts or network diagrams from spreadsheets and cloud accounts, so diagrams stay current, and a presentation mode turns diagrams into slides. AI features generate diagrams from a text description, suggest improvements, and summarize complex drawings. Lucidchart is part of the Lucid suite, which also includes Lucidspark for whiteboarding and Lucidscale for cloud diagrams.

item.title: Maze
item.description:
Maze helps product teams learn from users. Designers import a prototype from Figma, set tasks for participants, and share a link to run a test that records clicks, paths, and success rates. Surveys, card sorts, and interview studies are supported as well, and a panel service can recruit participants.

AI speeds up analysis. It transcribes sessions, pulls out themes and quotes, and writes summaries of what the data shows, so teams spend less time sorting through recordings. Reports can be shared with stakeholders.

item.title: MeetGeek
item.description:
MeetGeek joins your calendar’s online meetings, records them, and produces a transcript and summary after each one. The summary lists decisions, action items, and key points, and highlights flag important moments. Notes are sent automatically to attendees or to tools like Slack, Notion, HubSpot, and Google Docs, which cuts down on manual write-ups.

Beyond a single meeting, it organizes knowledge across your calls. Hubs group meetings by team or topic, and you can search past conversations or ask questions about them. Meeting templates tailor summaries for sales calls, interviews, or team check-ins, and analytics show participation and talk time. Teams can get insights into patterns across customer calls.

item.title: Metricool
item.description:
Metricool brings several marketing tasks into one dashboard. Users can plan and schedule posts across networks on a calendar, see analytics on posts, followers, and competitors, and manage Facebook, Instagram, Google, and TikTok ads reports. A link-in-bio tool, inbox for comments and messages, and web analytics help connect social activity to site traffic.

Reporting is a strong point. Customizable reports can be exported or scheduled for clients, and integrations connect with Looker Studio and other business intelligence tools, which suits agencies. AI features help write captions, suggest posting times, and generate content ideas, and a feature can plan a calendar from a brief. Plans cover multiple brands, so one account can manage several clients.

item.title: Microsoft Designer
item.description:
Microsoft Designer helps people make graphics quickly. You describe what you want, such as an invitation for a birthday party or a banner for a sale, and Designer produces several layout options with text, images, and styling, which you can edit. It offers templates for common formats, background removal, and tools for resizing a design for different platforms.

AI image generation is built in, powered by Microsoft’s and OpenAI’s image models, so you can create custom illustrations or photos to include in a design. It integrates with Microsoft 365 apps and Copilot, and is available on the web, as a mobile app, and inside tools such as Edge. Brand kits and shared templates are available on paid Microsoft 365 plans.

item.title: Microsoft Power Automate
item.description:
Power Automate connects apps and automates repetitive work. Users build flows that trigger on events, such as an email arriving or a form submission, and perform actions in hundreds of services. It works smoothly with Teams, SharePoint, Outlook, and Dynamics.

AI features extend it. Copilot lets people describe a flow in plain language, AI Builder processes documents and forms, and agent capabilities handle more open-ended tasks. Desktop flows use robotic process automation to control applications that have no API.

item.title: Microsoft Power Automate
item.description:
Power Automate helps people automate repetitive work without code. In a visual designer, users create flows that start from a trigger, such as an email arriving or a form being submitted, and then run actions like saving attachments, updating a spreadsheet, sending approvals, or posting to Teams. It connects to hundreds of services, with deep integration with SharePoint, Outlook, Excel, and Dynamics 365, and handles scheduled and event-driven tasks.

It also covers robotic process automation. Desktop flows record and replay actions on a computer, allowing automation of legacy applications that lack APIs. AI Builder adds capabilities such as reading text from documents, classifying content, and making predictions, and Copilot can build a flow from a plain-language description. Newer features support AI agents that use flows as tools.

item.title: Miro AI
item.description:
Miro provides an infinite shared canvas where teams place sticky notes, diagrams, documents, and images, and work together live or asynchronously. It’s used for brainstorming, retrospectives, user journey maps, roadmaps, and workshops, particularly for distributed teams. A large library of templates, integrations with tools such as Jira, Slack, and Google Drive, and facilitation features like timers and voting make it versatile.

AI features speed up creation and synthesis. Users can generate diagrams, flowcharts, and mind maps from a prompt, summarize and cluster hundreds of sticky notes into themes, and turn a board into a document or a prototype. Sidekicks are AI helpers with specific roles, such as a product manager or a retrospective facilitator, that give feedback and suggestions on the board. Flows connect several AI steps for repeatable processes.

item.title: Mixmax
item.description:
Mixmax turns Gmail into a sales workspace. It tracks opens, clicks, and replies, lets you schedule messages, and adds a calendar tool so recipients can book meetings from your email. Templates and snippets speed up repetitive writing, and polls, surveys, and documents can be embedded. It is used by sales, recruiting, and customer success teams that live in their inbox.

Sequences are a main feature: automated multi-step email campaigns that send follow-ups until someone replies, with rules for pausing and routing. Integrations connect with Salesforce, HubSpot, Outreach alternatives, Slack, and Zapier, so activity is logged in the CRM. AI helps draft emails, personalize at scale, and suggest next steps, and call recording and meeting notes have been added in some plans.

item.title: Monday.com
item.description:
Monday.com organizes work in colorful boards that resemble spreadsheets. Teams track projects, sales pipelines, marketing campaigns, and operations with columns for status, owners, dates, and more, and view the same data as a timeline, calendar, or chart. No-code automations handle routine updates and notifications.

The platform has expanded into products for sales CRM, service desks, and software development, built on the same foundation. AI assistants create boards from a description, summarize items and updates, write content, and extract information, and agents can take on tasks within workflows.

item.title: Murf
item.description: Murf is known for its studio, but its voice features are a separate reason people use it. The voice changer converts a recording of your own speech into a different voice from the library, keeping your timing and emotion, which suits people who want a polished sound without hiring talent. Voice cloning can create a custom voice for a brand or presenter, typically with consent and verification, and is offered mainly for business customers.

item.title: Murf
item.description:
Murf is aimed at people who need a professional voiceover without hiring a voice actor or booking a studio. In its browser-based studio, you paste a script, choose a voice, and adjust pitch, speed, and emphasis. Voices come in many accents and languages and suit narration, e-learning, product videos, ads, and presentations. You can add background music, line the audio up with video or slides, and export the result.

The platform has expanded to related audio jobs. Dubbing translates a video or audio file into other languages and keeps it timed to the original. An API gives developers text-to-speech for their own apps, including fast, streaming voices for conversational use. Murf Agents power voice calls and chat for customer service and similar needs, and a voice changer converts one voice into another. Team workspaces help companies share projects and keep audio consistent.

item.title: n8n
