item.description: n8n lets you build automations by connecting nodes on a canvas, similar to Zapier or Make, but with more room for code. Each node is a step: a trigger like a webhook or schedule, an action in an app, or a block that transforms data with JavaScript or Python. Hundreds of integrations are included, and a generic HTTP node covers the rest. Workflows can branch, loop, and call other workflows, so it handles anything from simple notifications to elaborate data pipelines.

item.title: Narrato
item.description:
Narrato helps teams manage the whole content process. A content calendar plans what to publish, assignments route work to writers and editors, and approval workflows track progress. The AI writer generates drafts, outlines, social posts, and ad copy in a team’s style, and SEO tools provide keyword suggestions and optimization scores.

Additional tools address agencies and publishers. Brief generation creates instructions for writers, a plagiarism checker and AI content detector help check originality, and a marketplace lets teams hire freelance writers for content that needs a human touch. Integrations publish directly to WordPress and other platforms, and an AI assistant helps with ideas and repurposing.

item.title: NotebookLM Plus
item.description: NotebookLM Plus gives heavier users more room in NotebookLM, Google’s tool for working with your own documents. The free version lets you add sources, ask questions with citations, and generate study aids, but it limits the number of notebooks, sources, and daily queries. The Plus tier lifts those limits, so people with large projects, such as researchers, students writing theses, or analysts working across many documents, can keep more material in one place.

item.title: Notion
item.description:
Notion lets people build their own workspace from simple pieces. A page can hold text, headings, checklists, images, embedded files, and databases, and databases can be shown as tables, boards, calendars, or galleries. Teams use it for wikis, meeting notes, project tracking, product roadmaps, and personal organization, and templates help people get started. Real-time collaboration, comments, and permissions make it work for teams as well as individuals.

The product has grown beyond notes. Notion Calendar and Notion Mail connect scheduling and email to the workspace, and Sites turns pages into public web pages. Notion AI adds writing help, summaries, translation, and question answering across your workspace and connected tools like Slack and Google Drive, plus agents that perform tasks. AI meeting notes capture and summarize calls. See the Notion AI entry for details on those features.

item.title: Notta
item.description: Notta turns speech into text for people who sit through many conversations. You can record in the mobile or web app, upload audio and video files, or let its assistant join Zoom, Google Meet, and Teams calls. The transcript appears in the app with speaker labels and timestamps, and you can search it, edit it, and share it. It supports a large number of languages, which suits international teams, journalists, and researchers.

item.title: Noty.ai
item.description:
Noty.ai is a lightweight tool for people who want meeting notes without much setup. It records and transcribes online meetings, then creates a summary that highlights the main discussion points, decisions, and tasks. The goal is to let participants focus on the conversation instead of typing, and to give everyone a shared record afterward.

Its integrations make the notes easy to reuse. Summaries can be pushed to Notion and other workspace tools, and the transcript is searchable, so you can find what was said about a topic in a past meeting. A browser extension handles recording in Google Meet and Zoom, and a free plan lets individuals try the product.

item.title: Numerous
item.description:
Numerous brings language models into the spreadsheet. After installing the add-in, you use a formula such as =AI(“prompt”, cell) in a cell to ask the model to do something with the data: categorize customer feedback, write product descriptions, extract names from messy text, translate, or summarize. Filling the formula down a column performs the task on hundreds or thousands of rows, which would take hours by hand.

It aims to be approachable for people who know spreadsheets but not code. Prompts are written in plain language, results appear in cells where you can filter and calculate with them, and features help with common tasks like cleaning, tagging, and brainstorming. Marketers, e-commerce teams, researchers, and operations staff use it to process lists of items quickly.

item.title: Open WebUI
item.description:
Open WebUI gives people a familiar chat interface for models they control. You run it on your own server or computer, connect it to local models through Ollama or to any OpenAI-compatible API, and get a polished web app with conversation history, model switching, prompt libraries, and voice input. It started as a front end for Ollama and has become a full platform.

Features target teams and power users. Retrieval-augmented generation lets users upload documents and chat with them, web search can add current information, and tools and functions extend what models can do. Administrators can manage multiple users, roles, and permissions, which suits organizations that want an internal AI assistant without sending data to a third party. It supports plugins and pipelines for custom behavior.

item.title: Otter.ai
item.description: Otter was one of the first widely used meeting transcription tools. You connect your calendar, and its assistant joins your Zoom, Google Meet, or Teams calls to record, transcribe, and label speakers. The transcript is available live, so participants can follow along, and afterward you get a summary, key points, and action items. Everything is searchable, so you can find what was said in a past meeting by keyword. It also works on phones for in-person conversations and lectures.

item.title: Otter.ai
item.description:
Otter.ai joins online meetings, transcribes the conversation as it happens, and produces notes people can search and share. Speakers are labeled, key points are summarized, and action items are pulled out, so attendees can focus on the discussion instead of taking notes.

Features include an assistant that can answer questions about a meeting or across past meetings, automatic sharing of notes with attendees, and integrations with calendars and collaboration tools. Mobile and web apps handle in-person conversations, lectures, and interviews.

item.title: PandaDoc AI
item.description:
PandaDoc helps sales teams close deals faster. Users build proposals and quotes from templates in a drag-and-drop editor, add pricing tables with live calculations, embed videos and payment links, and send them to clients, who can review and sign electronically. Tracking shows when a document is opened and viewed, so reps know when to follow up.

Automation and integration make it practical for teams. It connects with CRMs like Salesforce and HubSpot to populate documents with deal data and update records when documents are signed, offers approval workflows, content libraries, and a payment step. AI features help generate document content from a prompt, summarize contracts, suggest edits, and extract information, speeding up proposal creation.

item.title: Penpot
item.description:
Penpot is built for collaboration between designers and developers. It uses open web standards, so designs map to real code, and supports flexible layouts based on CSS grid and flex. Teams create prototypes, design systems, and shared components in a browser.

Being open source matters to some teams. They can host Penpot themselves, keep control of their data, and avoid vendor lock-in, and developers can inspect designs and get code in a familiar form. AI features and plugins extend the tool.

item.title: People.ai
item.description:
People.ai solves the data entry problem in sales. Instead of relying on reps to log everything, it connects to email, calendars, and phone systems and records contacts, meetings, and conversations, then matches them to the right accounts and opportunities in the CRM. That keeps records current and gives managers a more complete picture of how engaged each deal is.

On top of the data, it provides analytics and AI. Dashboards show activity, engagement with key contacts, and whether deals are at risk, and forecasting tools estimate which will close. AI agents can summarize accounts, answer questions about the pipeline in natural language, and prepare reps for meetings. The aim is to give sales leaders a reliable view without chasing updates.

item.title: Peppertype.ai
item.description:
Peppertype.ai started as a copywriting assistant and has grown into a broader content tool for marketers. Users pick a type of content, such as an ad, a product description, a blog outline, or a LinkedIn post, supply the topic and tone, and receive several drafts. Brand voice and knowledge settings help it reflect a company’s style, and templates cover many common marketing formats.

It is part of Pepper Content, a company that also runs a marketplace of freelance writers and managed content services, which is the source of the Peppertype name. That connection lets teams combine AI drafting with human writers and editors for higher-stakes content. Workflow tools support collaboration, review, and publishing, and the platform has added AI agents for tasks like research and repurposing content.

item.title: Phidata
item.description:
Phidata began as a Python framework for turning language models into agents. Developers define an agent with instructions, tools, memory, and a knowledge base, and the framework handles running it, storing history, and retrieving documents. It also supports teams of agents that work together.

The project was renamed Agno, and the same team and codebase continue under the new name, so documentation and packages now refer to Agno. Newer releases focus on speed, a lightweight design, and production features such as a runtime for serving agents.

item.title: Pictory
item.description:
Pictory is aimed at marketers and content creators who want video without editing skills. You paste a script or a blog URL, and the AI splits the text into scenes, picks stock clips and images for each, adds captions and music, and generates a voiceover. You can then edit scenes, swap visuals, and adjust the text with a simple storyboard-style editor.

Other features extend the same idea. Pictory can summarize a long video, such as a webinar or Zoom recording, into a short highlight reel, create captions, and generate text-to-video clips. A brand kit keeps colors and logos consistent, and integrations let teams pull content from articles. Typical uses are social media videos, explainers, and repurposing blog posts for video platforms.

item.title: Pipedrive
item.description: Pipedrive is designed by and for salespeople, with the pipeline at the center. Deals appear as cards that move across stages, from first contact to closed, so reps can see at a glance what needs attention. Each deal has activities, emails, notes, and files attached, and the system reminds you of follow-ups so nothing slips. Compared with big CRM suites, the interface is clean and quick to learn, which suits small and growing sales teams.

item.title: Pitch
item.description:
Pitch aims to make presentations that look good without wrestling with layouts. It provides modern templates, smart slide types, and a brand-aware design system that keeps a team’s decks consistent. Collaboration works like a shared document: several people edit at once, leave comments, and track versions, which suits startups, agencies, and sales teams that produce decks together.

Distinctive features include presentation analytics and sharing. You can send a deck as a link and see who viewed it and for how long, which is helpful for investor and sales decks, and recordings let you narrate a deck for asynchronous sharing. AI tools generate slide drafts from a prompt, rewrite text, and create visuals, and the platform integrates with tools like Slack, HubSpot, and Google Drive.

item.title: PlantNet
item.description: Pl@ntNet lets anyone identify a plant by taking a photo. You photograph a leaf, flower, fruit, or bark, and the app compares it with a large reference collection and returns a list of likely species with confidence scores and similar images. It covers wild plants and many cultivated ones, with regional floras for different parts of the world, and works best when you provide several views of the same plant.

item.title: Plus AI
item.description:
Plus AI takes the approach that you shouldn’t have to leave your slide editor to use AI. After installing the add-in in Google Slides or PowerPoint, you describe the presentation you want, and it drafts an outline and slides in the editor, which you can then adjust like any other deck. It can also build from a document, a set of notes, or a web page.

Editing features save time on existing decks. The remix tool can restyle or rework slides, and the rewrite function changes tone or length of text on a slide. It can convert content into a different layout, summarize, and create speaker notes. Because the output is native slides, the file remains fully editable and compatible with company templates and brand assets.

item.title: Promethean AI
item.description:
Promethean AI addresses the labor involved in building 3D environments. An artist describes what they want in a scene, such as a cluttered study or a forest clearing, and the assistant selects assets from a library, places them with sensible arrangement and variation, and assembles a draft environment. The aim is to automate repetitive dressing and layout so artists can focus on art direction.

The tool learns from the studio’s own assets and preferences, so output stays consistent with the project’s look, and it integrates with common creative software and engines. It was aimed at game studios, film and virtual production teams, and architectural visualization, where large environments must be filled with believable detail.

item.title: Proposify
item.description:
Proposify helps agencies and service companies create and send proposals. Teams build templates with sections, pricing tables, and brand styling, assemble a proposal quickly, and send it to clients who can review, comment, and sign electronically. Notifications show when a proposal is opened.

AI features help with writing content and suggest improvements based on what has worked in past proposals. Analytics reveal how long clients spend on each section, informing follow-ups. Integrations connect with CRMs and billing.

item.title: Raycast AI
item.description:
Raycast puts a command bar on your keyboard. Press a hotkey, type a few letters, and you can launch apps, search files, run calculations, manage windows, paste snippets, control music, and use hundreds of extensions that connect to tools such as GitHub, Linear, Notion, and Slack. Power users value how much it can cut mouse use and context switching.

Raycast AI adds chat and commands powered by leading language models. You can ask a question, rewrite selected text, summarize a page, translate, or run custom AI commands from any app, and switch among models from different providers. AI Extensions let the assistant act through extensions, such as creating an issue or checking a calendar, and Model Context Protocol support connects it to more tools. Chats and presets are synced across devices.

item.title: Replit
item.description:
Replit began as an online code editor and runtime that supported dozens of languages with no installation. Open a browser tab, start a project, and your code runs immediately on Replit’s servers. That made it popular in schools, coding bootcamps, and with beginners, and its multiplayer editing lets several people work in the same project at once. Projects are hosted, so sharing or deploying an app takes a click.

The current focus is Replit Agent, which builds software from natural language. You describe an app, and the agent writes code, sets up the environment, installs packages, creates a database, tests the result, and deploys it. You can keep chatting to refine features or fix bugs, or open the code and edit it directly. The aim is to let people without programming experience make working apps, and to let developers move faster. A mobile app lets you build and test from a phone.

item.title: Salesforce
item.description: Salesforce is the CRM that large companies tend to run their sales and customer operations on. It tracks leads, accounts, opportunities, and support cases, and it is sold as separate clouds for Sales, Service, Marketing, and Commerce, with Slack, Tableau, and MuleSoft added for collaboration, analytics, and integration. Underneath is a platform that lets companies build custom objects, workflows, and apps, which is why Salesforce setups can look very different from one company to the next.

item.title: SalesLoft
item.description:
Salesloft helps sales teams organize outbound and follow-up work. Reps follow cadences, which are structured sequences of emails, calls, and social touches, and the platform tells them who to contact next and records each activity in the CRM. Managers can see which messages and sequences generate replies and meetings, and coach reps with call recordings and analytics.

The platform has expanded into revenue orchestration. Conversation intelligence records and summarizes calls, deal management tracks stage progress and risk, and forecasting tools combine pipeline data with engagement signals. Salesloft acquired Drift for conversational marketing and has combined with Clari, a revenue forecasting company, to build a broader revenue platform. AI assistants prepare meeting briefs, draft messages, and suggest next steps.

item.title: SAP Ariba
item.description:
SAP Ariba helps large organizations buy what they need in an organized way. Procurement teams use it to find and evaluate suppliers, run sourcing events, manage contracts, process purchase orders and invoices, and monitor supplier risk. The Ariba Network connects buyers and suppliers electronically, so orders and invoices flow between systems without manual entry.

AI is being added to reduce manual work. SAP’s assistant, Joule, can help users search for information, draft sourcing documents, and answer questions about spend, and features analyze contracts, recommend suppliers, and flag unusual transactions. Integration with SAP’s ERP and other systems provides a connected view of purchasing, and spend analytics reveal savings opportunities.

item.title: Sembly AI
item.description:
Sembly joins your online meetings, records them, and produces a transcript with a structured summary. The summary highlights the main points, tasks, decisions, and risks mentioned, so teams can see what needs follow-up without rewatching. It also supports in-person meetings through its mobile app and uploads of audio files, and works in many languages.

Beyond single meetings, Sembly helps organize knowledge. Workspaces and meeting libraries let teams search past conversations and ask questions across them, and templates adjust the notes for different meeting types such as sales calls or interviews. Integrations push summaries and tasks into Slack, Notion, Asana, Jira, HubSpot, and other tools. Analytics track patterns like meeting time and topics.

item.title: simpleshow
item.description:
simpleshow is known for its hand-drawn, paper-cutout explainer style. A user pastes a script or topic, and the engine suggests images and structure, generates a video with narration, and lets the user edit scenes. The goal is to make complex subjects clear for training and communications.

Companies use it for onboarding, compliance, product explanations, and internal updates. The platform is aimed at non-designers and provides templates and a library of illustrations.

item.title: Smartsheet AI
item.description:
Smartsheet is built around the grid. Teams manage projects, requests, and processes in sheets that look like spreadsheets but add features such as attachments, comments, dependencies, and approvals. The same data can be viewed as a Gantt chart, calendar, board, or form, and reports and dashboards summarize progress for leaders. It’s used for project plans, marketing calendars, intake processes, and portfolio tracking in many large organizations.

Automation and AI reduce manual work. Rules can send alerts, request approvals, or update fields when conditions are met, and AI helps by generating formulas from plain language, summarizing sheets, creating content, and analyzing data to find trends. Newer features allow building workflows and agents with natural language. Integrations connect with Microsoft 365, Google Workspace, Slack, Salesforce, and more.

item.title: Spark Mail
item.description:
Spark is an email client that works with Gmail, Outlook, iCloud, Yahoo, and other accounts. Its Smart Inbox sorts messages into categories, putting people and important mail first and keeping newsletters and notifications out of the way. Features such as snooze, send later, follow-up reminders, and quick replies make it faster to process mail, and a unified inbox combines accounts.

Collaboration is a differentiator. Teams can share emails, comment privately on messages, and draft replies together before sending, which suits small teams who handle shared mailboxes. AI features in the paid tier help write and rewrite emails, summarize long threads, and suggest replies, and a feature can search by asking questions. The app is available on Apple devices, Android, and Windows.

item.title: Spline
item.description:
Spline brings 3D to web designers. In a browser editor that feels more like Figma than Blender, you create shapes, materials, lighting, and animations, then add interactions such as hover effects and clicks. Scenes can be published as links, embedded in websites, or exported to code, and they run in real time in the browser. It’s used for product landing pages, interactive hero sections, games, and design prototypes.

Collaboration and AI features set it apart from traditional 3D tools. Multiple people can edit a scene at once with comments and version history. AI tools can generate 3D objects and textures from text, help with animation, and create scenes from prompts. Physics, particles, and state-based interactions add depth, and integrations with Figma let designers bring in 2D elements.

item.title: Sprout Social
item.description:
Sprout Social is built for teams that manage social media as a function, not a side task. A calendar plans and schedules content across networks such as Instagram, Facebook, LinkedIn, X, and TikTok, and approval flows keep drafts under review before they go out. A smart inbox gathers messages, comments, and mentions from every channel into one stream that can be assigned, tagged, and replied to by a team.

Analytics are a major selling point. Reports show how posts perform, how audiences grow, and how competitors compare, and they can be exported or shared with clients and executives. Listening tools track brand mentions, topics, and sentiment across social and the web, which helps with crisis monitoring and market research. Influencer marketing and employee advocacy tools extend into related work. AI Assist helps write posts, change tone, and draft replies, and it can summarize sentiment from conversations.

item.title: StockImg AI
item.description:
StockImg AI turns a description into a usable image. Instead of searching a stock library for something close to what you imagine, you type what you want and the tool creates it. It offers separate generators geared to common needs: logo designs, ebook and book covers, posters, wallpapers, illustrations, and app screen mockups. Each has settings suited to its format, such as aspect ratios for covers and posters.

The tool also includes editing functions. You can adjust and regenerate images, remove backgrounds, and explore variations. Self-publishers, small businesses, bloggers, and social media managers use it to get covers and graphics without hiring a designer or paying for licenses. The output is meant to be unique to your prompt, which avoids the problem of the same stock photo showing up in many places.

item.title: Sunsama
item.description:
Sunsama is built around the idea that planning your day deliberately reduces overwhelm. Each morning, a guided ritual walks you through gathering tasks from different sources, choosing what you can realistically do, estimating the time each will take, and placing them on your calendar. The app shows your total planned hours against the day’s available time, which discourages overcommitting.

It connects to many other tools. Tasks from project managers, issue trackers, email, and Slack can be brought into your daily view without leaving Sunsama, and calendar events appear alongside them. An end-of-day shutdown ritual lets you review what you finished and move unfinished tasks forward. AI features help with suggestions for scheduling, summaries, and organizing tasks.

item.title: Supernormal
item.description:
Supernormal aims to make meeting notes require no effort. A bot joins your scheduled meetings, records and transcribes them, and creates notes organized by templates for different types of meetings, such as sales calls, interviews, one-on-ones, and standups. The notes list decisions, action items, and key points, and are shared with attendees or saved to the tools your team uses.

The product works across platforms, including Zoom, Google Meet, and Microsoft Teams, and also supports in-person meetings. Integrations push notes to Slack, Notion, HubSpot, Salesforce, and Google Docs. Search and chat features let you look back at past meetings and ask questions, and customization options allow you to adjust the format of the notes.

item.title: Surfer SEO
item.description: Surfer helps writers create content that matches what already ranks. You enter a keyword and it analyzes the top search results, then suggests the terms, headings, length, and structure those pages share. As you write in its editor, a content score updates, giving a quick sense of how well your page covers the topic. Writers and SEO teams use it to guide drafts and to update old posts that have dropped in rankings.

item.title: Swimm
item.description:
Swimm tackles documentation that rots. Developers write docs that reference specific code, and Swimm tracks those references. When the code changes, it detects the affected docs and either updates them automatically or alerts the owner.

AI helps generate documentation from code and answer questions about a codebase, which helps new hires learn a system. Integrations with IDEs and code hosts put docs where developers work. Large teams with legacy systems are the main audience.

item.title: Synthesia
item.description:
Synthesia produces videos with digital presenters. Users select from a library of avatars or create a custom one, paste a script, choose a voice and language, and receive a finished video. The editor handles slides, text, and media.

Companies use it for training, onboarding, product explainers, and communications, often replacing costly shoots. Translations let one video serve many markets. Recent features add interactive videos, screen recording, and avatars with more expressive delivery.

item.title: Synthesia
item.description:
Synthesia lets companies produce videos without cameras, studios, or actors. A user writes or pastes a script, selects an AI avatar from a library of presenters or creates a custom one, and the platform generates a video with natural speech and lip movement. Scenes, slides, screen recordings, and media can be combined, and editing the script and regenerating takes the place of a reshoot.

The platform is built for business use. It supports a large number of languages, so one video can be localized quickly, and offers templates, brand kits, and collaboration features. Interactive and agent-style avatars can respond to viewers, and an API lets teams automate video creation. Enterprise features cover security, compliance, and consent controls, since custom avatars require permission from the person depicted. Companies commonly use it for learning and development, onboarding, product explainers, and sales content.

item.title: Tableau
item.description:
Tableau is known for making data exploration feel visual and quick. Analysts connect to databases, spreadsheets, and cloud data warehouses, then drag fields onto a canvas to build charts, maps, and dashboards without writing code. It handles large data volumes well, and its interactivity lets viewers filter, drill down, and compare in ways static reports cannot. It is widely used in finance, healthcare, retail, government, and education.

Salesforce owns Tableau and has built AI into it. Tableau Pulse sends personalized, plain-language insights about key metrics to the people who care about them, and flags unusual changes without anyone opening a dashboard. Tableau Agent helps users build visualizations and analyze data by chatting with the tool. Tableau Prep cleans and combines data, and the platform integrates with Salesforce data and its Data Cloud.

item.title: Tabnine
item.description:
Tabnine was one of the earliest AI code completion tools, and it built its identity on privacy and control. It works inside VS Code, JetBrains IDEs, and other editors, suggesting lines and functions, answering questions in chat, writing tests and documentation, and explaining code. A distinguishing choice was letting companies run it in their own environment, including fully disconnected networks, and keeping code out of any third party’s training.

Its enterprise pitch centers on context. Tabnine can learn from a company’s repositories, style guides, and standards so suggestions match internal conventions, and administrators can choose which models are used, including options hosted in-house. It offers attribution and provenance controls for companies worried about generated code resembling open-source projects with restrictive licenses. Agents extend it to larger tasks such as code review and test generation.

item.title: Tactiq
item.description:
Tactiq takes a lightweight approach to meeting notes. Instead of sending a recording bot into the call, it runs as a browser extension that captures the meeting’s captions and audio on your device. A live transcript appears in a sidebar as people speak, and you can highlight key moments as the meeting happens. That makes it less intrusive in calls where an unfamiliar bot would raise eyebrows.

After the meeting, AI features produce summaries, action items, and custom outputs from prompts, such as a follow-up email or a status update. The transcript is saved in your account and can be exported to tools like Notion, Google Docs, Slack, and HubSpot. Templates adapt the output for different meeting types, and a search function finds past conversations.

item.title: Taskade
item.description:
Taskade merges project management and AI. A project can be viewed as a list, board, calendar, table, or mind map, and everything can be edited collaboratively in real time. Chat and video calls are built into the workspace so a team can discuss and track tasks in one place. It is flexible enough for personal to-do lists, team projects, wikis, and meeting notes.

AI agents are central. Users can create agents with specific roles and knowledge, such as a research assistant, a project manager, or a support bot, and let them generate content, break down projects, and respond to questions. Automations connect actions across tools and trigger agents on schedules or events, and templates cover common uses like content planning and sales processes. You can also generate whole projects from a prompt.

item.title: tl;dv
item.description:
tl;dv, short for “too long; didn’t view,” saves people from rewatching meetings. A bot joins your calls to record and transcribe them in many languages, and you can mark highlights during the call. Afterward, the recording is available with an AI-generated summary and a list of action items, plus timestamps so you can jump to the part that matters. Clips can be shared with people who missed the meeting.

The tool is popular with sales and product teams. It can fill in CRM fields in tools like HubSpot and Salesforce, produce reports across many meetings to spot patterns such as customer objections, and send notes to Slack and Notion. Templates tailor summaries to sales calls, user interviews, and team meetings, and search lets you find topics across your library.

item.title: Todoist
item.description: Todoist is a clean, fast task manager. You add tasks by typing in plain language, like “send report every Friday at 3pm,” and it turns that into a recurring due date. Tasks can be organized into projects and sections, given priorities and labels, and viewed as a list, board, or calendar. Filters let you build views such as everything due today across all projects. It syncs across phones, computers, browsers, and email clients.

item.title: VEED.io
item.description:
VEED is an online video editor that makes common edits simple. You upload clips, trim and arrange them on a timeline, add text, music, and effects, and export in formats for different platforms. It includes a screen and webcam recorder for tutorials and messages, templates for social videos, and stock media. Everything runs in the browser, which allows collaboration without installing software.

AI features are a big part of the draw. Auto subtitles transcribe and style captions in many languages, background removal and noise cleanup polish footage, eye contact correction makes you appear to look at the camera, and AI avatars and voices generate presenter videos from scripts. Tools for translation and dubbing help reach other markets, and an assistant can clean up speech by removing filler words and silences.

item.title: Venngage
item.description:
Venngage targets people who need to communicate information visually. Users start from thousands of templates for infographics, reports, flyers, presentations, and social graphics, replace the content, and customize colors, icons, and charts. Data can be imported to generate charts, and the tool includes maps and diagrams for explaining processes and comparisons.

It differentiates itself with business features. Brand kits apply logos, fonts, and colors automatically, team workspaces allow collaboration and approvals, and an accessibility checker flags color contrast and other issues. AI tools generate infographic designs from text, write copy, and suggest improvements, and designs can be exported or shared with analytics.

item.title: Visily
item.description:
Visily is built for people who need to mock up interfaces quickly without learning a full design tool. You can upload a screenshot of an app, a hand-drawn sketch, or a description of a screen, and the AI creates an editable wireframe made of real components. A library of templates, UI kits, and smart components helps assemble screens for web and mobile products.

Collaboration is part of the appeal. Teams can edit together, leave comments, and share clickable prototypes with stakeholders, and designs can be exported or moved into Figma for refinement. Product managers, business analysts, and founders use it to communicate ideas visually and gather feedback early, before engineering work starts.

item.title: Visme AI
item.description:
Visme is aimed at people who need to present information visually without design skills. It offers a drag-and-drop editor with thousands of templates for presentations, infographics, reports, charts, social media posts, and documents. Data widgets create charts and graphs from spreadsheets, and interactive elements such as links and animations can be added. Brand kits keep colors, fonts, and logos consistent across a team.

AI features speed up creation. An AI designer can generate a presentation or document from a prompt, write and rewrite text, create images, and suggest layouts. Teams can collaborate in real time with comments and workflows, and content can be exported as PDF, PowerPoint, or HTML, or shared by link with analytics. Visme is often used by marketers, educators, consultants, and communications teams.

item.title: Vyond
item.description:
Vyond focuses on business animation. Users build videos from libraries of characters, props, and backgrounds, choosing actions and expressions for each character and arranging scenes on a timeline. The style is a recognizable cartoon format popular in corporate training, compliance courses, and explainer videos, and the tool makes it possible to produce them without animation skills.

AI features reduce the work of getting started. A text-to-video capability generates a draft video from a script or prompt, including scenes, characters, and voiceover, which you can then edit. Other tools produce voices in many languages, help with translations, and match lip sync. Branded templates and shared libraries help teams keep their videos consistent, and enterprise features cover security and administration.

item.title: W&B Weave
item.description:
Weave addresses a common problem with LLM apps: it is hard to know what they are doing. Adding a few lines of code logs each call with its inputs, outputs, latency, cost, and the surrounding function calls, so a developer can inspect a failing response step by step instead of guessing. The traces cover nested calls, which matters for agents that chain several models and tools.

It also handles evaluation. Teams build datasets of test cases, define scorers (including LLM judges), and run experiments to compare prompts, models, and app versions before shipping. Results are tracked over time, which makes it easier to tell whether a change actually helped. Online evaluations can score live traffic and flag regressions in production.

item.title: Webflow
item.description:
Webflow sits between simple site builders and hand-coded sites. Designers work on a canvas that mirrors how the web works, setting classes, flexbox and grid layouts, and breakpoints, and the platform produces production code and hosts the result. That gives far more control than template-based builders, which is why agencies and in-house design teams like it.

The platform includes a CMS for blogs and collections, e-commerce, interactions and animations, localization, and tools for marketers to edit content without breaking the design. AI features generate sections and copy, suggest changes, and help with site structure and SEO. Developers can add custom code and use an API to connect Webflow to other services.

item.title: Whimsical AI
item.description:
Whimsical puts several lightweight visual tools in one place. You can draw flowcharts and sequence diagrams, sketch low-fidelity wireframes, brainstorm on mind maps, write docs, and arrange sticky notes on a board. The tools are designed around speed, with keyboard shortcuts, snapping, and a clean look that makes rough thinking easy to share.

AI features reduce the setup. Describe a process and Whimsical can draft a flowchart, turn a topic into a mind map, or produce a first-pass wireframe, which you then edit by hand. Teams use it for planning, product specs, and explaining systems, and sharing is simple with links, comments, and embeds in tools like Notion and Confluence.

item.title: Writerly
item.description:
Writerly is aimed at teams that want AI-written content to sound like them. Instead of generating generic text, it lets users supply samples of their existing writing and style guidelines, then drafts articles, emails, and social posts that follow that voice. That approach is common among brand-focused writing tools, and matters most for companies with several writers.

Features reported in directories include templates for common content types, collaboration for editors and reviewers, and options to reuse past content. Teams often use this kind of tool to keep messaging consistent across channels and to speed up first drafts, with humans editing for accuracy and judgment.

item.title: Writesonic
item.description:
Writesonic started as a template-based copywriter and has widened into a content and marketing suite. Users pick a tool for blog articles, ad copy, product descriptions, emails, or social posts, give a brief, and get a draft. A long-form article writer can produce SEO-minded posts from a keyword with outlines and sources, and a chat assistant answers questions and drafts on demand.

Recent additions center on search visibility. Writesonic has tools to see how a brand is mentioned in AI answer engines such as ChatGPT and Perplexity, plus recommendations for improving content. It also offers brand voice settings, an editor with SEO scoring, and integrations with WordPress and other platforms.

item.title: Writesonic
item.description: Writesonic began as a template-driven AI writer for marketing copy. You choose a type of content, such as a blog post, ad, product description, or social caption, fill in some details, and get a draft. A longer-form article writer builds full posts with an outline, headings, and optional SEO guidance, and a chat assistant answers questions and can search the web. A browser extension and integrations with WordPress and other tools help get content published.

item.title: Zed AI
item.description:
Zed is built for speed. Its editor, written in Rust, starts quickly and stays responsive on large projects, and multiplayer editing lets several people work in the same file with voice and chat.

AI is built in rather than added by extension. Users chat with models in an assistant panel, ask for inline edits, and run an agent that edits code across files, with support for several providers and local models. Edit predictions suggest the next change as you type, and the Agent Client Protocol lets other agents run inside.

item.title: Zendesk
item.description:
Zendesk is one of the most widely used help desk systems. Customer messages from email, web chat, phone, WhatsApp, and social media become tickets in a shared workspace, where they can be routed, prioritized, and tracked against service targets. A help center and community forum let customers find answers themselves, and reports show response times and satisfaction. It scales from small support teams to large contact centers.

The current product is built around AI. AI agents take on requests from start to finish, answering from help articles and past conversations, and taking actions in connected systems when allowed. A copilot assists human agents by suggesting replies, summarizing long threads, and flagging urgent or unhappy customers. The platform has added contact center, workforce management, and quality assurance tools, and an employee service product that applies the same ideas to internal IT and HR requests.

item.title: ZoomInfo
item.description:
ZoomInfo provides one of the largest databases of business contacts and companies. Sales and marketing teams search by title, industry, company size, location, and technology to build lists, and see verified email addresses, direct phone numbers, org charts, and firmographic details. Intent data shows which companies are researching topics related to a product, helping teams reach out when interest is high.

The platform has expanded from data into a workflow product. It includes tools for sales engagement, marketing advertising, conversation intelligence through Chorus, and enrichment that keeps CRM records up to date automatically. AI features include assistants that research accounts, draft outreach, and recommend who to contact, and agents that handle prospecting tasks. It integrates with Salesforce, HubSpot, and other systems.

item.title: Notion
item.description: Notion works as a set of building blocks. A team can create a company wiki, a project tracker with a board view, a product roadmap, a meeting notes database, and a documentation site, all in one workspace with permissions and comments. Databases are central: the same set of records can be viewed as a table, board, calendar, or timeline, and linked to other databases, which makes it possible to build custom systems without code.

item.title: Aide
item.description: Aide was an AI-first code editor from the London startup CodeStory. It was a fork of VS Code, so it looked familiar and could use extensions, but it added a layer of AI that understood the project. You could chat about the codebase, ask for changes across several files, and get completions informed by wider context. It was released as open source under the AGPL license, and the project drew substantial interest from developers looking for an alternative to Cursor.

item.title: Arize AI
item.description:
Arize helps teams see what their models are doing after deployment. For classic machine learning, it tracks performance, detects when input data drifts away from training data, and helps identify which segments of users a model is failing. Alerts point teams to problems before they affect the business.

For LLM applications, it traces each request through the chain of prompts, retrieval, and tool calls, and runs evaluations that score responses for relevance, hallucination, and safety. This helps developers find why an answer was wrong and test fixes. Arize Phoenix, the company’s open-source tool, offers tracing and evaluation that can run locally.

item.title: Ashby
item.description:
Ashby brings together tools that recruiting teams often buy separately. The core is an applicant tracking system for jobs, candidates, and interview plans. Around it sit scheduling that coordinates interviewers automatically, a CRM for sourcing and nurturing talent, and an analytics layer that shows pipeline health, time to hire, and source effectiveness.

AI features handle repetitive work, such as summarizing candidates, drafting outreach, and taking notes in interviews. Structured scorecards and interview plans promote consistent evaluation, and reporting is built into the product rather than added on, which analytics-minded recruiting teams like.

item.title: Attio
item.description:
Attio starts from the idea that every company sells differently. Instead of fixed objects like leads and opportunities, teams build their own structures, such as customers, partners, or investors, and link them. The interface feels more like a spreadsheet and a database than a traditional CRM, so it is easier to reshape.

Data fills in with little typing. Attio connects to email and calendar to log interactions, enriches company and contact details, and shows the strength of relationships. AI features summarize accounts, answer questions about the pipeline, and fill in fields from conversations. Workflow automation moves records, sends notifications, and updates data.

item.title: Cassidy AI
item.description:
Cassidy lets non-technical teams build AI workflows. A user connects sources such as documents, wikis, and apps, then designs assistants and multi-step workflows in a visual builder: take an input, retrieve company knowledge, draft an output, and send it onward.

Typical uses include drafting proposals and emails in the company’s voice, summarizing meetings, researching accounts, answering internal questions, and processing forms. Different model providers can be used, and permissions control who can see which sources. Teams share assistants so a good workflow becomes a reusable tool.

item.title: Cleanlab
item.description:
Cleanlab starts from the idea that model quality depends on data quality. Real datasets contain mistakes: images with wrong labels, duplicated examples, and outliers. Cleanlab’s open-source library uses statistical methods and model predictions to find the examples most likely to be wrong, so a team can correct them instead of reviewing everything.

The commercial platform, Cleanlab Studio, extends this with a no-code interface for cleaning and improving datasets and training models on the result. The company has also moved into reliability for generative AI, offering tools to score the trustworthiness of language model outputs and catch hallucinations in production systems.

item.title: ClearML
item.description:
ClearML helps machine learning teams keep their work organized and reproducible. Adding a couple of lines of code to a training script logs parameters, metrics, code versions, and outputs to a central server, so experiments can be compared and repeated. This replaces scattered notebooks and manual notes.

The suite goes beyond tracking. It includes dataset versioning, a task queue that sends jobs to available machines, pipelines that chain steps together, and model serving. For companies with expensive GPUs, resource scheduling shares hardware across teams. ClearML also supports orchestration for large language model workflows.

item.title: Close
item.description:
Close takes the position that sales reps should do their work from one screen. Calls, emails, and texts happen inside the CRM and are logged automatically, so there is less manual data entry and a complete history on each lead. Power dialers let reps work through lists quickly.

Sequences automate multi-step outreach that mixes email, calls, and texts, and workflows keep pipelines moving. AI features transcribe and summarize calls, suggest follow-ups, and score leads, which helps managers coach and helps reps decide where to spend time. Reporting shows activity and results by rep.

item.title: Codemod
item.description:
Codemod targets a chore every large codebase faces: changing the same pattern in hundreds or thousands of places. Codemods are scripts that rewrite code programmatically, for example moving from one version of a framework to the next. The platform provides a registry of community codemods, tools to run them, and a way to write new ones.

AI makes creating codemods easier. A developer describes a migration, and the tool helps produce the transformation and test it on examples, then applies it across repositories and opens pull requests for review. This turns weeks of manual edits into a reviewable change.

item.title: Comet ML
item.description:
Comet helps machine learning teams track and compare their work. A few lines of code log metrics, parameters, code, and datasets from training runs to a dashboard, where experiments can be compared and reproduced. A model registry stores approved versions and their lineage.

Production monitoring watches deployed models for drift and performance changes. For generative AI, Comet created Opik, an open-source tool for tracing and evaluating language model applications, which brings it into the same space as other LLM observability products.

item.title: ContractPodAi
item.description:
ContractPodAi was built for corporate legal departments that handle large volumes of contracts. Its platform covers the lifecycle: drafting from templates, routing for approval, negotiation, signature, storage in a searchable repository, and tracking of obligations and renewals. It connects with systems such as Salesforce, Microsoft 365, and ERP tools so contracts sit within the business processes they relate to.

The company has rebranded as Leah, after the name of its AI product, and now describes itself as an agentic AI platform. Its AI agents review contracts against playbooks, flag risks and deviations, extract key terms, answer questions about a contract portfolio, and handle repetitive tasks across legal, procurement, and finance. The change reflects a wider move in legal technology from software that stores documents to software that does the first pass of the work.

item.title: Copper
item.description:
Copper integrates with the tools its users already work in. Because it lives inside Gmail and connects with Google Calendar, Drive, and Docs, contacts and conversations are logged automatically, so reps do not have to copy information into a separate system.

The CRM covers the usual sales functions: contacts, companies, deals, pipelines, tasks, and reporting. Project management features track work after a deal closes, which suits agencies and service firms. AI features help summarize communication and suggest follow-ups, and workflow automation moves deals through stages.

item.title: Copysmith
item.description:
Copysmith targets online retailers that need lots of product copy. A merchant can generate descriptions for many products from a spreadsheet or catalog, create ad headlines and text, and draft emails and social posts. Bulk generation saves time when a store has hundreds of items.

Integrations connect it to Shopify and Google Ads, so content can flow into the tools where it is used. Team features allow collaboration and approval, and brand settings keep tone consistent. Some tools support SEO optimization by suggesting keywords.

item.title: CSM AI
item.description:
CSM turns simple inputs into 3D assets. A user uploads a picture, types a description, or draws a sketch, and the system produces a 3D model with textures that can be exported to common formats. It supports game developers, designers, and creators who need assets quickly.

Beyond single objects, it offers tools for character creation and animation preparation, and an API lets developers build 3D generation into their own apps. The output is often a starting point that artists clean up, since generated meshes can have topology problems that matter for animation and games.

item.title: Docsumo
item.description:
Docsumo turns documents into structured data. A company uploads or emails PDFs and scans such as invoices, receipts, bank statements, and forms, and the platform reads fields and tables, checks them against rules, and sends clean data to accounting, lending, or ERP systems. This replaces manual entry.

A review interface lets staff correct uncertain fields, and corrections improve accuracy over time. Pre-trained models cover common documents, while custom models handle company-specific layouts. Workflows include validation rules, approvals, and integrations through APIs. Lenders and finance teams are major users.

item.title: Dust
item.description:
Dust helps companies deploy AI assistants on their own information. Administrators connect sources such as Notion, Slack, Google Drive, GitHub, and Confluence, and create assistants for functions like support, sales, or engineering. Each assistant has instructions and access to selected data, so answers are grounded in the company’s content.

Employees use assistants in a chat interface or inside Slack, and assistants can take actions through connected tools. Teams share assistants they build, so a good one becomes common property. The platform works with models from several providers, and focuses on security and permissions.

item.title: Evisort
item.description:
Evisort uses AI to understand contracts. It ingests agreements, identifies clauses and key terms such as renewal dates, payment terms, and liability limits, and stores them as structured data. Teams can search across thousands of contracts, instead of hunting through PDFs.

It supports the contract lifecycle: drafting from templates, negotiating, tracking obligations, and getting alerts before renewals. Reports show risk and spend across the portfolio. Generative AI helps review contracts against playbooks and suggests changes.

item.title: Factory AI
item.description:
Factory sells AI agents for engineering teams. Droids take tasks from tickets or chat, explore a codebase, make changes, run tests, and open pull requests for review. Specialized droids handle different jobs, such as code review, incident response, or migrations.

The product works through a command line tool, IDE integrations, and a web interface, and connects to GitHub, Jira, Slack, and other tools so agents fit into existing workflows. Enterprise features address security, permissions, and model choice, with support for several model providers.

item.title: Folk
item.description:
Folk is a relationship manager for people who find traditional CRMs heavy. Users import contacts from email, LinkedIn, and spreadsheets, organize them into groups, and track conversations and deals in a clean interface. It suits agencies, recruiters, investors, and founders who manage many relationships.

AI and automation reduce the manual work. Enrichment fills in details like company and role, a browser extension saves profiles from LinkedIn, and sequences send personalized emails at scale. AI helps write messages and summarize history, and reminders prompt follow-ups so nobody falls through the cracks.

item.title: Freshsales
item.description:
Freshsales is a sales CRM that keeps lead and deal information in one view. Teams track contacts, run pipelines, and log calls and emails, with a built-in phone and chat so reps can contact prospects without switching tools. Automation moves leads through stages and assigns tasks.

Freddy AI assists with prioritization. It scores leads by likelihood to convert, predicts which deals will close, and suggests next best actions, while generative features draft emails and summarize conversations. Analytics show pipeline health, and integrations connect with Freshdesk, marketing tools, and common business apps.

item.title: Front
item.description:
Front treats shared inboxes like collaborative workspaces. Support, sales, and account teams manage messages from several channels in one place, assign conversations, leave internal comments, and see who is handling what. The interface resembles email, so adoption is easy.

Automation and AI reduce manual work. Rules route messages, tag them, and set priorities, while AI summarizes long threads, suggests replies, and answers common questions. Analytics show response times and workloads, and integrations with CRMs and helpdesk tools provide context.

item.title: Gem
item.description:
Gem helps recruiting teams build pipelines. Recruiters search for candidates across LinkedIn and other sources, add them to talent pools, and send sequences of personalized outreach. A candidate CRM tracks every interaction, so when a role opens, the team can reach people they have already engaged.

Analytics show how sourcing channels perform, how long hiring takes, and where candidates drop out. AI features help with search, writing outreach, and identifying candidates who may be open to new roles. An applicant tracking system component extends the suite for teams that want everything in one place.

item.title: Giskard
item.description:
Giskard focuses on quality and safety testing for AI. A team connects a model or an application, and the tool generates test cases and probes to find weaknesses. It checks for factual errors, harmful outputs, prompt injection, sensitive data exposure, and unfair behavior across groups.

Findings become a test suite that can run continuously, for example in a CI pipeline, so regressions are caught before release. For language model applications, Giskard supports retrieval-augmented systems and offers a red-teaming approach with automated attacks. A hub provides collaboration and reports for risk and compliance teams.

item.title: Helicone
item.description:
Helicone gives teams visibility into their language model usage. A developer changes the base URL of their API calls to route through Helicone, and each request is logged with its prompt, response, latency, cost, and user. Dashboards show spend by model, user, or feature, and flag errors.

Additional tools help manage production use. Caching saves cost on repeated requests, rate limits protect budgets, and prompt management lets teams version and test prompts. Sessions group multi-step agent traces, and evaluation features score outputs.

item.title: Humanloop
item.description:
Humanloop helped teams build reliable applications on language models. Developers managed and versioned prompts, ran automated and human evaluations, and monitored behavior in production. It was used by enterprises that needed to test changes before shipping and keep a record of how prompts evolved.

Anthropic hired the company’s co-founders and most of its team, without acquiring the product or its intellectual property. The standalone service was wound down shortly afterward, and customers were given guidance for migrating to other tools.

item.title: Jiminny
item.description:
Jiminny captures conversations between sales teams and customers. It records calls and meetings, creates transcripts, and uses AI to summarize them, extract action items, and detect topics, objections, and talk ratios. Managers use this to coach reps with specific examples.

Deal insights help forecast. The platform flags risks such as lack of next steps or missing stakeholders, and keeps the CRM updated with notes and fields without manual entry. Search across calls lets teams find how customers talk about competitors or pricing.

item.title: Jira
item.description:
Jira tracks work through issues in boards, backlogs, and timelines. Software teams use it for sprints, bug tracking, and roadmaps, and many other teams use it for requests and projects. Workflows are customizable, and it integrates with code hosts, chat tools, and the rest of Atlassian’s products.

Atlassian has added AI across Jira. It summarizes long ticket discussions, drafts descriptions and subtasks, and turns natural language into search queries. Rovo agents can take on work such as triaging issues or answering questions across connected tools, and the AI draws on a team’s own data.

item.title: Kixie
item.description:
Kixie speeds up phone outreach. A power dialer calls through a list automatically, local presence shows numbers with the prospect’s area code to improve answer rates, and voicemail drop leaves a prerecorded message with one click. Calls and texts sync with CRMs such as HubSpot, Salesforce, and Pipedrive.

Automation sends text messages and follow-ups triggered by call outcomes, and a coaching feature lets managers listen in. AI transcribes calls, summarizes them, and gives feedback on conversations. Analytics track activity, connect rates, and results by rep.

item.title: Langfuse
item.description:
Langfuse gives developers visibility into LLM applications. By adding its SDK or an integration, each request is traced with its prompts, model responses, tool calls, latency, and cost, including nested steps in agent workflows. Engineers inspect failures in a web interface and see usage across users and sessions.

Beyond observability, it supports quality work. Prompt management lets teams version and deploy prompts without code changes, evaluation features score outputs through LLM judges, user feedback, or custom checks, and datasets let teams run experiments before release. The product can be self-hosted, which suits privacy-sensitive teams.

item.title: Latitude
item.description:
Latitude makes interactive fiction with AI. Its best-known product, AI Dungeon, lets players describe any action in natural language, and an AI game master responds with the next part of the story. The result is open-ended storytelling that can go in any direction, from fantasy quests to comedy and mystery.

The studio has experimented with other AI-driven games and with platforms for creators who want to build their own AI-powered worlds. It uses a mix of language models, including models it trains and fine-tunes, and offers different tiers of models to subscribers.

item.title: Lever
item.description:
Lever pairs two things that recruiting teams often keep separate: an applicant tracking system for people who apply, and a relationship manager for people you want to attract. In one place, recruiters post jobs, move candidates through stages, schedule interviews, collect feedback, and build talent pools for roles that open later. The pipeline view is visual and quick to scan, which suits teams that hire continuously.

Sourcing and nurture are a focus. Lever can run email sequences to passive candidates, track responses, and bring prospects into the same pipeline as applicants. Interview scheduling is automated so recruiters spend less time on calendars, and scorecards keep feedback structured. Reporting covers the funnel, diversity data, and time to hire. Integrations link it to job boards, HR systems, and assessment tools.

item.title: Loomly
item.description:
Loomly supports the planning side of social media. Teams build a content calendar, get post ideas from trends and prompts, draft posts with images and links, and route them through an approval workflow before publishing. A brand asset library keeps logos and images handy.

The platform previews how a post will look on each network and schedules publishing. Analytics show performance, and ad management features support boosted posts. AI assists with captions and ideas.

item.title: Paradox
item.description:
Paradox focuses on hiring for roles with many applicants, such as retail, hospitality, and logistics. Olivia chats with candidates by text or on a career site, asks qualifying questions, answers common questions about the job and company, and books interviews directly on managers’ calendars.

That removes much of the scheduling and screening back and forth that slows recruiting. Candidates get fast responses, and recruiters spend time on interviews instead of coordination. The platform includes an applicant tracking tool and onboarding support.

item.title: Patronus AI
item.description:
Patronus AI helps teams find problems in AI applications. Developers run test sets through their systems, and Patronus scores the outputs with evaluators that check for hallucinations, unsafe content, leaks of sensitive data, and policy violations. Red-teaming tools probe for weaknesses with adversarial inputs.

The company has published benchmarks, including tests for financial question answering, and trained evaluation models such as a judge model for hallucination detection. Monitoring features watch production traffic and alert teams to drops in quality.

item.title: PromptLayer
item.description:
PromptLayer separates prompts from code. Teams store prompts in a registry, version them, test changes against datasets, and deploy new versions without redeploying the application. Non-engineers, such as product managers and domain experts, can edit prompts in a visual interface.

Observability features log every call with inputs, outputs, cost, and latency, and let teams search and analyze history. Evaluations compare prompt versions and models, and workflows chain steps for agents.

item.title: Publer
item.description:
Publer provides the essentials of social media planning at a modest price. Users connect accounts, build a calendar, schedule posts and recurring content, and see analytics on performance. Bulk scheduling and a library of media help manage volume.

Features include collaboration and approvals, link in bio pages, and a social inbox. The AI assistant writes captions, suggests hashtags, and repurposes content, and tools recycle evergreen posts.

Publer has a free plan with limits and paid tiers by social accounts. Alternatives include Buffer, Later, Metricool, Hootsuite, and Pallyy. Publer suits creators and small teams who want an affordable scheduler.

item.title: Quantified AI
item.description:
Quantified AI helps sales reps practice before they talk to real customers. A rep enters a simulated conversation with an AI buyer that responds in real time, raises objections, and changes direction, and the system scores the performance on things like discovery, handling pushback, and messaging.

Managers use the results to see who needs coaching and track progress over time, and companies can create scenarios that mirror their own sales motions and products. Practice is available any time, which helps new hires ramp faster than relying only on role-play with colleagues.

item.title: Reducto
item.description:
Reducto turns messy documents into clean data. A developer sends a PDF or image, and the API returns structured output that preserves layout, tables, and figures, which can feed language models or databases. It combines vision models and traditional techniques to handle difficult pages.

Applications include financial analysis, legal review, healthcare records, and RAG systems where poor parsing hurts answer quality. Options exist for extracting fields to a schema and for splitting documents by type. Enterprises can deploy it in their own environment.

item.title: Refact.ai
item.description:
Refact.ai gives developers an assistant they can control. It offers autocomplete, chat that understands the codebase, and an agent that can carry out tasks like fixing bugs, running tests, and refactoring. It plugs into popular editors.

Privacy is a key benefit: companies can run it on their own servers with open models so code never leaves their environment, or use cloud models. Fine-tuning on a codebase is available in some setups.

item.title: Relay
item.description:
Relay.app takes the Zapier-style approach and adds two things: AI steps and humans in the loop. A workflow can trigger on an event, call an AI to summarize or draft, then pause for a teammate to approve before the next action runs. This suits tasks where full automation is risky.

Integrations connect common business tools, and a visual builder makes flows easy to design. Examples include drafting replies for review, routing leads, and preparing reports. Approvals can be done in email or Slack.

item.title: Relevance AI
item.description:
Relevance AI lets teams create agents without code. A user defines what an agent does, gives it instructions and tools such as web search, email, or a CRM, and connects knowledge sources. Several agents can be assembled into a team, with one handing work to another.

Common uses are sales development, research, support, and operations. Templates give a starting point, and a monitoring layer shows what agents did and where they need help. Integrations connect with business tools, and agents can run on triggers or schedules.

item.title: Sapling
item.description:
Sapling helps support and sales teams write faster and more consistently. As an agent types in the help desk or CRM, Sapling suggests completions based on past replies, fixes grammar and tone, and inserts approved snippets. This reduces typing time and variation.

Managers use quality analytics to monitor response times and consistency, and see how suggestions are used. It integrates with Zendesk, Salesforce, Intercom, and other tools, and offers an API and an AI content detector.

item.title: Slab
item.description:
Slab gives teams a clean place to write and organize internal documentation. Content is arranged in topics, and the editor emphasizes readability. Engineering, support, and operations teams use it for runbooks, handbooks, and policies.

Search is the core feature. It queries Slab content and connected tools such as Google Drive, GitHub, and Slack in one place, and the AI answers questions in natural language with links to sources. Verification features prompt owners to keep pages up to date.

item.title: Speechmatics
item.description:
Speechmatics provides speech-to-text as a service. Developers send audio and get transcripts with timestamps, speaker labels, and language detection. The company emphasizes accuracy across accents and dialects, which is an area where many systems show bias.

Products include real-time transcription for live captioning and voice agents, batch processing, translation, and deployment options on premises for sensitive data. Customers include media, contact center, and healthcare companies.

Speechmatics is priced by usage. Alternatives include Deepgram, AssemblyAI, OpenAI Whisper, Gladia, and Google Cloud Speech-to-Text. Speechmatics suits organizations needing accurate multilingual transcription.

item.title: Spike
item.description:
Spike presents email like a chat. Threads become conversations, which can feel faster, and a unified view combines email with notes, tasks, and calendar. Teams can discuss messages privately without forwarding.

AI helps with summaries of long threads, drafting replies, and organizing the inbox, and shared inboxes support small teams. It works with many email providers.

Spike has a free tier and paid plans. Chat-style email is a taste, and some prefer traditional layouts. Alternatives include Superhuman, Shortwave, Hey, Gmail with Gemini, and Front. Spike suits people who want a conversational inbox.

item.title: Streak
item.description:
Streak adds pipeline management to Gmail. Users create boxes for deals, candidates, or projects, move them through stages, and see all related emails, notes, and files in one place. Because it sits in the inbox, there is little context switching.

Features include mail merge, email tracking, scheduling, shared inboxes, and automations. AI helps summarize threads and draft emails. It suits small teams that already run on Google Workspace.

Streak has a free plan and paid tiers. It is tied to Gmail. Alternatives include Copper, HubSpot, Pipedrive, Close, and Attio. Streak suits small teams working from the inbox.

item.title: Tettra
item.description:
Tettra helps teams keep answers in one place. Teams write pages for policies, processes, and FAQs, organize them in categories, and assign owners who verify content periodically so it stays accurate. Integrations with Slack make answers available where people ask questions.

An AI assistant searches the wiki and connected sources to respond to questions in chat. Requests that cannot be answered become tasks for subject experts, which grows the knowledge base over time.

item.title: Trieve
item.description:
Trieve packages the pieces of a search and RAG stack. Developers send documents, and Trieve indexes them for keyword and semantic search, supports filters and re-ranking, and offers APIs for chat with sources and recommendations.

It aims to reduce the work of stitching together a vector database, embedding service, and ranking logic, with features like analytics and a dashboard. It can be used for site search, support assistants, and product search.

item.title: Trint
item.description:
Trint speeds up working with recordings. Users upload interviews, press conferences, or footage and get transcripts that link to the audio, so editing the text is easy to verify. Teams can search across an archive, highlight quotes, and build stories from selections.

The platform supports many languages, translation, and subtitles, and offers collaboration for newsrooms with permissions and shared workspaces. AI features create summaries and help extract key moments.

Trint is paid, with plans by features and seats. Accuracy depends on audio quality. Alternatives include Otter.ai, Descript, Transkriptor, Verbit, and Rev. Trint suits media teams that work with large volumes of recorded content.

item.title: Vectara
item.description:
Vectara offers RAG as a service. Developers upload documents or connect sources, and the platform handles chunking, embedding, retrieval, and generation, returning answers with citations. Teams avoid assembling these components themselves.

The company emphasizes factual consistency, publishing a hallucination evaluation model and leaderboard, and offers agent features. Security options include private deployments for sensitive data.

Vectara has a free tier and paid plans by usage. Retrieval quality still depends on document quality. Alternatives include Pinecone with custom pipelines, Cohere, Azure AI Search, Glean, and LlamaIndex. Vectara suits teams that want RAG without building infrastructure.

item.title: Viz.ai
item.description:
Viz.ai is known for its stroke software. When a patient has a CT scan that may show a large vessel occlusion, a blockage in a major brain artery, the AI analyzes the images within minutes and alerts the stroke team on their phones, with images they can view immediately. Speeding up that notification can cut the time to treatment, which matters in stroke, where each minute affects outcomes.

The platform has expanded beyond stroke. It supports other conditions, including pulmonary embolism, aortic disease, and heart conditions, and uses AI to identify patients who may be eligible for treatment or follow-up. A care coordination layer links hospitals, so specialists at a distance can review cases, communicate, and arrange transfers. Several of its algorithms have received regulatory clearance in the United States.

item.title: Voiceflow
item.description:
Voiceflow lets teams design conversational agents together. On a visual canvas, designers and developers map out how an agent should respond, add steps that call language models, search knowledge bases, run logic, and connect to APIs and tools. Non-engineers can shape conversations while developers handle integrations, which makes it practical for cross-functional teams in customer support, sales, and operations.

The platform handles the whole lifecycle. You can add a knowledge base of company content so the agent answers from it, test the agent in a built-in environment, and deploy it to a website, messaging channels, phone lines, or via API. Analytics and transcripts show how conversations go, and versioning and collaboration features support teamwork. Voiceflow works with a choice of language models.

item.title: Wordware
item.description:
Wordware treats prompts as code. Users write workflows in an editor that feels like a document, mixing instructions in plain language with structure for loops, branches, and tool calls. The aim is to let people who understand a problem, not only engineers, build AI apps.

Workflows can be published as apps or APIs, and the platform supports several model providers and integrations. Teams use it for research agents, content workflows, and internal tools.

item.title: ZenML
item.description:
ZenML helps teams move ML work from notebooks to production. Developers write pipelines as Python functions, and ZenML runs them on a chosen orchestrator, such as Kubeflow, Airflow, or a cloud service, tracking artifacts and metadata along the way.

A stack concept separates pipeline code from infrastructure, so the same pipeline can run locally during development and in the cloud in production. The framework has extended to support LLM workflows and agents.

item.title: Activepieces
item.description: Activepieces is an alternative to Zapier built with openness in mind. Users build automations called flows by chaining a trigger, such as a new form entry, to actions across apps like Google Sheets, Slack, Gmail, and CRMs. The editor is friendly to non-developers, and code steps are available for custom logic. The integrations, called pieces, are open-source and community-contributed, and each can also work as a tool for AI agents.

item.title: Akiflow
item.description: Akiflow is built for people whose tasks are scattered across many apps. A task might arrive as an email, a Slack message, a Jira ticket, or an Asana item, and Akiflow collects them in a universal inbox so you can decide what to do and when. You drag tasks onto a calendar to block out time for them, which turns a long to-do list into a realistic day. Keyboard shortcuts and a command bar make it fast to use.

item.title: Amazon Q Developer
item.description: Amazon Q Developer is the successor to CodeWhisperer, and it is built around AWS knowledge.
